<div class="no-margin"><h4>Current ChromeOS updates</h4>

<p><a id="chromeOSA152" name="chromeOSA152"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Google Certificate Authority Connector on ChromeOS</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>This feature extends the functionality of the Google Certificate Authority Connector to Chrome browser users on ChromeOS, by allowing Google to act as a customer-specific certificate authority. Previously, Chrome browser on ChromeOS did not support the Google Certificate Authority Connector; it was supported on Windows, Mac, and Linux only.</p>

    <p>For more information, see&nbsp;<a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/11053129"><u>Use the Google Cloud Certificate Connector</u></a> in the Chrome Help Center.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>
</div>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Upcoming ChromeOS changes</h4>

<p><a id="upChromeOSA152" name="upChromeOSA152"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Upcoming change to ChromeOS release numbering&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>Starting with ChromeOS 154, ChromeOS will continue to be released every 4 weeks, but the release number will be incremented by 2 (instead of 1). This change is to align numbering with the new Chrome browser 2-week release cadence. You can find more details in the <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-two-week-release" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome for Developers</u></a> blog post.</p>

    <p>For customers on the Long-term Support channel, the duration between LTS releases is not changing; LTS will continue to release every 6 months. With the transition to the new release numbering, LTS versioning will&nbsp; increment every 12 versions. For more information, see the <a href="https://chromiumdash.appspot.com/schedule" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chromium release schedule</u></a> and <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/12239814"><u>Long-term Support (LTS) release notes</u></a> in the Chrome Enterprise and Education Help Center.</p>

    <p><img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/k8mx9CikAVGLAYHrS3DotQTdRGhK5T5k5-qXtv52-S-3n4nTRoxq6izsmJU_pfycS3A=w895" width="2048" height="854" alt="" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/k8mx9CikAVGLAYHrS3DotQTdRGhK5T5k5-qXtv52-S-3n4nTRoxq6izsmJU_pfycS3A"></p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><a id="upChromeOSB152" name="upChromeOSB152"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Mandatory migration to Certificate Provisioning API&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>At the end of November 2026, ChromeOS will stop supporting certificate enrollment without using the Certificate Provisioning API. If you do not migrate, no new certificates will be issued.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>For instructions, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/11338941"><u>Configuring Certificate Provisioning for ChromeOS via SCEP - Chrome Enterprise and Education Help</u></a>.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

Find them exclusively on our website: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/resources/release-notes/" rel="noopener" target="_blank">chromeenterprise.google</a>. Please update your bookmarks. (Note that ChromeOS release notes will continue to be published at this current link and will not move.)</p>

<h2>Chrome browser changes</h2>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><strong>Chrome 151 removes support for macOS 12</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 150 is the last release to support macOS 12; Chrome 151+ will no longer support macOS 12, which is outside of its support window with Apple. To maintain security, it is essential to run Chrome browser on a supported operating system.</p>

<p>On Macs running macOS 12, Chrome continues to work, showing a warning infobar, but it will not update any further. If users wish to have Chrome updated, they need to update their computer to a supported version of macOS.</p>

<p>For new installations of Chrome 151+, macOS 13+ is required.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 151 on Windows, macOS, Linux No rollout step</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Auto-hide for bookmark bar</strong></p>

<p>To provide a cleaner <strong>New tab</strong> page experience and improve user productivity, Chrome introduces new ways to control the visibility of the bookmark bar. Starting in Chrome 151 on Windows, macOS, Linux, and ChromeOS, the bookmark bar can automatically hide if it is not being used regularly. If the bookmark bar is automatically hidden due to low usage, affected users see a notification that allows them to easily restore the bar.</p>

<p>Chrome 151 introduces new bookmark visibility settings, under <strong>Settings &gt; Appearance</strong>, giving users explicit control over whether the bar appears on the <strong>New tab</strong> page.</p>

<p>Admins can manage this feature using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#BookmarkBarEnabled"><u>BookmarkBarEnabled</u></a> policy. To prevent the bookmark bar from automatically hiding, admins must set the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#BookmarkBarEnabled"><u>BookmarkBarEnabled</u></a> policy to mandatory. When this policy is enforced, the new visibility settings still appear in the browser but will not be clickable.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 151 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Enhanced Safe Browsing protections when using Gemini in Chrome</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 151 expands Safe Browsing protections to provide an even safer experience when using Gemini in Chrome. By triggering real-time Safe Browsing verdicts for active pages, this update increases coverage to protect against newly-created malicious sites and keep AI-assisted browsing secure.</p>

<p>This update introduces no new enterprise policies. Existing enterprise policies governing Safe Browsing protections (such as <a href="http://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SafeBrowsingProtectionLevel"><u>SafeBrowsingProtectionLevel</u></a>) and generative AI features (such as <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a>) continue to govern user access and warning behaviors across managed devices.</p>

<p>For more information, see <a href="https://safebrowsing.google.com/"><u>Google Safe Browsing</u></a> and <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16291696"><u>Gemini in Chrome</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 151 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Enterprise sign-in on personal Windows devices</strong></p>

<p>Previously, when signing in with a work or school account (such as Office 365) on personal Windows devices, some users experienced unintended enterprise policy enforcement. Chrome is currently resolving an issue on Windows where signing-in incorrectly classified personal machines as enterprise-managed.</p>

<p>Starting in Chrome 154 on Windows, Chrome will include additional checks to ensure that personal devices are not treated as enterprise-managed based solely on an account login. This change will not impact devices that are fully joined to Entra ID or Active Directory (AD).</p>

<p>Users on personal Windows devices will experience a standard consumer browsing environment. Specifically:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>UI changes</strong>: The management disclaimer UI will no longer appear, and enterprise-specific error messages for SSL errors will be disabled.</li>
  <li><strong>Consumer features enabled:</strong> Features that explicitly exclude enterprise environments will become available, including new AI features, the Platform Experience Helper, and specific heuristics for HTTPS-First Mode.</li>
</ul>

<p>Because these personal devices will correctly no longer be treated as enterprise-managed, IT administrators should be aware of the following impacts on their controls:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Policy functionality</strong>: Policies that strictly require an enterprise-managed device will stop functioning on these personal machines. Examples of affected policies include <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HomepageLocation"><u>HomepageLocation</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AutoOpenFileTypes"><u>AutoOpenFileTypes</u></a>, and all Google Update policies. For more details, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/6350036"><u>Manage Chrome updates</u></a>.</li>
  <li><strong>Enterprise features</strong>: Certain enterprise-only capabilities, such as <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/7125792?hl=en"><u>Chrome Downgrade</u></a> snapshots, will no longer be generated for these devices.</li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 151 on Windows Policies that strictly require an enterprise-managed device will consider additional checks.</li>
  <li>Chrome 154 on Windows All other features will consider additional checks</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Gemini in Chrome</strong></p>

<p>Gemini is now integrated into Chrome on macOS, Windows, iOS, Android and selective ChromeOS devices, and can understand the content of your current page. Users can now seamlessly get key takeaways, clarify concepts, and find answers, all without leaving their Chrome tab. This integration includes both chat, where users can interact with Gemini via text, and Gemini Live, with which users can interact with Gemini via voice.</p>

<p>In Chrome 143, <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16291696"><u>Gemini in Chrome</u></a> started to roll out to most Google Workspace users with access to the Gemini app in the US. Admins can turn off this feature (value 1) using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiSettings"><u>GeminiSettings</u></a> policy or by using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> (value 2). For more details, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16291696"><u>Gemini in Chrome</u></a> in the Help Center or this <a href="https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/chrome-enterprise/supercharging-employee-productivity-with-ai-securely-with-gemini-in-chrome-enterprise"><u>blog post</u></a>.</p>

<p>In Chrome 143, we announced the multi-tab context feature. Gemini in Chrome can now see more of your opened tabs (10 max) so you can ask questions across multiple pages to help you compare, find information more efficiently. Gemini in Chrome also serves as a productivity agent. Gemini in Chrome automatically uses public information from these Google services: Google Search, Google Maps, YouTube. With your permission, Gemini in Chrome can help you connect your personal information and content in Google Workspace services (Gmail, Drive, Keep, Calendar, and Tasks).</p>

<p>In Chrome 144, auto browse in Gemini in Chrome was made available to some users (non-enterprise). An enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebSettings"><u>GeminiActOnWebSettings</u></a> is available.</p>

<p>In Chrome 147, Auto browse in Gemini in Chrome became available to Enterprise users. Enterprise policies <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebSettings"><u>GeminiActOnWebSettings</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebAllowedForURLs"><u>GeminiActOnWebAllowedForURLs</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebBlockedForURLs"><u>GeminiActOnWebBlockedForURLs</u></a> are available to control auto browse.</p>

<p>In Chrome 149, Gemini in Chrome became available to users in 118 additional countries and territories.</p>

<p>In Chrome 150, Gemini Spark can use Chrome auto browse to complete tasks that need web actuation. Enterprise policy is <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiSparkSettings"><u>GeminiSparkSettings</u></a>. Chrome will also now suggest Gemini in Chrome features at relevant moments. Enterprise policy is <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ChromeSuggestionsSettings"><u>ChromeSuggestionsSettings</u></a>.</p>

<p>In Chrome 151, Gemini in Chrome is available to users in the United Kingdom and 14 additional countries and territories. This release also includes new Gemini in Chrome features, such as:</p>

  <li>File generation</li>
  <li>Improved scam blocking</li>
</ul>

For more information, see <a href="https://safebrowsing.google.com/"><u>Google Safe Browsing</u></a> and <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16291696"><u>Gemini in Chrome</u></a>.</li>

<p><strong>URL filtering updates</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 151 introduces two updates to URL filtering behavior to ensure consistent security enforcement and more accurate administrative reporting across all platforms. This results in changes to the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#URLBlocklist"><u>URLBlocklist</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#URLAllowlist"><u>URLAllowlist</u></a> policies.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Consistent policy enforcement in Incognito mode</strong>: To enhance security and privacy, the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#URLBlocklist"><u>URLBlocklist</u></a> policy will now be strictly enforced on Incognito pages. Previously, the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#IncognitoModeUrlAllowlist"><u>IncognitoModeUrlAllowlist</u></a> could override blocklist settings in certain scenarios. This update ensures that administrators have reliable control over restricted content, regardless of the user's browsing mode.</li>
  <li><strong>Improved wildcard (*) handling in URLAllowlist</strong>: When a wildcard (*) is used in the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#URLAllowlist"><u>URLAllowlist</u></a>, Chrome no longer categorizes every URL as <em>explicitly allowed</em>. While users are still permitted to navigate to these URLs (unless blocked by a more specific policy), this change ensures that internal status checks and reporting tools accurately reflect the difference between a global allowlisting and a targeted allowlist entry.</li>
  <li>Chrome 151 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>AI chat button for preferred search engine</strong></p>

<p>To ensure all Chrome users can quickly get AI-powered answers to their questions, regardless of their default search engine, the Omnibox now displays an AI chat button for supported third-party search engines. This provides a seamless, one-click experience to access their preferred search engine's AI chat capabilities.</p>

<p>Admins can manage this capability using the new <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ThirdPartyAiChatSettings"><u>ThirdPartyAiChatSettings</u></a> policy, which interacts with existing AI management policies:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Enabling Third-Party Chat</strong>: For users to see the AI chat button when their Default Search Engine is a supported third party, administrators must enable both the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AIModeSettings"><u>AIModeSettings</u></a> and the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ThirdPartyAiChatSettings"><u>ThirdPartyAiChatSettings</u></a> policies.</li>
  <li><strong>Default &amp; Fallback Behavior</strong>: If the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ThirdPartyAiChatSettings"><u>ThirdPartyAiChatSettings</u></a> policy is left unset, it will automatically fall back to the value defined in the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAIDefaultSettings"><u>GenAIDefaultSettings</u></a> policy.</li>
  <li><strong>Google Default Search Engine</strong>: The existing <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AIModeSettings"><u>AIModeSettings</u></a> policy remains unchanged. It will continue to exclusively control the visibility of the Google chat button for users who use Google as their Default Search Engine.</li>

<p><strong>XML parsing in Rust for non XSLT scenarios</strong></p>

<p>To improve browser security and protect users against memory-related vulnerabilities, Chrome 151 is changing its XML parsing engine to a memory-safe Rust implementation for several common scenarios. This foundational update eliminates potential memory corruption bugs while maintaining full compatibility with existing web standards.</p>

<p>Chrome has already begun to deprecate and remove XSLT. While this process continues, the new, safer parser will handle the following scenarios where no XSLT is required:</p>

<ol>
  <li>DOMParser Web API.</li>
  <li>Accessing responseXML of XMLHttpRequest.</li>
  <li>SVG standalone images (that is, accessing a image.svg document directly as a top level navigation).</li>
  <li>SVG external images (including a main document embedding an SVG as an external image resource).</li>
</ol>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 151 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android No rollout step</li>
</ul>

<h2>Chrome Enterprise Core changes</h2>

<p><strong>Gen AI and SaaS app usage reporting</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 151 introduces a new <strong>Gen AI and SaaS app usage</strong> reporting feature in the Google <strong>Admin console</strong>. This report brings visibility into an organization's use of generative AI tools and SaaS sites, allowing admins to monitor usage of their enterprise IT resources.</p>

<p>This new report tracks usage for popular Gen AI and enterprise SaaS websites in Chrome, providing metrics on visits, unique managed profiles, unique managed browsers, and access to sensitive content transfer events. With these insights, admins can assess risk and determine where controls are needed. Using Chrome Enterprise Premium data protection controls, admins can then restrict usage using Data Loss Prevention (DLP) rules.</p>

<p>The <strong>Gen AI and SaaS app usage reporting</strong> policy will be available in the Admin console to disable this reporting.</p>

<p>Chrome 147 allowed a <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/engage/trusted-testers/sign-up/"><u>Trusted Tester</u></a> preview, with the feature gradually rolling out in Chrome 151.</p>

<div class="no-margin"><h2>Chrome Enterprise Premium changes</h2>

<p>Read more about the differences between <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/products/chrome-enterprise-premium" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Enterprise Core and Chrome Enterprise Premium</u></a>.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><span id="cke_bm_114490S">&nbsp;</span></p>

<p><strong>Block extensions using Chrome Web Store categories</strong></p>

<p>As early as Chrome 148, admins can enhance security by automatically blocking Chrome extensions based on their Chrome Web Store categories, for example, blocking all <em>Games</em> extensions. This feature prevents extensions from blocked categories being installed and disables them if already present. <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/6306504"><u>Force-installed</u></a> and allow-listed extensions remain unaffected.</p>

<p>This setting is only available in the Google Admin console under <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/6177447"><u>Apps &amp; Extensions &gt; Settings</u></a>, within the new <strong>Advanced extension blocking</strong> section. The setting name is <strong>Block by category</strong>. It can also be configured using the <a href="https://developers.google.com/chrome/management"><u>Chrome Management APIs</u></a>. This setting is not available for locally-managed devices.</p>

<p>Chrome 148 allows a <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/engage/trusted-testers/sign-up/"><u>Trusted Tester</u></a> preview, with the feature gradually rolling out in Chrome 151.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 148 on Linux, macOS, Windows - Early preview available to Chrome Enterprise Trusted Tester</li>
  <li>Chrome 151 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>MIP label integration for DLP</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 151 can now understand and enforce Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies based on Microsoft Information Protection (MIP) sensitivity labels applied to Office 365 documents.</p>

<p>To enable this feature, administrators must authorize the connection between Chrome Enterprise Premium and their Microsoft Azure tenant using the MIP label config under the Connectors API. Once connected, admins can create permanent DLP rules using these labels to block, warn, or audit user actions, for example:</p>

<ul>
  <li>copying and pasting to external sites, specifically targeting risks like GenAI data leakage</li>
  <li>downloading</li>
  <li>printing</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p>In Chrome 151, a <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/engage/trusted-testers/sign-up/"><u>Trusted Tester preview</u></a> of Microsoft Information Protection (MIP) label integration becomes available on Windows, macOS and ChromeOS.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 151 on ChromeOS, macOS, Windows - Early preview available to Chrome Enterprise Trusted Tester</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>DLP support for virtual files on ChromeOS</strong></p>

<p>On ChromeOS, files stored in non-native virtual folders (such as Microsoft OneDrive via extension-based File System Providers) were previously bypassed during enterprise file scans.</p>

<p>With this update, Chrome now supports Data Loss Prevention (DLP) scanning for these virtual files during user-initiated file uploads, drag-and-drop actions, and clipboard pastes. To perform the scan, ChromeOS securely streams a temporary local copy of the virtual file. Once the scan is completed and evaluated, the temporary file is immediately deleted. This update closes a security gap, ensuring consistent policy enforcement across all storage locations on ChromeOS.</p>

<p>This capability is governed by the existing, permanent <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnFileAttachedEnterpriseConnector"><u>OnFileAttachedEnterpriseConnector</u></a> policy. If you have already configured file-upload scanning for your organization, no further action is required; ChromeOS will automatically begin scanning virtual files.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 151 on ChromeOS - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>
</div>

<h2>Coming soon</h2>

<p><strong>Note:</strong> The items listed below are experimental or planned updates. They might change, be delayed, or canceled before launching to the Stable channel.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Upcoming Chrome browser changes</h4>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><strong>CPU Performance API</strong></p>

<p>Starting in Chrome 152, Chrome will introduce the CPU Performance API, which allows web applications to determine the CPU performance of a user's device. This API targets web applications that will use this information to provide an improved user experience, possibly in combination with the Compute Pressure API, which provides information about the user device’s CPU pressure or utilization and allows applications to react to changes in CPU pressure.</p>

<p>Users can override the reported performance in Chrome's Performance settings. Administrators can also control this behavior using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#CpuPerformanceTierOverride"><u>CpuPerformanceTierOverride</u></a> policy (which takes precedence over the user setting).</p>

<p>For more details, see <a href="https://github.com/WICG/cpu-performance"><u>CPU Performance API Explainer</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 152 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android No rollout step</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Deprecate and remove XSLT</strong></p>

<p><a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/xslt-10/"><u>XSLT v1.0</u></a>, which all browsers adhere to, was standardized in 1999. In the meantime, XSLT has evolved to v2.0 and v3.0, adding features, and growing apart from the old version frozen into browsers. This lack of advancement, coupled with the rise of JavaScript libraries and frameworks that offer more flexible and powerful DOM manipulation, has led to a significant decline in the use of client-side XSLT. Its role within the web browser has been largely superseded by JavaScript-based technologies, such as JSON and React.</p>

<p>Chromium uses the <strong>libxslt</strong> library to process these transformations, and <a href="https://discourse.gnome.org/t/stepping-down-as-libxslt-maintainer/27615"><u>libxslt was unmaintained</u></a> for ~6 months of 2025. Libxslt is a complex, aging C codebase of the type notoriously susceptible to memory safety vulnerabilities like buffer overflows, which can lead to arbitrary code execution. Because client-side XSLT is now a niche, rarely-used feature, these libraries receive far less maintenance and security scrutiny than core JavaScript engines, yet they represent a direct, potent attack surface for processing untrusted web content. Indeed, XSLT is the source of several recent high-profile security exploits that continue to put browser users at risk.</p>

<p>For these reasons, Chromium (along with both other browser engines, Gecko and WebKit) plans to deprecate and remove XSLT from the web platform. The modern web is powered by three major browser engines: <a href="https://www.chromium.org/blink/"><u>Blink</u></a> (Chromium), <a href="https://firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org/overview/gecko.html"><u>Gecko</u></a> (Firefox), and <a href="https://webkit.org/"><u>WebKit</u></a> (Safari). They interpret code to render pages.</p>

<p>For more details, see this <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/deprecating-xslt"><u>Chrome for Developers article</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 143 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows Deprecation (but not removal) of the APIs.</li>
  <li>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows Origin Trial (OT) and Enterprise Policy go live for testing. These allow sites and enterprises to continue using features past the removal date.</li>
  <li>Chrome 158 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows XSLT stops functioning on Stable releases, for all users other than Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy participants.</li>
  <li>Chrome 176 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy stop functioning. XSLT is disabled for all users.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Deprecation and removal of Privacy Sandbox APIs</strong></p>

<p>Chrome has <a href="https://privacysandbox.com/news/update-on-plans-for-privacy-sandbox-technologies/"><u>recently announced</u></a> that the current approach to third-party cookies is to be maintained, following which, we plan to deprecate and remove the following APIs:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Topics</li>
  <li>Protected Audience</li>
  <li>Shared Storage</li>
  <li>Attribution Reporting</li>
  <li>Private Aggregation</li>
  <li>Related Web Sites</li>
  <li>requestStorageAccessFor</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p>The following are the enterprise policies associated with the above APIs.</p>

<ul>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PrivacySandboxSiteEnabledAdsEnabled"><u>PrivacySandboxSiteEnabledAdsEnabled</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PrivacySandboxAdTopicsEnabled"><u>PrivacySandboxAdTopicsEnabled</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PrivacySandboxAdMeasurementEnabled"><u>PrivacySandboxAdMeasurementEnabled</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#RelatedWebsiteSetsOverrides"><u>RelatedWebsiteSetsOverrides</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#RelatedWebsiteSetsEnabled"><u>RelatedWebsiteSetsEnabled</u></a></li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p>Deprecation began with Chrome 144, and removal is planned for Chrome 152. After deprecation, the APIs will continue to exist, and most users will see no disruptions. However, some users who rely on server-side integrations (such as k-anonymity server, or coordinators) will see a break in the services. We have proactively reached out to users of the APIs with our deprecation plans. At the time of removal, Chrome 152, all the policies associated with these APIs will also be removed.</p>

<p>None of the APIs are enabled by default to enterprise users. Enterprise teams may want to review the status for any managed profile in their <strong>Admin console</strong>.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 144 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows Deprecation launch</li>
  <li>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows APIs and the associated policies removal</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Navigation capturing for PWAs</strong></p>

<p>To streamline the Progressive Web App (PWA) experience and improve user productivity, Chrome is updating how links are handled. Previously, users had to manually configure their app settings for a PWA to capture associated links. Starting in Chrome 152 on ChromeOS, this process is automated, and all installed PWAs will capture links by default.</p>

<p>To ensure users remain in control of their browsing experience, Chrome will display a notification when this occurs. This notification will guide users to the <strong>Settings</strong> page, allowing them to easily turn off the feature if they wish to opt out of the default link capturing behavior.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 152 on ChromeOS - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Notification attribution for PWAs on macOS</strong> Chrome is rolling out notification attribution for installed Progressive Web Apps (PWAs) on macOS. When a PWA is installed on macOS, its notifications will now be natively attributed to the PWA itself (using its own name and icon in the Notification Center) rather than Google Chrome.</p>

<p>This update also changes how notifications are displayed to the user, aligning PWA notifications with native macOS applications. It introduces two changes that align with current behavior in <a href="https://webkit.org/"><u>WebKit</u></a>:</p>

<ul>
  <li>For app notifications, Chrome will no longer support the requireInteraction field for notifications. On macOS, the user controls whether the notification is temporary or persistent on a per-app basis.</li>
  <li>For app badging, the Badging API now requires notifications permissions for the app badge to show up. If the user does not grant notifications permission, the API will silently do nothing.</li>
</ul>

<p>Administrators who pre-grant notification permissions using Chrome policies must update their configurations if they want to keep that behavior for PWAs on macOS.</p>

<p>In addition to the Chrome origin-based policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#NotificationsAllowedForUrls"><u>NotificationsAllowedForUrls</u></a>, administrators must deploy a macOS MDM configuration profile to pre-grant notification permissions to the PWA's specific bundle ID.</p>

<p><strong>Process isolation on Windows</strong></p>

To enable early testing prior to Chrome 152:</p>

<ol>
  <li>Toggle the chrome://flags/#enable-process-isolation-ui flag to <strong>Enabled</strong>.</li>
  <li>Navigate to chrome://settings/system and enable <strong>Process Isolation</strong>.</li>

<p><strong>SafeBrowsing API v4 to v5 migration</strong></p>

<p><strong>Unframed display mode for Isolated Web Apps</strong></p>

<p>Unframed display mode allows <a href="https://chromeos.dev/en/web/isolated-web-apps"><u>Isolated Web Apps</u></a> to occupy the entire browser window, which optimizes the workspace available. By removing standard window borders and title bars, developers can implement unique user experiences with branding and menu hierarchies that match the look-and-feel of native applications.</p>

<p>Administrators can manage this feature with existing policies for window management:</p>

<ul>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DefaultWindowManagementSetting"><u>DefaultWindowManagementSetting</u></a> configures the default state for the window management for all apps. The policies below can override this default.</li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WindowManagementAllowedForUrls"><u>WindowManagementAllowedForUrls</u></a> allows IWAs with specified origins to enter unframed mode without any user interaction.</li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WindowManagementBlockedForUrls"><u>WindowManagementBlockedForUrls</u></a> blocks unframed mode for IWAs with specified origins, forcing Chrome to fallback to other available display modes.</li>
  <li>Chrome 152 on ChromeOS - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Window Shape API</strong></p>

<p>Window Shape API enables allowlisted <a href="https://chromeos.dev/en/web/isolated-web-apps"><u>Isolated Web Apps</u></a> on ChromeOS to have a customized window shape. By enabling non-rectangular and non-contiguous window layouts, developers can implement unique user experiences (such as widgets, floating panels, and overlays) that match the look-and-feel of native applications. The window.chromeos.isolatedWebApp.setShape API requires the window to be in <em>unframed</em> display mode and requires the window-management permission to be granted.</p>

<p>Administrators can manage this feature with existing policies for window management:</p>

<ul>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DefaultWindowManagementSetting"><u>DefaultWindowManagementSetting</u></a> configures the default state for the window management for all apps. The policies below can override this default.</li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WindowManagementAllowedForUrls"><u>WindowManagementAllowedForUrls</u></a> allows IWAs with specified origins to enter unframed mode and set custom window shapes without any user interaction.</li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WindowManagementBlockedForUrls"><u>WindowManagementBlockedForUrls</u></a> blocks the permission for specified origins, forcing Chrome to remove any custom window shapes and fallback to other available display modes.</li>
  <li>Chrome 152 on ChromeOS - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>

Building on our history of adapting our release process to match the demands of a modern web, we are announcing this significant step to further increase our development velocity and Chrome Stable is moving to a 2-week release cycle. The 2-week Stable option remains the most secure choice and should be utilized if security is a larger concern than maintenance costs.</p>

<p><strong>Sub apps</strong></p>

<p>Sub apps allow developers to create multiple apps under a single Isolated Web App (<a href="https://chromeos.dev/en/web/isolated-web-apps"><u>IWA</u></a>) installation. Each Sub app has its own distinct name, icons and OS integrations.</p>

<p>Sub apps appear on the desktop shelf with a distinct identity from the parent IWA, offering separate OS capabilities, such as file type association. This allows a single software package to present different, isolated functionalities to the user while maintaining a single, unified IWA install and update process.</p>

<p>There are three new enterprise policies available to control the Sub apps API:</p>

<ul>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DefaultSubAppsWithoutPromptsSetting"><u>DefaultSubAppsWithoutPromptsSetting</u></a> specifies globally (for all IWAs) if user permission prompts are required to install Sub apps. The policies below can override this default.</li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SubAppsWithoutPromptsAllowedForOrigins"><u>SubAppsWithoutPromptsAllowedForOrigins</u></a> specifies a list of IWA URLs that can add or update Sub apps without user permission prompts.</li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SubAppsWithoutPromptsBlockedForOrigins"><u>SubAppsWithoutPromptsBlockedForOrigins</u></a> specifies a list of IWA URLs that can add Sub apps with user permission prompts only.</li>
  <li>Chrome 153 on Windows, macOS, Linux No rollout step</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Always use secure connections by default</strong></p>

<p>Prior to enabling it by default for all users, Chrome 150 enables <strong>Always use secure connections</strong> for users who have opted in to <a href="https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/11577602"><u>Enhanced Safe Browsing protections in Chrome</u></a>.</p>

<p>Chrome 154 will enable the <strong>Always use secure connections</strong> setting in the <em>public sites only</em> mode by default. This means Chrome will ask for the user's permission before the first access to any public site without HTTPS. Public sites are defined as sites that have a globally unique name, and excludes direct navigation to <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1918"><u>RFC 1918</u></a> addresses (192.168.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8, and so on), as well as shortnames such as go/.</p>

<p>If you are a website developer or IT professional, and you have users who may be impacted by this feature, we very strongly recommend enabling the <strong>Always use secure connections</strong> setting today to help identify sites that you may need to work to migrate. Admins can use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HttpAllowlist"><u>HttpAllowlist</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HttpsOnlyMode"><u>HttpsOnlyMode</u></a> policies to override this behavior.</p>

<p>For more information, see our <a href="https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/docs/security/ask-before-http/ask-before-http-adoption-guide.md"><u>adoption guide</u></a> and <a href="https://security.googleblog.com/2025/10/https-by-default.html"><u>announcement blog post</u></a>.</p>
&nbsp;

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 150 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia Enable "Always use secure connections" for users who have opted in to Enhanced Safe Browsing. This applies to Desktop only.</li>
  <li>Chrome 154 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia Enable "Always use secure connections" by default for all users.</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Optional browser optimization for Service Workers</strong></p>

<p><strong>ServiceWorkerAutoPreload</strong> is an optional browser optimization that changes the existing service worker behavior. In ServiceWorkerAutoPreload mode, the browser issues the network request in parallel with the service worker bootstrap. If the fetch handler returns the response with respondWith(), the browser consumes the network request result inside the fetch handler. If the fetch handler result is fallback, it passes the network response directly to the browser.</p>

<p>Admins can control this feature using an enterprise policy called <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled"><u>ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 140 on Android, Windows <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled"><u>ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled</u></a> policy will be available</li>
  <li>Chrome 154 on Android, Windows <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled"><u>ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled</u></a> policy will be removed.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Post-quantum cryptography for Chrome Browser CUP</strong></p>

<p>To proactively protect the integrity of browser updates against future quantum computing threats, Chrome is upgrading the security of its <a href="https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src.git/+/master/docs/updater/cup.md"><u>Client Update Protocol (CUP)</u></a>.</p>

<p>CUP secures communication with the update server, which delivers critical executable code like security patches and recovery components.</p>

<p>Starting in Chrome 155 across all platforms (Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS, Android, and iOS), Chrome will update from classical signatures (ECDSA) to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) for Chrome Component and Extension updates.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 155 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows - Feature rolls out gradually Some enterprise users might begin to experience secure Component and Extension updates with quantum resilient cryptography.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Local network access restrictions</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 142 restricted the ability to make requests to the user's local network, gated behind a permission prompt. A local network request is any request from a public website to a local IP address or loopback, or from a local website (for example, intranet) to loopback.</p>

<p>Gating the ability for websites to perform these requests behind a permission mitigates the risk of cross-site request forgery attacks against local network devices such as routers, and reduces the ability of sites to use these requests to fingerprint the user's local network.</p>

<p>This permission is restricted to secure contexts. If granted, the permissions additionally relax mixed content blocking for local network requests (since many local devices are not able to obtain publicly trusted TLS certificates for various reasons).</p>

<p>This work supersedes a prior effort called <a href="https://chromestatus.com/feature/5737414355058688"><u>Private Network Access</u></a>, which used preflight requests to have local devices opt in. For more information on this feature, see <a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QQkqehw8umtAgz5z0um7THx-aoU251p705FbIQjDuGs/edit?usp=sharing"><u>Adapting your website for new Local Network Access restrictions in Chrome</u></a>.</p>

<p>Chrome 145 introduced more granular permissions for websites requesting access to a user's local network. The previous single local-network-access permission is being split into two distinct permissions:</p>

<ul>
  <li>local-network: Grants access to IP addresses in the local network space (for example, intranets, internal devices).</li>
  <li>loopback-network: Grants access to loopback IP addresses (for example, localhost, 127.0.0.1).</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p>The old local-network permission will remain as an alias, ensuring existing configurations and permissions policies continue to function as expected.</p>

<p>This change provides both users and Admins with more precise control over how websites interact with internal network resources. Current enterprise policies managing local network access will not be affected by this change.</p>

<p>Chrome 146 introduces two new enterprise policies for managing local network access restrictions: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides"><u>LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled"><u>LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled</u></a>. These policies can be set using <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/14749672"><u>custom configurations</u></a>.</p>

<p>Chrome 147 expands Local Network Access restrictions to include WebSocket and WebTransport connections.</p>

<p>In Chrome 156, the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut"><u>LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut</u></a> policy will be removed.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 145 on Android, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia The permission split is rolled out.</li>
  <li>Chrome 146 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia Two new enterprise policies will be available for managing local network access restrictions:
    <ul>
      <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides"><u>LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides</u></a> could be used to mark IPv4 and IPv6 address blocks as public or private. IP ranges that are treated as public will not cause permission prompts when accessed by other pages. For example, CGNAT 100.64.0.0/10 can be marked as public. This is useful for certain VPN and proxy setups. Marking 0.0.0.0/0&nbsp; and ::/0 as public is equivalent to disabling the local network access restrictions.</li>
      <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled"><u>LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled</u></a> can be used to cause the LNA permission to be automatically delegated to iframes by the parent frame, without requiring explicit annotation of the child iframes. This is useful in situations where local network access is performed by an embedded SaaS tool inside of a different SaaS tool. This includes certain locally hosted documentation and knowledgebase software.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>Chrome 147 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows Local Network Access restrictions expanded to include WebSocket and WebTransport connections.</li>
  <li>Chrome 156 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut"><u>LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut</u></a> policy will be removed.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Disallow spaces in non-file:// URL hosts</strong></p>

<p>According to the <a href="https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#forbidden-host-code-point"><u>URL Standard specification</u></a>, URL hosts cannot contain the space character, but currently URL parsing in Chromium allows spaces in the host. This causes Chromium to fail several tests included in the <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/websockets?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2024-websockets"><u>Interop2024 HTTPS URLs for WebSocket</u></a> and <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/url?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2023-url"><u>URL focus</u></a> areas. To bring Chromium into spec compliance, we would like to remove spaces from URL hosts altogether, but a difficulty with this is that they are used in the host part in Windows file:// URLs. For more details, see this <a href="https://github.com/whatwg/url/issues/599"><u>Github discussion</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 157 on Android, ChromeOS, LaCrOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Post-quantum cryptography for DTLS in WebRTC</strong> This feature will enable the use of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) with WebRTC connections. The motivation for PQC is to get WebRTC media traffic up to date with the latest cryptography protocols and prevent <em>Harvest Now to Crack Later</em> scenarios.</p>

<p>Admins will be able to control this feature using an enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement"><u>WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement</u></a>, to allow enterprise users to opt out of PQC. The policy is temporary and is planned to be removed by Chrome 159.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 149 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
  <li>Chrome 159 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia Remove <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement"><u>WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement</u></a> enterprise policy</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Protocol filtering in Digital Credential API</strong></p>

<p>Starting in Chrome 151, Chrome will begin deprecating support for unspecified presentation and issuance protocols in the <strong>Digital Credentials API</strong>, with final removal scheduled for Chrome 160.</p>

<p>The Digital Credentials API was originally designed to be an opaque pipeline for arbitrary exchange protocols. In November 2025, the <a href="https://github.com/w3c-fedid/digital-credentials/issues/396"><u>FedID WG resolved</u></a> to change this so that the spec normatively referenced only a specific set of exchange protocols.</p>

<p>The removal of support for arbitrary, opaque pipelines ensures that only verified protocols are used, enabling a more robust privacy and security threat model for identity verification. This change aligns Chromium with updated industry specifications that normatively reference only a specific set of exchange protocols.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 160 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android No rollout step</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Isolated Web Apps</strong></p>

<p><a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/iwa/introduction"><u>Isolated Web Apps</u></a> (IWAs) are an extension of existing work on PWA installation and Web Packaging that provide stronger protections against server compromise and other tampering that is necessary for developers of security-sensitive applications. Rather than being hosted on live web servers and fetched over HTTPS, these applications are packaged into Web Bundles, signed by their developer, and distributed to end-users through one or more of the potential methods described in the <a href="https://github.com/WICG/isolated-web-apps/blob/main/README.md"><u>explainer</u></a>.</p>

<p>In Chrome 128, IWAs became installable through an admin policy only on enterprise-managed ChromeOS devices.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 161 on Windows This rollout adds support for Isolated Web Apps in enterprise-managed browser configurations on Windows.</li>
</ul>

<h4><strong>Upcoming Chrome Enterprise Core updates</strong></h4>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><strong>Custom HTTP headers</strong></p>

<p>Chrome Enterprise will soon offer custom HTTP header injection, a feature that injects custom headers into network requests matching configured URL patterns. This generic capability allows enterprises to reduce their reliance on complex SSL-inspection proxies for a variety of security workflows. For example, administrators can use this feature to enforce SaaS tenant restrictions and prevent data exfiltration. By applying these controls directly at the browser’s network stack, this functionality guarantees the injected headers cannot be modified, disabled, or bypassed by user-installed extensions.</p>

<p>This feature will operate transparently in the background with minimal impact on browsing performance. Administrators will be able to control this feature using a new HttpHeaderInjection policy.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 152 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows Custom HTTP headers feature becomes available on desktop platforms</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Chrome browser rule UX refactor</strong></p>

<p>To enhance the <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/13876556"><u>Data Loss Prevention</u></a> (DLP) rule creation experience, the Google <strong>Admin console</strong> has streamlined how administrators define policies for different applications. Building on the foundation of mutually-exclusive application groups, which separated Workspace, Chrome browser, and ChromeOS rules, the Chrome browser rule workflow has been fundamentally redesigned.</p>

<p>Administrators can now configure multiple actions and protections within a single Chrome browser DLP rule. The new interface consolidates Chrome triggers and introduces support for per-trigger actions. This means admins no longer need to create separate rules to manage different behaviors for the same website; they can now, for example, audit visits to a specific URL while simultaneously blocking file downloads and applying a watermark, all within one unified rule. The workflow is divided into logical sections:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Websites (URL targeting)</li>
  <li>Full-website protection</li>
  <li>Content-transfer protection</li>
</ul>

<p>Existing rules are fully backward compatible. No new enterprise policies are introduced with this update; the changes are applied directly to the rule configuration interface.</p>

<p>For more information, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/11587610"><u>What are ChromeOS data controls? - Chrome Enterprise and Education Help</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 142 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows Enables mutually exclusive app selection for DLP rule configuration in Admin console.</li>
  <li>Chrome 155 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows Introduces multi-action support and per-trigger configurations for Chrome browser DLP rules.</li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

<div class="no-margin"><p>&nbsp;</p>

<h4><strong>Upcoming Chrome Enterprise Premium updates</strong></h4>

<p><strong>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</strong></p>

<p><strong>Custom HTTP headers</strong></p>

<p>Chrome Enterprise will soon offer custom HTTP header injection, a feature that injects custom headers into network requests matching configured URL patterns. This generic capability allows enterprises to reduce their reliance on complex SSL-inspection proxies for a variety of security workflows. For example, administrators can use this feature to enforce SaaS tenant restrictions and prevent data exfiltration. By applying these controls directly at the browser’s network stack, this functionality guarantees the injected headers cannot be modified, disabled, or bypassed by user-installed extensions.</p>

<p>This feature will operate transparently in the background with minimal impact on browsing performance. Administrators will be able to control this feature using a new HttpHeaderInjection policy.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 152 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows Custom HTTP headers feature becomes available on desktop platforms</li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><strong>Chrome browser rule UX refactor</strong></p>

<p>To enhance the <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/13876556"><u>Data Loss Prevention</u></a> (DLP) rule creation experience, the Google <strong>Admin console</strong> has streamlined how administrators define policies for different applications. Building on the foundation of mutually-exclusive application groups, which separated Workspace, Chrome browser, and ChromeOS rules, the Chrome browser rule workflow has been fundamentally redesigned.</p>

<p>Administrators can now configure multiple actions and protections within a single Chrome browser DLP rule. The new interface consolidates Chrome triggers and introduces support for per-trigger actions. This means admins no longer need to create separate rules to manage different behaviors for the same website; they can now, for example, audit visits to a specific URL while simultaneously blocking file downloads and applying a watermark, all within one unified rule. The workflow is divided into logical sections:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Websites (URL targeting)</li>
  <li>Full-website protection</li>
  <li>Content-transfer protection</li>
</ul>

<p>Existing rules are fully backward compatible. No new enterprise policies are introduced with this update; the changes are applied directly to the rule configuration interface.</p>

<p>For more information, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/11587610"><u>What are ChromeOS data controls? - Chrome Enterprise and Education Help</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 142 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows Enables mutually exclusive app selection for DLP rule configuration in Admin console.</li>
  <li>Chrome 155 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows Introduces multi-action support and per-trigger configurations for Chrome browser DLP rules.</li>
</ul>
</div>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Current ChromeOS updates</h4>

<p><a id="chromeOSA151" name="chromeOSA151"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Chrome Apps Kiosk mode deprecation&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>Starting with ChromeOS 151, Chrome apps on ChromeOS will stop working in Kiosk sessions.</p>

    <p>Apps that are force-installed through the Admin console for Managed guest sessions and user sessions will continue to be supported.</p>

    <p>For more details, see<a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/15950395"> <u>End of support for Chrome apps</u></a>.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeOSB151" name="chromeOSB151"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>IWA Apps management and web capabilities&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>As early as ChromeOS 151, administrators will be able to define new web configurations for Isolated Web Apps (IWAs) for Managed Guest Sessions.&nbsp; On the Admin console, admins can now select <strong>Menu &gt; Devices &gt; Chrome &gt; Web capabilities &gt; Managed guest sessions</strong> to set default and per-origin web configurations for IWAs. .</p>

    <p>For more details, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/15820883"><u>Set web capabilities policies for websites and Isolated Web Apps</u></a>.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeOSC151" name="chromeOSC151"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Updates blocked for certain ChromeOS Flex devices&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>From ChromeOS 151&nbsp;onwards, we will begin blocking updates for devices unable to meet the minimum requirements for the Chrome Browser. This will affect devices using the following:</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Intel and AMD graphics from 2010 and older&nbsp;</li>
      <li>Nvidia graphics from 2014 and older&nbsp;</li>
    </ul>

    <p>This does not affect any <a href="https://support.google.com/chromeosflex/answer/11513094" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>certified devices</u></a>. If unexpected devices are affected, reach out to Google <a href="https://support.google.com/chromeosflex/answer/4594885" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ChromeOS Flex support</u></a>.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Upcoming ChromeOS changes</h4>

<p><a id="upChromeOSA151" name="upChromeOSA151"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Mandatory migration to Certificate Provisioning API &nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>ChromeOS 158 (planned release mid-November, 2026) is the last release to support certificate enrollment without using the Certificate Provisioning API. If you do not migrate, no new certificates will be issued. For instructions, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/11338941"><u>Configuring Certificate Provisioning for ChromeOS via SCEP - Chrome Enterprise and Education Help</u></a>.</p>

    <p>Note the upcoming changes to ChromeOS release numbering in the <a href="https://chromiumdash.appspot.com/schedule"><u>ChromeOS release schedule</u></a>.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeOSB151" name="upChromeOSB151"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Upcoming change to ChromeOS release numbering&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>Starting with ChromeOS 154, ChromeOS will continue to be released every 4 weeks, but the release number will be incremented by 2 (instead of 1). This change is to align numbering with the new Chrome browser 2-week release cadence. You can find more details in the <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-two-week-release" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome for Developers</u></a> blog post.</p>

    <p>For customers on the Long-term Support channel, the duration between LTS releases is not changing; LTS will continue to release every 6 months. With the transition to the new release numbering, LTS versioning will&nbsp; increment every 12 versions. For more information, see the <a href="https://chromiumdash.appspot.com/schedule" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chromium release schedule</u></a> and <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/12239814"><u>Long-term Support (LTS) release notes</u></a> in the Chrome Enterprise and Education Help Center.</p>

  </li>

<h2>Chrome browser changes &nbsp;</h2>

<p><strong>Always use secure connections by default</strong></p>

<p>Prior to enabling it by default for all users, Chrome 150 enables <strong>Always use secure connections</strong> for users who have opted in to <a href="https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/11577602"><u>Enhanced Safe Browsing protections in Chrome</u></a>.</p>

<p>Chrome 154 will enable the <strong>Always use secure connections</strong> setting in the <em>public sites only</em> mode by default. This means Chrome will ask for the user's permission before the first access to any public site without HTTPS. Public sites are defined as sites that have a globally unique name, and excludes direct navigation to <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1918"><u>RFC 1918</u></a> addresses (192.168.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8, and so on), as well as shortnames such as go/.</p>

<p>If you are a website developer or IT professional, and you have users who may be impacted by this feature, we very strongly recommend enabling the <strong>Always use secure connections</strong> setting today to help identify sites that you may need to work to migrate. Admins can use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HttpAllowlist"><u>HttpAllowlist</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HttpsOnlyMode"><u>HttpsOnlyMode</u></a> policies to override this behavior.</p>

<p>For more information, see our <a href="https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/docs/security/ask-before-http/ask-before-http-adoption-guide.md"><u>adoption guide</u></a> and <a href="https://security.googleblog.com/2025/10/https-by-default.html"><u>announcement blog post</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia - Feature rolls out gradually</strong>: Enable "Always use secure connections" for users who have opted in to Enhanced Safe Browsing. This applies to Desktop only.</li>
  <li>Chrome 154 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia - Feature rolls out gradually: Enable "Always use secure connections" by default for all users.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Credential exchange for Google Password Manager</strong></p>

<p>To improve the security of credential migration and to enable passkey portability, Chrome on Android now supports the <a href="https://fidoalliance.org/specifications-credential-exchange-specifications/"><u>FIDO Alliance Credential Exchange</u></a> standard. This feature allows users to securely import and export passwords and passkeys between Google Password Manager and third-party credential providers using an end-to-end encrypted protocol. Admin can control this feature using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PasswordManagerEnabled"><u>PasswordManagerEnabled</u></a> policy.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Android - Feature rolls out gradually</strong></li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Gemini in Chrome</strong></p>

<p>Gemini is now integrated into Chrome on macOS, Windows, Android and selective ChromeOS devices, and can understand the content of your current page. Users can now seamlessly get key takeaways, clarify concepts, and find answers, all without leaving their Chrome tab. This integration includes both chat—where users can interact with Gemini via text, and Gemini Live, with which users can interact with Gemini via voice.</p>

<p>In Chrome 143, <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16291696"><u>Gemini in Chrome</u></a> started to roll out to most Google Workspace users with access to the Gemini app in the US. Admins can turn off this feature (value 1) using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiSettings"><u>GeminiSettings</u></a> policy or by using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> (value 2). For more details, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16291696"><u>Gemini in Chrome</u></a> in the Help Center or this <a href="https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/chrome-enterprise/supercharging-employee-productivity-with-ai-securely-with-gemini-in-chrome-enterprise"><u>blog post</u></a>.</p>

<p>In Chrome 143, we announced the multi-tab context feature. Gemini in Chrome can now see more of your opened tabs (10 max) so you can ask questions across multiple pages to help you compare, find information more efficiently. Gemini in Chrome also serves as a productivity agent. Gemini in Chrome automatically uses public information from these Google services: Google Search, Google Maps, YouTube. With your permission, Gemini in Chrome can help you connect your personal information and content in Google Workspace services (Gmail, Drive, Keep, Calendar, and Tasks).</p>

<p>In Chrome 144, auto browse in Gemini in Chrome was made available to some users (non-enterprise). An enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebSettings"><u>GeminiActOnWebSettings</u></a> is available.</p>

<p>In Chrome 147, Auto browse in Gemini in Chrome became available to Enterprise users.</p>

<p>In Chrome 149, Gemini in Chrome became available to users in 118 additional countries and territories.</p>

<p>In Chrome 150, Gemini Spark can use Chrome auto browse to complete tasks that need web actuation. Enterprise policy is <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiSparkSettings"><u>GeminiSparkSettings</u></a>.</p>

<p>For more details, see our <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16291696"><u>Gemini in Chrome</u></a> Help Center article.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 147 on ChromeOS, macOS, Windows: Auto browse in Gemini in Chrome available to enterprise users. Enterprise policies <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebSettings"><u>GeminiActOnWebSettings</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebAllowedForURLs"><u>GeminiActOnWebAllowedForURLs</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebBlockedForURLs"><u>GeminiActOnWebBlockedForURLs</u></a> are available to control auto browse.</li>
  <li>Chrome 149 on ChromeOS, macOS, Windows - Feature rolls out gradually: Gemini in Chrome is now available to users in 118 additional countries and territories. More details in our <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16291696"><u>Gemini in Chrome</u></a> Help Center article.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on ChromeOS, macOS, Windows</strong>:
    <ul>
      <li>Chrome will now suggest Gemini in Chrome features at relevant moments. Enterprise policy ChromeSuggestions will be available at launch.</li>
      <li>As early as Chrome 150 users will be able to connect Chrome to Gemini Spark. This permits the Gemini Spark agent to perform autonomous, multi-step actions on Chrome clients using the active browser session. Enterprise policy GeminiSparkSettings will be available at launch.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Opaque origin for data: URLs</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 150 updates how Dedicated and Shared Workers handle <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2397"><u>data: URLs</u></a>. Rather than automatically inheriting the security origin of the script or page that created them, these workers will now be assigned a unique opaque origin.</p>

<p>This alignment with the worker <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/2021/NOTE-workers-20210128/#worker"><u>HTML specification</u></a> enhances security by isolating these workers from the creator's same-origin state, preventing them from accessing sensitive data via mechanisms like BroadcastChannel or same-origin storage. To maintain correct isolation boundaries, these workers still reside within the same storage partition (for example, by preserving the top-level site or nonce) as their creator.</p>

<p>This security adjustment is enabled by default across desktop and mobile platforms. Administrators can review or verify security boundaries using their centralized configurations. For technical implementation details and specification references, see Step 3 of the <a href="https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/workers.html#script-settings-for-workers"><u>HTML Living Standard Worker Settings</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong>: No rollout step.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>WebMCP Tooling</strong></p>

<p>This feature allows inspection and debugging for WebMCP tools defined on a page. For more information on WebMCP, see <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/ai/webmcp"><u>Chrome for Developers article</u></a>.</p>

<p>The DevTools UI, browser automation tools (for example, puppeteer), and agents (for example, via chrome-devtools-mcp) are able to inspect defined tools, to trigger tool calls themselves, and to observe tool calls triggered by another agent interacting with the page. Similar to other DevTools features, you can control WebMCP Tooling using <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#RemoteDebuggingAllowed"><u>RemoteDebuggingAllowed</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DeveloperToolsAvailability"><u>DeveloperToolsAvailability</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong></li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Connection limit randomization for proxy pools</strong></p>

<p>Starting in Chrome 150, Chrome introduces randomization to the connection limits for TCP socket proxy pools. This security enhancement is designed to mitigate cross-site state leakage. Currently, by exploiting limits in the connection pool size on Chrome, knowledge can be gained about cross-site state that would otherwise be inaccessible. Specifically, it’s possible (with some statistical certainty) to evaluate the login state, visited history, or even something more specific like whether Gmail has pending messages in the inbox.</p>

<p>To mitigate this risk, Chrome is adding randomization to the way that TCP socket pools are limited so that an observing site cannot infer this information with high certainty.</p>

<p>Admins can disable this feature using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AllowSocketPoolSizeRandomizationForProxies"><u>AllowSocketPoolSizeRandomizationForProxies</u></a> policy.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows - Feature rolls out gradually</strong></li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Disable SVG filters on plugins and iFrames</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 150 will prevent Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) filters from being applied to embedded plugins (for example, PDFs) and cross-origin or restricted iFrames (for example, sandboxed ones). When a plugin or iFrame would be painted with an SVG filter effect, the effect tree is traversed to find the highest ancestor without SVG filters, and that effect is then applied instead.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong>: No rollout step.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Keychain error message on macOS</strong></p>

<p>To ensure data availability and security, Chrome on macOS now includes a notification to help users resolve keychain configuration errors. If Chrome cannot access the macOS system keychain during startup, sensitive profile data—including cookies, autofill information, and passwords—might become unavailable. This feature introduces an infobar that alerts the user to the issue and provides a direct path to re-authorize keychain access by relaunching the browser.</p>

<p>In managed environments, resolving this state may require administrative privileges to fulfill the macOS system security prompt. Admins should be aware that users encountering this message may require assistance from support teams to restore full access to their encrypted profile data. Chrome remains functional even if keychain access is denied, though access to previously-saved data will be restricted until the permission is granted.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on macOS - Feature rolls out gradually</strong></li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>New Chrome Desktop visual updates</strong></p>

<p>With Google's design language evolving for the AI era, we have an opportunity to modernize the desktop browser's UI across operating systems and to reduce clutter. The first wave of updates will roll out with Chrome 150, including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Icons will be updated with softer edges and animations on buttons, like the three dot Chrome menu and page refresh.</li>
  <li>Context menus will be simplified by removing or re-homing low usage and duplicate items.</li>
  <li>Settings, Downloads, and Bookmark pages will get a visual re-skin to align with the latest design language.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows - Feature rolls out gradually</strong>:</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Windows, macOS, Linux</strong>: updated icons (increased roundedness).</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS</strong>: simplified tab strip and context menus, updated tab group colors, visual update to chrome://settings, downloads, and bookmarks, updated dark mode color.</li>
  <li>Chrome 152 on macOS: "glass" effect on tab strip.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>PWA origin migration</strong></p>

<p>When a user installs a Progressive Web App (PWA), its identity and security context are tightly bound to its web origin, for example, app.example.com. This presents a significant challenge for developers who need to change their PWA's origin due to rebranding, domain restructuring, or technical re-architecture. Currently, such a change forces users to manually uninstall the old app and reinstall the new one, leading to a disruptive experience and a potential increase in user loss rate. Chrome 150 introduces a mechanism for developers to seamlessly migrate an installed PWA to a new, same-site origin, preserving user trust and permissions.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebAppInstallForceList"><u>WebAppInstallForceList</u></a> policy will block migration. Since enterprise policies around web applications are primarily based on URLs and origins, there is a risk that a migration would bypass certain policies an admin might have configured. No migration will be offered to the user when an app is force-installed by their enterprise administrator, and instead a banner will be shown explaining this to the user.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Windows, macOS, Linux</strong>: No rollout step.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Support for ML-DSA in TLS</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 150 adds support for Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) signing algorithms and certificates in TLS. This will enable the use of ML-DSA (post-quantum) certificates in chrome://certificate-manager, and associated enterprise policies. There are no changes to the Chrome Root Store. The relevant policies are:</p>

<ul>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#CACertificateManagementAllowed"><u>CACertificateManagementAllowed</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#CACertificates"><u>CACertificates</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#CACertificatesWithConstraints"><u>CACertificatesWithConstraints</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#CADistrustedCertificates"><u>CADistrustedCertificates</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#CAHintCertificates"><u>CAHintCertificates</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#CAPlatformIntegrationEnabled"><u>CAPlatformIntegrationEnabled</u></a></li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p>This feature will be available on all non-iOS platforms.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong>: Support for ML-DSA in TLS enabled by default. Users or administrators must explicitly configure a trusted root for ML-DSA to be used, as it is not currently possible to issue a publicly trusted ML-DSA certificate.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Update to autofill address synchronization</strong></p>

<p>As part of ongoing infrastructure upgrades to unify our data sync services, Chrome is temporarily pausing the synchronization of autofill addresses across Chrome Enterprise devices.</p>

<p>During this period, all previously saved addresses will remain completely secure and accessible locally on the specific device where they were originally saved. This change does not delete any existing data. We are refining our enterprise address integration and plan to re-enable cross-device syncing in a future release.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows - Feature rolls out gradually</strong></li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>New Autofill and passwords screen on mobile devices</strong></p>

<p>Starting in Chrome 150 for Android and Chrome 151 for iOS, the <strong>Passwords and Autofill</strong> settings category is being replaced with a new, unified <strong>Autofill and password</strong> screen. This update also reorganizes the <strong>Addresses and more</strong> screen by splitting <strong>Enhanced Autofill</strong> management into two distinct categories: <strong>Identity docs</strong> and <strong>Travel</strong>.</p>

<p>The primary goal of this change is to provide users and admins with a more comprehensive overview of all the stored browser data, including passwords, passkeys, addresses, and ID cards. This is a user interface change within the settings.</p>

<p>Existing policies for Autofill and Password management continue to function as expected, without any disruption. Admins can continue to manage these settings through the following existing policies: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PasswordManagerEnabled"><u>PasswordManagerEnabled</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AutofillAddressEnabled"><u>AutofillAddressEnabled</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AutofillCreditCardEnabled"><u>AutofillCreditCardEnabled</u></a>.</p>

<p>For more information, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/answer/142893"><u>Fill out forms automatically in Chrome</u></a> in the Google Chrome Help Center.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Android - Feature rolls out gradually</strong>: Whole feature being rolled out.</li>
  <li>Chrome 151 on iOS - Feature rolls out gradually: Whole feature being rolled out.</li>
</ul>
