<h2>Chrome Enterprise Core changes</h2>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><strong>Deprecation of roaming profile policies</strong></p>

<p>Chrome Enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#RoamingProfileSupportEnabled"><u>RoamingProfileSupportEnabled</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#RoamingProfileLocation"><u>RoamingProfileLocation</u></a> were due to be deprecated in Chrome 150 but will remain functional until Chrome 161.</p>

<p>Admins should plan to migrate away from these configurations before their full removal in January 2027, after which Chrome will no longer use or update data from roaming profiles.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Policies are deprecated but remain functional.</li>
  <li>Chrome 161 on Linux, macOS, Windows: Policies removed. Chrome will no longer use data from roaming profiles or update them.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Gen AI and SaaS app usage reporting</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 150 introduces a new <strong>Gen AI and SaaS app usage</strong> reporting feature in the Google <strong>Admin console</strong>. This report brings visibility into an organization's use of generative AI tools and SaaS sites, allowing admins to monitor usage of their enterprise IT resources.</p>

<p>This new report tracks usage for popular Gen AI and enterprise SaaS websites in Chrome, providing metrics on visits, unique managed profiles, unique managed browsers, and access to sensitive content transfer events. With these insights, admins can assess risk and then, leverage Chrome Enterprise Premium data protection controls to restrict usage using Data Loss Prevention (DLP) rules.</p>

<p>The <strong>Gen AI and SaaS app usage reporting</strong> policy will be available in the Admin console to disable this reporting.</p>

<p>Chrome 147 allowed a <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/engage/trusted-testers/sign-up/"><u>Trusted Tester</u></a> preview, with the feature gradually rolling out in Chrome 150 and Chrome 151.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Early preview available to Chrome Enterprise Trusted Tester.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Feature rolls out gradually.</li>
  <li>Chrome 151 on ChromeOS: Feature rolls out gradually. ChromeOS support is gradually rolling out.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>SSO with Microsoft Entra ID on Android</strong></p>

<p>Chrome on Android now supports seamless Single Sign-On (SSO) with Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD). This feature allows users to access Microsoft web applications, such as Outlook and SharePoint, without repeatedly entering credentials, if they are already signed into a Microsoft app on the same device. This update aligns Chrome on Android with SSO features available Chrome on Windows and macOS.</p>

<p>Admins can use <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AndroidEntraSsoEnabled"><u>AndroidEntraSsoEnabled</u></a> policy to control this functionality, which is disabled by default. To work, the device must have a Microsoft broker app installed (such as Microsoft Authenticator, Intune Company Portal, or Link to Windows) and the user must be signed into a Microsoft app. This feature is an add-on for managed users and improves user productivity by reducing authentication friction while leveraging secure, on-device credential handling.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Android - Feature rolls out gradually</strong>: Single Sign-On (SSO) with Microsoft Entra ID becomes available on Android.</li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

<div class="no-margin"><h2>Chrome Enterprise Premium changes</h2>

<p>Read more about the differences between <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/products/chrome-enterprise-premium" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Enterprise Core and Chrome Enterprise Premium</u></a>.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><strong>Microsoft Information Protection (MIP) label integration</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 150 can now understand and enforce Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies based on Microsoft Information Protection (MIP) sensitivity labels applied to Office 365 documents.</p>

<p>To enable this feature, administrators must authorize the connection between Chrome Enterprise Premium and their Microsoft Azure tenant using the MIP label config under the Connectors API. Once connected, admins can create permanent DLP rules using these labels to block, warn, or audit user actions, for example:</p>

<ul>
  <li>copying and pasting to external sites, specifically targeting risks like GenAI data leakage</li>
  <li>downloading</li>
  <li>printing</li>
</ul>

<p>In Chrome 150, a <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/engage/trusted-testers/sign-up/"><u>Trusted Tester preview</u></a> of Microsoft Information Protection (MIP) label integration becomes available on Windows, macOS and ChromeOS.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on ChromeOS, macOS, Windows</strong>: Early preview available to Chrome Enterprise Trusted Tester.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Asynchronous file hashing for large DLP uploads</strong></p>

<p>In Chrome 150, Chrome Enterprise Premium optimizes how it processes files larger than 50MB during Data Loss Prevention (DLP) scans. This update moves the file hash computation to a background process, thereby significantly reducing file upload times and browser delays for users. When the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnFileAttachedEnterpriseConnector"><u>OnFileAttachedEnterpriseConnector</u></a> or <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnFileDownloadedEnterpriseConnector"><u>OnFileDownloadedEnterpriseConnector</u></a> policies are enabled, this performance improvement applies automatically. Full file hashes will continue to be securely generated and sent for reporting purposes once the background task completes.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows - Feature rolls out gradually</strong></li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Enterprise file download protection on Android</strong></p>

<p>Admins can now prevent Chrome on Android users from downloading files considered to contain sensitive data by creating a DLP OnFileDownload rule to send a file for analysis when it is downloaded from a specific page. Based on the scanning result, it will warn or block the download if sensitive information is detected.</p>

<p>Admins can control this feature using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnFileDownloadedEnterpriseConnector"><u>OnFileDownloadedEnterpriseConnector</u></a> policy, which enables the download connector. Configuring this policy extends your established desktop content scanning and DLP rules directly to Chrome on Android, if they are available on mobile platforms.</p>

<p>This update allows you to enforce consistent data security policies across both desktop and mobile environments, effectively closing a critical security gap and mitigating the risk of sensitive data exfiltration to managed and unmanaged mobile endpoints.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Android - Feature rolls out gradually</strong>: Feature becomes available on Android.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Screenshot protections for specific URLs</strong></p>

<p>Admins can prevent users from taking screenshots or screen sharing specific web pages considered to contain sensitive data. Admins create a DLP URL filtering rule to block users taking screenshots or screen sharing specific URLs or categories of URLs.</p>

<p>This feature can be controlled via the same <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#EnterpriseRealTimeUrlCheckMode"><u>EnterpriseRealTimeUrlCheckMode</u></a> Chrome Enterprise policy that enables all real-time URL lookups.</p>

<p>In Chrome 150, this feature becomes available on iOS and iPadOS.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 129 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Trusted Tester program.</li>
  <li>Chrome 131 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Feature rolls out.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on iOS - Feature rolls out gradually</strong>: Feature becomes available on iOS and iPadOS.</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>CPU Performance API</strong></p>

<p>Starting in Chrome 151, Chrome will introduce the CPU Performance API, which allows web applications to determine the performance tier of a user's device. This API targets web applications that will use this information to provide an improved user experience, possibly in combination with the Compute Pressure API, which provides information about the user device’s CPU pressure/utilization and allows applications to react to changes in CPU pressure.</p>

<p>Users can override the reported performance tier in Chrome's Performance settings. Administrators can also control this behavior using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#CpuPerformanceTierOverride"><u>CpuPerformanceTierOverride</u></a> policy (which takes precedence over the user setting).</p>

<p>For more details, see <a href="https://github.com/WICG/cpu-performance"><u>CPU Performance API Explainer</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 151 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong>: No rollout step.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Chrome will remove support for macOS 12</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 150 will be the last release to support macOS 12; Chrome 151+ will no longer support macOS 12, which is outside of its support window with Apple. Running on a supported operating system is essential to maintaining security.</p>

<p>On Macs running macOS 12, Chrome will continue to work, showing a warning infobar, but will not update any further. If users wish to have Chrome updated, they need to update their computer to a supported version of macOS.</p>

<p>For new installations of Chrome 151+, macOS 13+ will be required.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 151 on Windows, macOS, Linux</strong>: No rollout step.</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Process isolation on Windows</strong></p>

<p>Starting in Chrome 151, Chrome will apply Windows security Access Control Lists (ACLs) to prevent other applications from reading or injecting into Chrome's memory space. This security enhancement is designed to protect Chrome's memory from unauthorized access, though it may cause interoperability issues with older antivirus, Data Loss Prevention (DLP), or accessibility software.</p>

<p>The admins will be able to control and disable this feature using the <strong>WindowsProcessIsolation</strong> policy. Enterprises are encouraged to begin testing the feature manually before the policy becomes available to identify potential software incompatibilities. To enable early testing:</p>

<ol>
  <li>Toggle the chrome://flags/#enable-process-isolation-ui flag to <strong>Enabled</strong>.</li>
  <li>Navigate to chrome://settings/system and enable <strong>Process Isolation</strong>.</li>
</ol>

<p>Process isolation will eventually be enabled by default on all Chrome installations on Windows.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 151 on Windows - Feature rolls out gradually</strong></li>
</ul>

<p><strong>SafeBrowsing API v4 to v5 migration</strong></p>

<p>Chrome calls into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/v4"><u>SafeBrowsing v4 API</u></a> will be migrated to call into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference"><u>v5 API</u></a> instead. The method names are also different between v4 and v5.</p>

<p>If admins have any v4-specific URL allowlisting to allow network requests to https://safebrowsing.googleapis.com/v4*, these should be modified to allow network requests to the whole domain instead: safebrowsing.googleapis.com. Otherwise, rejected network requests to the v5 API will cause security regressions for users.</p>

<p>For more details, see <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference/Migration.From.V4"><u>Migration From V4 - Safe Browsing</u></a>.</p>

</ul>

<p><strong>URLAllowlist and URLBlocklist policy update</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 151 introduces two refinements to URL filtering behavior to ensure consistent security enforcement and more accurate administrative reporting across all platforms.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Consistent Policy Enforcement in Incognito Mode</strong>: To enhance security and privacy, the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#URLBlocklist"><u>URLBlocklist</u></a> policy will now be strictly enforced on Incognito pages. Previously, the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#IncognitoModeUrlAllowlist"><u>IncognitoModeUrlAllowlist</u></a> could override blocklist settings in certain scenarios. This update ensures that administrators have reliable control over restricted content, regardless of the user's browsing mode.</li>
  <li><strong>Improved Wildcard (*) Handling in URLAllowlist</strong>: When a wildcard (*) is used in the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#URLAllowlist"><u>URLAllowlist</u></a>, Chrome will no longer categorize every URL as "explicitly allowed." While users will still be permitted to navigate to these URLs (unless blocked by a more specific policy), this change ensures that internal status checks and reporting tools accurately reflect the difference between a global allowlisting and a targeted allowlist entry.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 151 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows - Feature rolls out gradually</strong></li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>XML Parsing in Rust for non XSLT scenarios</strong></p>

<p>To improve browser security and protect users against memory-related vulnerabilities, Chrome 151 is changing its XML parsing engine to a memory-safe Rust implementation for several common scenarios. This foundational update eliminates potential memory corruption bugs while maintaining full compatibility with existing web standards.</p>

<p>Chrome has already begun to deprecate and remove XSLT. While this process continues, the new, safer parser will handle the following scenarios where no XSLT is required:</p>

<ol>
  <li>DOMParser Web API.</li>
  <li>Accessing responseXML of XMLHttpRequest.</li>
  <li>SVG standalone images (that is, accessing a image.svg document directly as a top level navigation).</li>
  <li>SVG external images (including a main document embedding an SVG as an external image resource).</li>
</ol>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 151 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong>: No rollout step.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Connection Allowlists</strong></p>

<p>Connection Allowlists is a feature designed to provide explicit control over external endpoints by restricting connections initiated via the Fetch API or other web platform APIs from a document or worker.</p>

<p>The proposed implementation involves the distribution of an authorized endpoint list from the server through an HTTP response header. Prior to the establishment of any connection by the user agent on behalf of a page, the agent will evaluate the destination against this allowlist; connections to verified endpoints will be permitted, while those failing to match the entries in the list will be blocked.</p>

<p>More details on the proposal can be found here: <a href="https://github.com/WICG/connection-allowlists"><u>https://github.com/WICG/connection-allowlists</u></a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong>: No rollout step.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Deprecate and remove XSLT</strong></p>

<p><a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/xslt-10/"><u>XSLT v1.0</u></a>, which all browsers adhere to, was standardized in 1999. In the meantime, XSLT has evolved to v2.0 and v3.0, adding features, and growing apart from the old version frozen into browsers. This lack of advancement, coupled with the rise of JavaScript libraries and frameworks that offer more flexible and powerful DOM manipulation, has led to a significant decline in the use of client-side XSLT. Its role within the web browser has been largely superseded by JavaScript-based technologies, such as JSON and React.</p>

<p>Chromium uses the <strong>libxslt</strong> library to process these transformations, and <a href="https://discourse.gnome.org/t/stepping-down-as-libxslt-maintainer/27615"><u>libxslt was unmaintained</u></a> for ~6 months of 2025. Libxslt is a complex, aging C codebase of the type notoriously susceptible to memory safety vulnerabilities like buffer overflows, which can lead to arbitrary code execution. Because client-side XSLT is now a niche, rarely-used feature, these libraries receive far less maintenance and security scrutiny than core JavaScript engines, yet they represent a direct, potent attack surface for processing untrusted web content. Indeed, XSLT is the source of several recent high-profile security exploits that continue to put browser users at risk.</p>

<p>For these reasons, Chromium (along with both other browser engines) plans to deprecate and remove XSLT from the web platform.</p>

<p>For more details, see this <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/deprecating-xslt"><u>Chrome for Developers article</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 143 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Deprecation (but not removal) of the APIs.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Origin Trial (OT) and Enterprise Policy go live for testing. These allow sites and enterprises to continue using features past the removal date.</li>
  <li>Chrome 158 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: XSLT stops functioning on Stable releases, for all users other than Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy participants.</li>
  <li>Chrome 176 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy stop functioning. XSLT is disabled for all users.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Deprecation and removal of Privacy Sandbox APIs</strong></p>

<p>Chrome has <a href="https://privacysandbox.com/news/update-on-plans-for-privacy-sandbox-technologies/"><u>recently announced</u></a> that the current approach to third-party cookies is to be maintained, following which, we plan to deprecate and remove the following APIs:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Topics</li>
  <li>Protected Audience</li>
  <li>Shared Storage</li>
  <li>Attribution Reporting</li>
  <li>Private Aggregation</li>
  <li>Related Web Sites</li>
  <li>requestStorageAccessFor</li>
</ul>

<p>The following are the enterprise policies associated with the above APIs.</p>

<ul>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PrivacySandboxSiteEnabledAdsEnabled"><u>PrivacySandboxSiteEnabledAdsEnabled</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PrivacySandboxAdTopicsEnabled"><u>PrivacySandboxAdTopicsEnabled</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PrivacySandboxAdMeasurementEnabled"><u>PrivacySandboxAdMeasurementEnabled</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#RelatedWebsiteSetsOverrides"><u>RelatedWebsiteSetsOverrides</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#RelatedWebsiteSetsEnabled"><u>RelatedWebsiteSetsEnabled</u></a></li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p>Deprecation began with Chrome 144, and removal is planned for Chrome 152. After deprecation, the APIs will continue to exist, and most users will see no disruptions. However, some users who rely on server-side integrations (such as k-anonymity server, or coordinators) will see a break in the services. We have proactively reached out to users of the APIs with our deprecation plans. At the time of removal, Chrome 152, all the policies associated with these APIs will also be removed.</p>

<p>None of the APIs are enabled by default to enterprise users. Enterprise teams may want to review the status for any managed profile in their <strong>Admin console</strong>.</p>

<ul>

  <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: APIs and the associated policies removal.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Local network access restrictions</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 142 restricted the ability to make requests to the user's local network, gated behind a permission prompt. A local network request is any request from a public website to a local IP address or loopback, or from a local website (for example, intranet) to loopback.</p>

<p>Gating the ability for websites to perform these requests behind a permission mitigates the risk of cross-site request forgery attacks against local network devices such as routers, and reduces the ability of sites to use these requests to fingerprint the user's local network.</p>

<p>This permission is restricted to secure contexts. If granted, the permissions additionally relaxes mixed content blocking for local network requests (since many local devices are not able to obtain publicly trusted TLS certificates for various reasons).</p>

<p>This work supersedes a prior effort called <a href="https://chromestatus.com/feature/5737414355058688"><u>Private Network Access</u></a>, which used preflight requests to have local devices opt in. For more information on this feature, see <a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QQkqehw8umtAgz5z0um7THx-aoU251p705FbIQjDuGs/edit?usp=sharing"><u>Adapting your website for new Local Network Access restrictions in Chrome</u></a>.</p>

<p>Chrome 145 introduced more granular permissions for websites requesting access to a user's local network. The previous single local-network-access permission is being split into two distinct permissions:</p>

<ul>
  <li>local-network: Grants access to IP addresses in the local network space (for example, intranets, internal devices).</li>
  <li>loopback-network: Grants access to loopback IP addresses (for example, localhost, 127.0.0.1).</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p>The old local-network permission will remain as an alias, ensuring existing configurations and permissions policies continue to function as expected.</p>

<p>This change provides both users and Admins with more precise control over how websites interact with internal network resources. Current enterprise policies managing local network access will not be affected by this change.</p>

<p>Chrome 146 introduces two new enterprise policies for managing local network access restrictions: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides"><u>LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled"><u>LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled</u></a>. These policies can be set using <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/14749672"><u>custom configurations</u></a>.</p>

<p>Chrome 147 expands Local Network Access restrictions to include WebSocket and WebTransport connections.</p>

<p>In Chrome 152, the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut"><u>LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut</u></a> policy will be removed.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 145 on Android, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: The permission split is rolled out.</li>
  <li>Chrome 146 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: Two new enterprise policies will be available for managing local network access restrictions:
    <ul>
      <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides"><u>LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides</u></a> could be used to mark IPv4 and IPv6 address blocks as public or private. IP ranges that are treated as public will not cause permission prompts when accessed by other pages. For example, CGNAT 100.64.0.0/10 can be marked as public. This is useful for certain VPN and proxy setups. Marking 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 as public is equivalent to disabling the local network access restrictions.</li>
      <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled"><u>LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled</u></a> can be used to cause the LNA permission to be automatically delegated to iframes by the parent frame, without requiring explicit annotation of the child iframes. This is useful in situations where local network access is performed by an embedded SaaS tool inside of a different SaaS tool. This includes certain locally hosted documentation and knowledgebase software.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>Chrome 147 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Local Network Access restrictions expanded to include WebSocket and WebTransport connections.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut"><u>LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut</u></a> policy will be removed.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Smarter autofill suggestions</strong></p>

  <li>Chrome 140 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: The existing <em>Autofill with AI</em> feature will be renamed to <em>Enhanced autofill</em>. This feature allows users to save and fill additional types of information, and with this update becomes available in more countries and languages.</li>

<p><strong>Moving to a 2-week release cycle</strong></p>

<p>From September 2026 (Chrome 153), Chrome will move to a 2-week release cycle, from the current four-week cycle. The web platform is constantly advancing, and our goal at Chrome is to ensure developers and users have immediate access to the latest capabilities, fixes, and performance improvements. Building on our history of adapting our release process to match the demands of a modern web, we are announcing this significant step to further increase our development velocity and Chrome Stable is moving to a 2-week release cycle. You can find more details in the <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-two-week-release"><u>Chrome for Developers</u></a> blog post.</p>

<p>Extended Stable is available for customers who might have concerns about the maintenance costs. For more information about Extended Stable, see this <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16942104"><u>Help Center</u></a> article. The 2-week Stable option remains the most secure choice and should be utilized if security is a larger concern than maintenance costs.</p>

<ul>

<p><strong>ServiceWorkerAutoPreload browser mode</strong></p>

<p><strong>ServiceWorkerAutoPreload</strong> is a mode where the browser issues the network request in parallel with the service worker bootstrap. If the fetch handler returns the response with respondWith(), the browser consumes the network request result inside the fetch handler. If the fetch handler result is fallback, it passes the network response directly to the browser. ServiceWorkerAutoPreload is an optional browser optimization that changes the existing service worker behavior.</p>

<p>Admins can control this feature using an enterprise policy called <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled"><u>ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 140 on Android, Windows: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled"><u>ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled</u></a> policy will be available.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 154 on Android, Windows</strong>: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled"><u>ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled</u></a> policy will be removed.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Disallow spaces in non-file:// URL hosts</strong></p>

<p>According to the <a href="https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#forbidden-host-code-point"><u>URL Standard specification</u></a>, URL hosts cannot contain the space character, but currently URL parsing in Chromium allows spaces in the host. This causes Chromium to fail several tests included in the <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/websockets?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2024-websockets"><u>Interop2024 HTTPS URLs for WebSocket</u></a> and <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/url?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2023-url"><u>URL focus</u></a> areas. To bring Chromium into spec compliance, we would like to remove spaces from URL hosts altogether, but a difficulty with this is that they are used in the host part in Windows file:// URLs. For more details, see this <a href="https://github.com/whatwg/url/issues/599"><u>Github discussion</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 157 on Android, ChromeOS, LaCrOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong></li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>PostQuantum cryptography for DTLS in WebRTC</strong></p>

<p>This feature will enable the use of PostQuantum Cryptography (PQC) with WebRTC connections. The motivation for PQC is to get WebRTC media traffic up to date with the latest cryptography protocols and prevent <em>Harvest Now to Crack Later</em> scenarios.</p>

<p>Admins will be able to control this feature using an enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement"><u>WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement</u></a>, to allow enterprise users to opt out of PQC. The policy is temporary and is planned to be removed by Chrome 159.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 149 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 159 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong>: Remove <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement"><u>WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement</u></a> enterprise policy.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Protocol filtering in Digital Credential API</strong></p>

<p>Starting in Chrome 151, Chrome will begin deprecating support for unspecified presentation and issuance protocols in the <strong>Digital Credentials API</strong>, with final removal scheduled for Chrome 160.</p>

<p>The Digital Credentials API was originally designed to be an opaque pipeline for arbitrary exchange protocols. In November 2025, the <a href="https://github.com/w3c-fedid/digital-credentials/issues/396"><u>FedID WG resolved</u></a> to change this so that the spec normatively referenced only a specific set of exchange protocols.</p>

<p>The removal of support for arbitrary, opaque pipelines ensures that only verified protocols are used, enabling a more robust privacy and security threat model for identity verification. This change aligns Chromium with updated industry specifications that normatively reference only a specific set of exchange protocols.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 160 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong>: No rollout step.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Isolated Web Apps</strong></p>

<p><a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/iwa/introduction"><u>Isolated Web Apps</u></a> (IWAs) are an extension of existing work on PWA installation and Web Packaging that provide stronger protections against server compromise and other tampering that is necessary for developers of security-sensitive applications. Rather than being hosted on live web servers and fetched over HTTPS, these applications are packaged into Web Bundles, signed by their developer, and distributed to end-users through one or more of the potential methods described in the <a href="https://github.com/WICG/isolated-web-apps/blob/main/README.md"><u>explainer</u></a>.</p>

<p>In Chrome 128, IWAs became installable through an admin policy only on enterprise-managed ChromeOS devices.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 161 on Windows</strong>: This rollout adds support for Isolated Web Apps in enterprise-managed browser configurations on Windows.</li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<h4><strong>Upcoming Chrome Enterprise Core updates</strong></h4>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p>No upcoming feature announcements in this release.</p>
</div>

<div class="no-margin"><p>&nbsp;</p>

<h4><strong>Upcoming Chrome Enterprise Premium updates</strong></h4>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><strong>Custom HTTP headers</strong></p>

<p>Chrome Enterprise will soon offer custom HTTP header injection, a feature that injects custom headers into network requests matching configured URL patterns. This generic capability allows enterprises to reduce their reliance on complex SSL-inspection proxies for a variety of security workflows. For example, administrators can use this feature to enforce SaaS tenant restrictions and prevent data exfiltration. By applying these controls directly at the browser’s network stack, this functionality guarantees the injected headers cannot be modified, disabled, or bypassed by user-installed extensions.</p>

<p>This feature will operate transparently in the background with minimal impact on browsing performance. Administrators can manage this via the HttpHeaderInjection policy.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 151 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Custom HTTP headers feature becomes available on desktop platforms.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>DLP support for virtual files on ChromeOS</strong></p>

<p>On ChromeOS, files stored in non-native virtual folders (such as Microsoft OneDrive via extension-based File System Providers) were previously bypassed during enterprise file scans because they lacked a native local path.</p>

<p>With this update, Chrome will soon support Data Loss Prevention (DLP) scanning for these virtual files during user-initiated file uploads, drag-and-drop actions, and clipboard pastes. To perform the scan, ChromeOS securely streams a temporary local copy of the virtual file. Once the scan is completed and evaluated, the temporary file is immediately deleted. This update closes a security gap, ensuring consistent policy enforcement across all storage locations on ChromeOS.</p>

<p>This capability is governed by the existing, permanent <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnFileAttachedEnterpriseConnector"><u>OnFileAttachedEnterpriseConnector</u></a> policy. If you have already configured file-upload scanning for your organization, no further action is required; ChromeOS will automatically begin scanning virtual files.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 151 on ChromeOS - Feature rolls out gradually</strong></li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Enterprise file download protection on iOS</strong></p>

<p>Admins will soon be able to prevent users downloading files considered to contain sensitive data, by creating a DLP OnFileDownload rule to send a file for analysis when it is downloaded from a specific page. Based on the scanning result, it will warn or block the download if sensitive information is detected.</p>

<p>This feature can be controlled via the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnFileDownloadedEnterpriseConnector"><u>OnFileDownloadedEnterpriseConnector</u></a> Chrome Enterprise policy that enables the download connector.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 151 on iOS - Feature rolls out gradually</strong>: Feature becomes available on iOS and iPadOS.</li>
</ul>
</div>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Current ChromeOS updates</h4>

<p><a id="chromeOSA150" name="chromeOSA150"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Gemini in Class Tools&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>As early as ChromeOS 150, Class Tools allows educators to lock students to Gemini’s Guided Learning mode during class time, reducing distractions and keeping students focused on their assignments. This functionality also extends across teacher-led experiences available in Google Classroom, such as restricting test prep sessions, preventing device navigation beyond Search, and locking student screens to NotebookLM to anchor class time to approved research material.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>Available with Google Workspace for Education Plus or Teaching and Learning add-on only. For more information, see <a href="https://edu.google.com/workspace-for-education/editions/compare-editions/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Compare Editions - Google for Education</u></a>.</p>

    <p>&nbsp;</p>
    <img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/SZSrvtElDabPZEO6zghpP4KOuPYP1yRqO8elX83J7QdzRBCXDu7HZlWfesff-moahg=w800" width="800" height="1400" alt="" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/SZSrvtElDabPZEO6zghpP4KOuPYP1yRqO8elX83J7QdzRBCXDu7HZlWfesff-moahg"></li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeOSB150" name="chromeOSB150"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>End of support for Chrome Apps in Kiosk sessions&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>ChromeOS 150 is the last ChromeOS release supporting Chrome Apps in Kiosk sessions. Starting with ChromeOS 151, Chrome apps on ChromeOS will stop working in Kiosk sessions. Apps that are force-installed through the Admin console for Managed Guest sessions (MGS) and user sessions will continue to be supported</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeOSC150" name="chromeOSC150"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Local PIN and password on managed Chromebooks&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>ChromeOS 150 adds two new enterprise policies that allow users to enable local PIN and passwords for their managed Chromebooks. Additionally, Admins can configure minimum complexity requirements for local PINs or passwords. For more details on these policies, see:</p>

    <ul>
      <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AllowedLocalAuthFactors" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>AllowedLocalAuthFactors</u></a></li>

<p><a id="chromeOSD150" name="chromeOSD150"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Automatic migration for local PIN or password users&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>Starting in ChromeOS 150, a small percentage of managed Enterprise and Education users who added an account on ChromeOS in late June 2026, who configured a local PIN or password, will be automatically switched back to standard online password authentication.</p>

    <p>After updating to ChromeOS 150 and signing in, affected users will see a one-time informational screen explaining that their device authentication has reverted to their online account password. Their local PIN or password will be removed and these users will have to sign in with their online Google account authentication method.</p>

    <p><strong>Note: </strong>No action is required by Admins; this switch occurs automatically to ensure device authentication aligns with organizational identity policies. User profiles, local files, and device data remain completely unaffected.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeOSE150" name="chromeOSE150"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Isolated Web Apps unmanaged install&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>ChromeOS 150 lets users manually install Isolated Web Apps. Admins can control this feature using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#IsolatedWebAppUserInstallationEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>IsolatedWebAppUserInstallationEnabled</u></a> policy.</p>

    <p>To set the policy, open your <a href="http://admin.google.com" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Google Admin console</u></a> and navigate to <strong>Devices &gt; Chrome &gt; Apps &amp; Extensions &gt; User app settings &gt; Isolated Web App Installation</strong>.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeOSF150" name="chromeOSF150"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Enhanced </strong><strong>reauthentication mechanisms&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>ChromeOS 150 improves the reliability of reauthentication mechanisms, leading to less unexpected reauthentication requests on the login screen. This update optimizes checks and fetches for token handles stored against the user’s account.</p>

    <p>For more detail, see related policies for login frequency and reauthentication settings in <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/2657289"><u>Set Chrome policies for users or browsers&nbsp; - Chrome Enterprise and Education Help</u></a>.</p>

    <p>Starting with ChromeOS 154, ChromeOS will continue to be released every 4 weeks, but the release number will be incremented by 2 (instead of 1). This change is to align numbering with the new Chrome browser 2-week release cadence. You can find more details in the <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-two-week-release" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome for Developers</u></a> blog post.</p>

    <p>For customers on the Long-term Support channel, the duration between LTS releases is not changing; LTS will continue to release every 6 months. With the transition to the new release numbering, LTS versioning will&nbsp; increment every 12 versions. For more information, see the <a href="https://chromiumdash.appspot.com/schedule" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chromium release schedule</u></a> and <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/12239814"><u>Long-term Support (LTS) release notes</u></a> in the Chrome Enterprise and Education Help Center.</p>

<h2>Chrome browser changes &nbsp;</h2>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><strong>Chrome Profile Bootstrapping via Custom URI</strong></p>

<p>This feature introduces a new custom URI scheme (google-chrome://) that allows external applications and web portals to launch Chrome directly into a specific managed profile. If the specified profile does not exist, the user will be guided through a streamlined profile creation flow pre-populated with their work email. This enables a seamless transition for users jumping from arbitrary browsers or built-in app catalogs into a secure, managed Chrome environment. Admins can control this behavior using the <strong>ChromeURILaunchEnabled</strong> policy. Chrome 149 will offer an early preview to <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/9036081"><u>Chrome Enterprise Trusted Testers</u></a>.</p>
&nbsp;

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 149 on macOS, Windows</strong> - Early preview available to Chrome Enterprise Trusted Tester</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Remove search provider overrides from initial preferences</strong></p>

<p>From Chrome 149 onwards, the search_provider_overrides and search_provider_overrides_version properties of the <a href="https://www.chromium.org/administrators/configuring-other-preferences"><u>initial_preferences file</u></a> are no longer supported.</p>

<p>Existing profiles that had imported initial preferences will stop responding to these properties. As an alternative, admins can use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/intl/en_au/policies/#DefaultSearchProvider"><u>DefaultSearchProvider</u></a> policy.</p>
&nbsp;

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 149 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Custom spelling suggestions support</strong>&nbsp;</p>

<p>Chrome for Android is updating its spell check interface to achieve parity with the built-in Android experience. This update adds support for the Input Method Editor (IME) suggestion bar, such as the one provided by Gboard. For more information, see <a href="https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/views/touch-and-input/creating-input-method"><u>Work with IMEs on Android for Developers</u></a>.</p>
&nbsp;

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 149 on Android</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Restrict background fetch for Service Workers</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 149 restricts the ability for a Service Worker to perform downloads using the <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/background-fetch">Background Fetch API</a>. The <strong>RestrictBackgroundFetchFromServiceWorkerEnabled</strong> policy allows administrators to re-enable background fetch for cases where download-related functionality is no longer working. The policy can be set through Chrome Enterprise custom configurations. For more details, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/14749672">Set Chrome policies using the Custom Configurations page</a> in the Help Center.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 149 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong><br>
    Enterprise policy <strong>RestrictBackgroundFetchFromServiceWorkerEnabled</strong> becomes available.</li>
  <li>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows<br>
    Enterprise policy <strong>RestrictBackgroundFetchFromServiceWorkerEnabled</strong> will be deprecated</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Updated PDF file icon and description on Windows</strong></p>

<p>When Chrome is set as the default PDF handler, Chrome 149 updates the file icon displayed in Windows Explorer from the standard Chrome browser icon to a customized white document icon featuring both the Chrome logo and the text <em>PDF</em>. Additionally, the file type description in Windows Explorer changes from <em>Chrome HTML Document</em> to <em>Chrome PDF Document</em>.</p>

<p>Previously, Chrome registered PDF files under the ChromeHTML ProgID, causing PDFs to share the same icon and description as web pages. Chrome now registers under a dedicated ChromePDF ProgID. This separates PDF files visually and textually from standard HTML files. This update brings Chrome into alignment with standard Windows file-handling conventions and makes it easier for users to identify PDF files in Windows Explorer.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 149 on Windows</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Chrome for ARM64 Linux devices</strong></p>

<p>We’re excited to announce that Google will launch Chrome for ARM64 Linux devices in Q2 2026, following the successful expansion of Chrome to Arm-powered macOS devices in 2020 and Arm-powered Windows devices in 2024.</p>

<p>Launching Chrome for ARM64 Linux devices allows more users to enjoy the seamless integration of Google’s most helpful services into their browser. This move addresses the growing demand for a browsing experience that combines the benefits of the open-source Chromium project with Google's ecosystem of apps and features.</p>

<p>To read more, see this <a href="https://blog.chromium.org/2026/03/bringing-chrome-to-arm64-linux-devices.html"><u>Chromium blog</u></a> post.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 149 on Linux</strong> This is a new build of Chrome. It will become available for download once available.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Enhanced autofill</strong> From Chrome 137 onwards, users can turn on <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/answer/142893"><u>Enhanced autofill</u></a>, a feature that helps users fill out online forms more easily. On relevant forms, Chrome can use AI to better understand the form and to then offer users the option to automatically fill in the form using previously saved info. Admins can control the feature using the existing <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> policy and a new <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AutofillPredictionSettings"><u>AutofillPredictionSettings</u></a> policy.</p>

<p>Enhanced autofill will also be available to users of Chrome on Android (Chrome 148 onwards) and Chrome on iOS (Chrome 149 onwards).</p>
&nbsp;

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 137 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 140 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> The existing <em>Autofill with AI</em> feature will be renamed to <em>Enhanced autofill</em>. This feature allows users to save and fill additional types of information, and with this update becomes available in more countries and languages.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 148 on Android</strong> Enhanced autofill will be made available to users of Chrome on Android.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 149 on iOS</strong> Enhanced autofill will be made available to users of Chrome on iOS.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> Enhanced autofill will be available to all users by default, including the highest-quality form field predictions, as it will be migrated to use Private Inference for data processing.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Update to No HTTPS warning</strong> The warning displayed when a user opts in to the <strong>Always Use Secure Connections</strong> on chrome://settings/security is changing from an interstitial to a dialog. Full page load remains blocked, and the functionality remains the same. The URL content security indicator on the warning is changing from the *indicator to the broken lock. Some users may see this warning automatically when visiting HTTP sites. Users can opt in to the warning on chrome://settings/security.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 141 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> New warning design on desktop platforms.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 149 on Android</strong> Similar updated warning design on Android, using a warning bubble instead of a full interstitial.</li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

  <li><strong>New policies in Chrome browser&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

<h2>Chrome Enterprise Core changes</h2>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>No updates in Chrome 149.</li>
</ul>

<div class="no-margin"><h2>Chrome Enterprise Premium changes</h2>

<p>Read more about the differences between <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/products/chrome-enterprise-premium" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Enterprise Core and Chrome Enterprise Premium</u></a>.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><span>&nbsp;</span></p>

<p><strong>Microsoft Information Protection (MIP) label integration</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 149 can now understand and enforce Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies based on Microsoft Information Protection (MIP) sensitivity labels applied to Office 365 documents.</p>

<p>To enable this feature, administrators must authorize the connection between Chrome Enterprise Premium and their Microsoft Azure tenant using the new Microsoft 365 card in the <strong>Data Connectors</strong> section of the <strong>Google Admin console</strong>. Once connected, admins can create permanent DLP rules using these labels to block, warn, or audit user actions, for example:</p>

<ul>
  <li>copying and pasting to external sites, specifically targeting risks like GenAI data leakage</li>
  <li>downloading</li>
  <li>printing</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 149 on ChromeOS, macOS, Windows</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually Microsoft Information Protection (MIP) label integration becomes available on Windows, macOS and ChromeOS.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>New policy setting for DataControlRules</strong></p>

<p>Chrome is enhancing the existing <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DataControlsRules"><u>DataControlsRules</u></a> policy by introducing a new setting labeled <strong>Pasting restrictions across management boundaries</strong>. This update provides admins with a context-based mechanism to block against sensitive web content being pasted into or from managed Chrome profiles without requiring specific source or destination URLs.</p>

<p>Starting in Chrome 149, administrators can use new settings in the <strong>Google Admin console</strong> to establish data boundaries specifically for:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Incognito mode</li>
  <li>Unmanaged Chrome profiles</li>
  <li>Applications outside of Chrome browser</li>
</ul>

<p>This enhancement strengthens data loss prevention for Chrome Enterprise Premium customers by preventing corporate data exfiltration into unmanaged environments. To ensure transparency, managed users will receive immediate on-browser notifications if a paste action is restricted by these organizational security policies.</p>

<p>For more details, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/2657289#data_controls"><u>Set Chrome policies for users or browsers - Data Controls</u></a>.</p>
&nbsp;

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 149 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, macOS, Windows</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Telemetry for extensions in third-party SIEM tools</strong></p>

<p>Chrome is expanding telemetry capabilities for extension security, by allowing managed events to be exported to all supported third-party Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) platforms via the Chrome Reporting Connector.</p>

<p>Extension telemetry events monitor risky browser behaviors like:</p>

<ul>
  <li>dynamic code injection</li>
  <li>process invocation</li>
  <li>unauthorized data access</li>
</ul>

<p>Previously, these events were restricted solely to Google Security Operations (SecOps). With this update, enterprise administrators can route these high-fidelity security signals to their preferred external SIEM provider for centralized threat correlation and incident investigation.</p>

<p>To safeguard user privacy and optimize performance, extension telemetry events are handled as follows:</p>

<ul>
  <li>evaluated against a stateless filter</li>
  <li>exist purely in memory without local disk logging</li>
  <li>are completely deactivated within Incognito profiles</li>
</ul>

<p>This capability is restricted to organizations with active Chrome Enterprise Premium licensing. If a managed device does not possess a valid license, extension telemetry events will not be automatically generated and transmitted.</p>

<p>Administrators can configure and opt in to this feature using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnSecurityEventEnterpriseConnector"><u>OnSecurityEventEnterpriseConnector</u></a> policy.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 149 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Asynchronous file hashing for large DLP uploads</strong></p>

<p>In Chrome 149, Chrome Enterprise Premium optimizes how it processes files larger than 50MB during Data Loss Prevention (DLP) scans. This update moves the file hash computation to a background process, thereby significantly reducing file upload times and browser delays for users. When the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnFileAttachedEnterpriseConnector">OnFileAttachedEnterpriseConnector</a> or <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnFileDownloadedEnterpriseConnector">OnFileDownloadedEnterpriseConnector</a> policies are enabled, this performance improvement applies automatically. Full file hashes will continue to be securely generated and sent for reporting purposes once the background task completes.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 149 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows - Feature rolls out gradually</strong></li>
</ul>
</div>

<p class="align-right"><a href="#top">↑ back to top</a> &nbsp;</p>

<h2>Coming soon</h2>

<p><strong>Note:</strong> The items listed below are experimental or planned updates. They might change, be delayed, or canceled before launching to the Stable channel.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Upcoming Chrome browser changes</h4>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><strong>Always use secure connections by default</strong></p>

<p>Prior to enabling it by default for all users, Chrome 150 will enable <strong>Always use secure connections</strong> for users who have opted in to <a href="https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/11577602"><u>Enhanced Safe Browsing protections in Chrome</u></a>.</p>

<p>Chrome 154 will enable the <strong>Always use secure connections</strong> setting in the <em>public sites only</em> mode by default. This means Chrome will ask for the user's permission before the first access to any public site without HTTPS. Public sites are defined as sites that have a globally unique name, and excludes direct navigation to <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1918"><u>RFC 1918</u></a> addresses (192.168.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8, and so on), as well as shortnames such as go/.</p>

<p>If you are a website developer or IT professional, and you have users who may be impacted by this feature, we very strongly recommend enabling the <strong>Always use secure connections</strong> setting today to help identify sites that you may need to work to migrate. Admins can use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HttpAllowlist"><u>HttpAllowlist</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HttpsOnlyMode"><u>HttpsOnlyMode</u></a> policies to override this behavior.</p>

<p>For more information, see our <a href="https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/docs/security/ask-before-http/ask-before-http-adoption-guide.md"><u>adoption guide</u></a> and <a href="https://security.googleblog.com/2025/10/https-by-default.html"><u>announcement blog post</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually Enable "Always use secure connections" for users who have opted in to Enhanced Safe Browsing. This applies to Desktop only.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 154 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually Enable "Always use secure connections" by default for all users.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Deprecation and removal of Privacy Sandbox APIs</strong></p>

<p>Chrome has <a href="https://privacysandbox.com/news/update-on-plans-for-privacy-sandbox-technologies/"><u>recently announced</u></a> that the current approach to third-party cookies is to be maintained, following which, we plan to deprecate and remove the following APIs:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Topics</li>
  <li>Protected Audience</li>
  <li>Shared Storage</li>
  <li>Attribution Reporting</li>
  <li>Private Aggregation</li>
  <li>Related Web Sites</li>
  <li>requestStorageAccessFor</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p>The following are the enterprise policies associated with the above APIs.</p>

<ul>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PrivacySandboxSiteEnabledAdsEnabled"><u>PrivacySandboxSiteEnabledAdsEnabled</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PrivacySandboxAdTopicsEnabled"><u>PrivacySandboxAdTopicsEnabled</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PrivacySandboxAdMeasurementEnabled"><u>PrivacySandboxAdMeasurementEnabled</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#RelatedWebsiteSetsOverrides"><u>RelatedWebsiteSetsOverrides</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#RelatedWebsiteSetsEnabled"><u>RelatedWebsiteSetsEnabled</u></a></li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p>Deprecation began with Chrome 144, and removal is planned for Chrome 150. After deprecation, the APIs will continue to exist, and most users will see no disruptions. However, some users who rely on server-side integrations (such as k-anonymity server, or coordinators) will see a break in the services. We have proactively reached out to users of the APIs with our deprecation plans. At the time of removal, Chrome 150, all the policies associated with these APIs will also be removed.</p>

<p>None of the APIs are enabled by default to enterprise users. Enterprise teams may want to review the status for any managed profile in their <strong>Admin console</strong>.</p>
&nbsp;

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 144 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> Deprecation launch</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> APIs and the associated policies removal</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Disable SVG filters on plugins and cross-origin or restricted iframes</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 150 will prevent Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) filters from being applied to cross-origin or restricted iFrames (for example, sandboxed ones) and embedded plugins (for example, PDFs). When a frame or plugin would be painted with an SVG filter effect, the effect tree is traversed to find the highest ancestor without SVG filters, and that effect is then applied instead.</p>
&nbsp;

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong> No rollout step</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>ML-DSA in TLS</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 150 adds support for Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) signing algorithms and certificates in TLS. This will enable the use of ML-DSA (post-quantum) certificates in chrome://certificate-manager, and associated enterprise policies. There are no changes to the Chrome Root Store. The relevant policies are:</p>

<ul>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#CACertificateManagementAllowed"><u>CACertificateManagementAllowed</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#CACertificates"><u>CACertificates</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#CACertificatesWithConstraints"><u>CACertificatesWithConstraints</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#CADistrustedCertificates"><u>CADistrustedCertificates</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#CAHintCertificates"><u>CAHintCertificates</u></a></li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#CAPlatformIntegrationEnabled"><u>CAPlatformIntegrationEnabled</u></a></li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p>This feature will be available on all non-iOS platforms.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong> Support for ML-DSA in TLS enabled by default. Users or administrators must explicitly configure a trusted root for ML-DSA to be used, as it is not currently possible to issue a publicly trusted ML-DSA certificate.</li>
</ul>
