<p><strong>New Chrome Desktop visual updates</strong></p>

<p>With Google's design language evolving for the AI era, we have an opportunity to modernize the desktop browser's UI across operating systems and to reduce clutter. The first wave of updates will roll out with Chrome 150, including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>A <em>glass</em> effect tab strip that allows desktop backgrounds to subtly show through.</li>
  <li>Updated iconography with softer edges and animations on buttons like the three dot Chrome menu and page refresh.</li>
  <li>Context menus will be simplified by removing or re-homing low usage and duplicative items.</li>
  <li>Settings, Downloads, and Bookmark pages will get a visual reskin to align with the latest design language.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
  <li>Chrome 150 on Windows, macOS: "glass" effect on tab strip</li>
  <li>Chrome 150 on Windows, maxOS, Linux: updated iconography (increased roundedness)</li>
  <li>Chrome 150 on Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS: simplified tab strip and context menus, updated tab group colors, visual update to chrome://settings, downloads, and bookmarks, updated dark mode color</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Opaque origin for data: URLs</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 150 updates how Dedicated and Shared Workers handle <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2397"><u>data: URLs</u></a>. Rather than automatically inheriting the security origin of the script or page that created them, these workers will now be assigned a unique opaque origin.</p>

<p>This alignment with the worker <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/2021/NOTE-workers-20210128/#worker"><u>HTML specification</u></a> enhances security by isolating these workers from the creator's same-origin state, preventing them from accessing sensitive data via mechanisms like BroadcastChannel or same-origin storage. To maintain correct isolation boundaries, these workers still reside within the same storage partition (for example, by preserving the top-level site or nonce) as their creator.</p>

<p>This security adjustment is enabled by default across desktop and mobile platforms. Administrators can review or verify security boundaries via their centralized configurations. For technical implementation details and specification references, see Step 3 of the <a href="https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/workers.html#script-settings-for-workers"><u>HTML Living Standard Worker Settings</u></a>.</p>
&nbsp;

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong> No rollout step</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>PWA origin migration</strong></p>

<p>When a user installs a Progressive Web App (PWA), its identity and security context are tightly bound to its web origin, for example, app.example.com. This presents a significant challenge for developers who need to change their PWA's origin due to rebranding, domain restructuring, or technical re-architecture. Currently, such a change forces users to manually uninstall the old app and reinstall the new one, leading to a disruptive experience and potential user loss. Chrome 150 introduces a mechanism for developers to seamlessly migrate an installed PWA to a new, same-site origin, preserving user trust and permissions.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebAppInstallForceList"><u>WebAppInstallForceList</u></a> policy will block migration. Since enterprise policies around web applications are primarily based on URLs and origins, there is a risk that a migration would bypass certain policies an admin might have configured. No migration will be offered to the user when an app is force-installed by their enterprise administrator, and instead a banner will be shown explaining this to the user.</p>
&nbsp;

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Windows, macOS, Linux</strong> No rollout step</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Redesign of profile creation flows</strong></p>

<p>In Chrome 148, existing profile creation flows on Desktop (Windows only) get a visual update to provide a contemporary and streamlined onboarding experience. During First Run and Secondary profile creation, we introduce a new design to the onboarding flow, which includes management screens, to harmonize with the current Chrome brand identity.</p>

<p>This update only includes visual improvements. There are no functional changes to the onboarding process, and your existing workflows and policies remain unaffected.</p>

<p>Chrome 150 introduces this visual update on Desktop for macOS and Linux.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 148 on Windows</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Linux, macOS</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Chrome will remove support for macOS 12</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 150 will be the last release to support macOS 12; Chrome 151+ will no longer support macOS 12, which is outside of its support window with Apple. Running on a supported operating system is essential to maintaining security.</p>

<p>On Macs running macOS 12, Chrome will continue to work, showing a warning infobar, but will not update any further. If users wish to have Chrome updated, they need to update their computer to a supported version of macOS.</p>

<p>For new installations of Chrome 151+, macOS 13+ will be required.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 151 on Windows, macOS, Linux</strong> No rollout step</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Process isolation on Windows</strong></p>

<p>Chrome will apply Windows security Access Control Lists (ACLs) to prevent other applications from reading or injecting into Chrome's memory space. This may cause interoperability issues with older antivirus, DLP, or accessibility software.</p>

<p>Admins will be able to control and disable this feature with the upcoming <strong>WindowsProcessIsolation</strong> policy. Process isolation will eventually be enabled by default on all Windows installations.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 151 on Windows</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>SafeBrowsing API v4 to v5 migration</strong></p>

<p>Chrome calls into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/v4"><u>SafeBrowsing v4 API</u></a> will be migrated to call into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference"><u>v5 API</u></a> instead. The method names are also different between v4 and v5. If admins have any v4-specific URL allowlisting to allow network requests to https://safebrowsing.googleapis.com/v4*, these should be modified to allow network requests to the whole domain instead: safebrowsing.googleapis.com. Otherwise, rejected network requests to the v5 API will cause security regressions for users. For more details, see <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference/Migration.From.V4"><u>Migration From V4 - Safe Browsing</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 151 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Deprecate and remove XSLT</strong></p>

<p><a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/xslt-10/"><u>XSLT v1.0</u></a>, which all browsers adhere to, was standardized in 1999. In the meantime, XSLT has evolved to v2.0 and v3.0, adding features, and growing apart from the old version frozen into browsers. This lack of advancement, coupled with the rise of JavaScript libraries and frameworks that offer more flexible and powerful DOM manipulation, has led to a significant decline in the use of client-side XSLT. Its role within the web browser has been largely superseded by JavaScript-based technologies, such as JSON and React.</p>

<p>Chromium uses the libxslt library to process these transformations, and <a href="https://discourse.gnome.org/t/stepping-down-as-libxslt-maintainer/27615"><u>libxslt was unmaintained</u></a> for ~6 months of 2025. Libxslt is a complex, aging C codebase of the type notoriously susceptible to memory safety vulnerabilities like buffer overflows, which can lead to arbitrary code execution. Because client-side XSLT is now a niche, rarely-used feature, these libraries receive far less maintenance and security scrutiny than core JavaScript engines, yet they represent a direct, potent attack surface for processing untrusted web content. Indeed, XSLT is the source of several recent high-profile security exploits that continue to put browser users at risk.</p>

<p>For these reasons, Chromium (along with both other browser engines) plans to deprecate and remove XSLT from the web platform. For more details, see this <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/deprecating-xslt"><u>Chrome for Developers article</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 143 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> Deprecation (but not removal) of the APIs.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> Origin Trial (OT) and Enterprise Policy go live for testing. These allow sites and enterprises to continue using features past the removal date.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 158 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> XSLT stops functioning on Stable releases, for all users other than Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy participants.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 176 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy stop functioning. XSLT is disabled for all users.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Local network access restrictions</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 142 restricted the ability to make requests to the user's local network, gated behind a permission prompt. A local network request is any request from a public website to a local IP address or loopback, or from a local website (for example, intranet) to loopback.</p>

<p>Gating the ability for websites to perform these requests behind a permission mitigates the risk of cross-site request forgery attacks against local network devices such as routers, and reduces the ability of sites to use these requests to fingerprint the user's local network.</p>

<p>This permission is restricted to secure contexts. If granted, the permissions additionally relaxes mixed content blocking for local network requests (since many local devices are not able to obtain publicly trusted TLS certificates for various reasons).</p>

<p>This work supersedes a prior effort called <a href="https://chromestatus.com/feature/5737414355058688"><u>Private Network Access</u></a>, which used preflight requests to have local devices opt in. For more information on this feature, see <a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QQkqehw8umtAgz5z0um7THx-aoU251p705FbIQjDuGs/edit?usp=sharing"><u>Adapting your website for new Local Network Access restrictions in Chrome</u></a>.</p>

<p>Chrome 145 introduced more granular permissions for websites requesting access to a user's local network. The previous single local-network-access permission is being split into two distinct permissions:</p>

<ul>
  <li>local-network: Grants access to IP addresses in the local network space (for example, intranets, internal devices).</li>
  <li>loopback-network: Grants access to loopback IP addresses (for example, localhost, 127.0.0.1).</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p>The old local-network permission will remain as an alias, ensuring existing configurations and permissions policies continue to function as expected.</p>

<p>This change provides both users and Admins with more precise control over how websites interact with internal network resources. Current enterprise policies managing local network access will not be affected by this change.</p>

<p>Chrome 146 introduces two new enterprise policies for managing local network access restrictions: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides"><u>LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled"><u>LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled</u></a>. These policies can be set using <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/14749672"><u>custom configurations</u></a>.</p>
&nbsp;

<p>Chrome 147 expands Local Network Access restrictions to include WebSocket and WebTransport connections.</p>
&nbsp;

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 145 on Android, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong> The permission split is rolled out.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 146 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong> Two new enterprise policies will be available for managing local network access restrictions:</li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides"><u>LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides</u></a> could be used to mark IPv4 and IPv6 address blocks as public or private. IP ranges that are treated as public will not cause permission prompts when accessed by other pages. For example, CGNAT 100.64.0.0/10 can be marked as public. This is useful for certain VPN and proxy setups. Marking 0.0.0.0/0 &nbsp;and ::/0 as public is equivalent to disabling the local network access restrictions.</li>
  <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled"><u>LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled</u></a> can be used to cause the LNA permission to be automatically delegated to iframes by the parent frame, without requiring explicit annotation of the child iframes. This is useful in situations where local network access is performed by an embedded SaaS tool inside of a different SaaS tool. This includes certain locally hosted documentation and knowledgebase software.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> Local Network Access restrictions expanded to include WebSocket and WebTransport connections.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut"><u>LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut</u></a> policy will be removed.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>PostQuantum cryptography for DTLS in WebRTC</strong></p>

<p>This feature will enable the use of PostQuantum Cryptography (PQC) with WebRTC connections. The motivation for PQC is to get WebRTC media traffic up to date with the latest cryptography protocols and prevent <em>Harvest Now to Crack Later</em> scenarios.</p>

<p>Admins will be able to control this feature using an enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement"><u>WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement</u></a>, to allow enterprise users to opt out of PQC. The policy is temporary and is planned to be removed by Chrome 152.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 142 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong> Remove <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement"><u>WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement</u></a> enterprise policy</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Moving to a 2-week release cycle</strong></p>

<p>From September 2026 (Chrome 153), Chrome will move to a 2-week release cycle, from the current four-week cycle. The web platform is constantly advancing, and our goal at Chrome is to ensure developers and users have immediate access to the latest capabilities, fixes, and performance improvements. Building on our history of adapting our release process to match the demands of a modern web, we are announcing this significant step to further increase our development velocity and Chrome Stable is moving to a 2-week release cycle. You can find more details in the <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-two-week-release"><u>Chrome for Developers</u></a> blog post.</p>

<p>Extended Stable is available for customers who might have concerns about the maintenance costs. For more information about Extended Stable, see this <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16942104"><u>Help Center</u></a> article. The 2-week Stable option remains the most secure choice and should be utilized if security is a larger concern than maintenance costs.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 153 on Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> Chrome moves to a 2-week release cycle</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Disallow spaces in non-file:// URL hosts</strong></p>

<p>According to the <a href="https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#forbidden-host-code-point"><u>URL Standard specification</u></a> URL hosts cannot contain the space character, but currently URL parsing in Chromium allows spaces in the host. This causes Chromium to fail several tests included in the <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/websockets?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2024-websockets"><u>Interop2024 HTTPS URLs for WebSocket</u></a> and <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/url?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2023-url"><u>URL focus</u></a> areas. To bring Chromium into spec compliance, we would like to remove spaces from URL hosts altogether, but a difficulty with this is that they are used in the host part in Windows file:// URLs. For more details, see this <a href="https://github.com/whatwg/url/issues/599"><u>Github discussion</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 157 on Android, ChromeOS, LaCrOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong></li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Isolated Web Apps</strong></p>

<p><a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/iwa/introduction"><u>Isolated Web Apps</u></a> (IWAs) are an extension of existing work on PWA installation and Web Packaging that provide stronger protections against server compromise and other tampering that is necessary for developers of security-sensitive applications. Rather than being hosted on live web servers and fetched over HTTPS, these applications are packaged into Web Bundles, signed by their developer, and distributed to end-users through one or more of the potential methods described in the <a href="https://github.com/WICG/isolated-web-apps/blob/main/README.md"><u>explainer</u></a>.</p>

<p>In Chrome 128, IWAs became installable through an admin policy only on enterprise-managed ChromeOS devices.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 161 on Windows</strong> This rollout adds support for Isolated Web Apps in enterprise-managed browser configurations on Windows.</li>
</ul>

<h4><strong>Upcoming Chrome Enterprise Core updates</strong></h4>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><strong>Gen AI and SaaS app usage reporting</strong></p>

<p>As early as Chrome 147, admins will have access to a new <strong>Gen AI and SaaS app usage</strong> reporting feature in the Google Admin console. This report brings visibility into their organization's use of generative AI tools and SaaS sites, allowing admins to monitor usage of their enterprise IT resources.</p>

<p>This report is available for <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/products/chrome-enterprise-core/"><u>Chrome Enterprise Core (CEC)</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/products/chrome-enterprise-premium/"><u>Chrome Enterprise Premium (CEP)</u></a> customers only.</p>

<p>This new report tracks usage for popular Gen AI and enterprise SaaS websites in Chrome, providing metrics on visits, unique managed profiles, unique managed browsers, and access to sensitive content transfer events. With these insights, admins can assess risk and restrict usage by making informed licensing decisions or creating usage restrictions, such as Data Loss Prevention (DLP) rules.</p>

<p>Chrome 147 allows a <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/engage/trusted-testers/sign-up/"><u>Trusted Tester</u></a> preview, with the feature gradually rolling out in Chrome 150.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> - Early preview available to Chrome Enterprise Trusted Tester</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually</li>

<p><strong>SSO with Microsoft Entra ID on Android</strong></p>

<p>Chrome on Android now supports seamless Single Sign-On (SSO) with Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD). This feature allows users to access Microsoft web applications, such as Outlook and SharePoint, without repeatedly entering credentials, if they are already signed into a Microsoft app on the same device. This brings Chrome on Android to feature parity with Chrome on Windows and macOS.</p>

<p>Admins can use <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AndroidEntraSsoEnabled"><u>AndroidEntraSsoEnabled</u></a> policy to control this functionality, which is disabled by default. To work, the device must have a Microsoft broker app installed (such as Microsoft Authenticator, Intune Company Portal, or Link to Windows) and the user must be signed into a Microsoft app. This feature is an add-on for managed users and improves user productivity by reducing authentication friction while leveraging secure, on-device credential handling.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Android</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually Single Sign-On (SSO) with Microsoft Entra ID becomes available on Android</li>
</ul>

<h4><strong>Upcoming Chrome Enterprise Premium updates</strong></h4>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><strong>Custom HTTP headers</strong></p>

<p>Chrome Enterprise now offers custom HTTP header injection, a feature that injects custom headers into network requests matching configured URL patterns. This generic capability allows enterprises to reduce their reliance on complex SSL-inspection proxies for a variety of security workflows. For example, administrators can use this feature to enforce SaaS tenant restrictions and prevent data exfiltration. By applying these controls directly at the browser’s network stack, this functionality guarantees the injected headers cannot be modified, disabled, or bypassed by user-installed extensions.</p>

<p>This feature operates transparently in the background with minimal impact on browsing performance. Administrators can manage this via the HttpHeaderInjection policy.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> Custom HTTP headers feature becomes available on desktop platforms</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Screenshot protections</strong></p>

<p>Admins can prevent users from taking screenshots or screen sharing specific web pages considered to contain sensitive data. Admins create a DLP URL filtering rule to block users taking screenshots or screen sharing specific URLs or categories of URLs.</p>

<p>This feature can be controlled via the same <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#EnterpriseRealTimeUrlCheckMode"><u>EnterpriseRealTimeUrlCheckMode</u></a> Chrome Enterprise policy that enables all real-time URL lookups.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 129 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> Trusted Tester program</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 131 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong> Feature rolls out</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on iOS</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually Feature becomes available on iOS and iPadOS</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Data Controls enforcement for context menu search</strong></p>

<p>Chrome is enhancing the existing <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DataControlsRules"><u>DataControlsRules</u></a> policy by introducing enforcement on the "Search [Default Search Engine] for ..." context menu item. This update provides admins with a mechanism to secure data against a known exfiltration vector, as this search action previously bypassed copy restrictions.</p>

<p>Administrators can rely on their existing <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DataControlsRules"><u>DataControlsRules</u></a> to evaluate the current tab's URL before allowing a context menu search. This enhancement strengthens data loss prevention for enterprise customers by preventing corporate data exfiltration without requiring the creation of new policies. To ensure transparency, managed users will receive an immediate warning dialog if the action triggers a WARN rule, or the menu item will be completely hidden if blocked by organizational security policies.</p>

<p>For more details, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/2657289#data_controls"><u>Set Chrome policies for users or browsers - Data Controls</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 151 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong></li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Enterprise file download protection on iOS</strong></p>

<p>Admins can prevent users from downloading files considered to contain sensitive data by creating a DLP OnFileDownload rule to send a file for analysis when it is downloaded from a specific page. Based on the scanning result, it will warn or block the download if sensitive information is detected.</p>

<p>This feature can be controlled via the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnFileDownloadedEnterpriseConnector"><u>OnFileDownloadedEnterpriseConnector</u></a> Chrome Enterprise policy that enables the download connector.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 151 on iOS</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually Feature becomes available on iOS and iPadOS</li>
</ul>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Current ChromeOS updates</h4>

<p><a id="chromeOSA149" name="chromeOSA149"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Locate managed ChromeOS device&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>Using a new remote <strong>Locate device</strong> command, administrators can now better secure and recover lost or stolen hardware. When a ChromeOS device is disabled using the Admin console, admins can choose to enable location tracking. This allows the Admin console to detect the approximate location of the device as soon as it connects to the Internet. To prioritize user privacy, a clear notification and lock screen message inform the user that their location is being shared. Location data is only accessible for 24 hours before expiring. This enhancement provides a critical tool for fleet management while maintaining transparency and data security.</p>
    <img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/kKnsbk07GyXEug2zs19j10H_s5a_EB8Yh9KhDGlgZgfrKwPc4tSr4x6ir9rrvx6aSio=w895" width="958" height="542" alt="" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/kKnsbk07GyXEug2zs19j10H_s5a_EB8Yh9KhDGlgZgfrKwPc4tSr4x6ir9rrvx6aSio"></li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeOSB149" name="chromeOSB149"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Connectivity troubleshooting&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>ChromeOS has a built-in <strong>Diagnostics</strong> app, which allows users to troubleshoot their issues. To open the <strong>Diagnostics</strong> app, use this key sequence:</p>

    <ul>
      <li>[Ctrl] + Search Key + Esc&nbsp;</li>
    </ul>

    <p>ChromeOS 149 adds a <strong>Connectivity</strong> troubleshooting function to the <strong>Diagnostics</strong> app, to help users diagnose connectivity problems to a pre-defined list of Google services. This tool helps troubleshoot customer networking-related problems, such as the inability to access specific Google services.</p>
    <img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/2IZpu9ZBf92HNrkQQrAelFR_K4tqH-OQ5cCBXX6auqr3L78L1v0n5jsHXnrRdeskxw=w848" width="848" height="560" alt="" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/2IZpu9ZBf92HNrkQQrAelFR_K4tqH-OQ5cCBXX6auqr3L78L1v0n5jsHXnrRdeskxw"></li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeOSC149" name="chromeOSC149"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Accessibility settings sync&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>ChromeOS 149 introduces synchronization for the following <strong>Accessibility</strong> settings:</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Reduced animations</li>
      <li>Caption customization&nbsp;</li>
    </ul>

    <p>These settings can now be synced for a user across all ChromeOS devices where the user is signed in. This feature helps reduce friction during setup of a new device, by syncing accessibility settings from the old device first.&nbsp;In future releases, more <strong>Accessibility</strong> settings will be synced in this way.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>In&nbsp;ChromeOS<strong> Settings</strong>, select <strong>Privacy and security &gt; Sync and Google services &gt; Manage what you sync &gt; Sync data</strong>,&nbsp;and then toggle the <strong>Settings </strong>option as required.&nbsp;</li>
      <li>For managed users, Admins can control Accessibility settings sync by adding or removing the <b>preferences</b>&nbsp;option as required in the&nbsp;<a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SyncTypesListDisabled"><u>SyncTypesListDisabled</u></a> policy.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Upcoming ChromeOS changes</h4>

<p><a id="upChromeOSA149" name="upChromeOSA149"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Enhanced </strong><strong>reauthentication mechanisms</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>ChromeOS 150 improves the reliability of reauthentication mechanisms, leading to less unexpected reauthentication requests on the login screen. This update optimizes checks and fetches for token handles stored against the user’s account.</p>

    <p>For more detail, see related policies for login frequency and reauthentication settings in <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/2657289"><u>Set Chrome policies for users or browsers&nbsp; - Chrome Enterprise and Education Help</u></a>.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeOSB149" name="upChromeOSB149"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Enhanced local authentication for managed ChromeOS devices</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>Administrators can now allow Chrome Enterprise and Education users to set up local PINs and passwords. This reduces reliance on password scraping and enables a smoother, passwordless-style experience for subsequent sign-ins. To ensure security, admins can define specific complexity requirements (Low, Medium, or High) for these local factors.</p>

    <p>Settings are managed using new policies in the <strong>Admin console</strong>. When requirements change, users are notified to update their credentials during their next session. This update simplifies the sign-in flow for third-party Identity Providers and ensures that even during account recovery, local security standards are strictly maintained.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeOSC149" name="upChromeOSC149"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Isolated Web Apps unmanaged install</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>ChromeOS 150 lets users manually install Isolated Web Apps. Admins can control this feature using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#IsolatedWebAppUserInstallationEnabled"><u>IsolatedWebAppUserInstallationEnabled</u></a> policy.</p>

    <p>To set the policy, open your <a href="http://admin.google.com"><u>Google Admin console</u></a> &nbsp;and navigate to <strong>Devices &gt; Chrome &gt; Apps &amp; Extensions &gt; User app settings &gt; Isolated Web App Installation</strong>.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeOSD149" name="upChromeOSD149"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Unframed display mode for Isolated Web Apps</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>ChromeOS 150 introduces the unframed display mode that extends the Isolated Web App (IWA) client area to encompass the entire window, including the regions normally reserved for the title bar and system window controls. This provides developers with complete control over the application's visual layout, enabling bespoke, immersive experiences and custom window branding.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeOSE149" name="upChromeOSE149"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Inverted color option for mouse cursor</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>ChromeOS already allows users to change their mouse cursor size and color. ChromeOS will soon add a new color option that inverts the content underneath the cursor. This can be especially helpful for users with large cursor sizes, because content underneath the cursor is still visible.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeOSF149" name="upChromeOSF149"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>ChromeOS 150 includes n</strong><strong>ext available long-term candidate (LTC) release&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>ChromeOS 150, due for release on Tuesday, July 21, 2026, includes the next available LTC release. For more details, see the <a href="https://chromiumdash.appspot.com/schedule"><u>Chromium release schedule</u></a> and <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/11333726"><u>Long-term Support (LTS) on ChromeOS</u></a> in the Chrome Enterprise and Education Help Center.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeOSG149" name="upChromeOSG149"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Updates blocked for certain ChromeOS Flex devices&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>From ChromeOS 150 onwards, we will begin blocking updates for devices unable to meet the minimum requirements for the Chrome Browser. This will affect devices using the following:</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Intel and AMD graphics from 2010 and older&nbsp;</li>
      <li>Nvidia graphics from 2014 and older&nbsp;</li>
    </ul>

    <p>This does not affect any <a href="https://support.google.com/chromeosflex/answer/11513094" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>certified devices</u></a>. If unexpected devices are affected, reach out to Google <a href="https://support.google.com/chromeosflex/answer/4594885" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ChromeOS Flex support</u></a>.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeOSH149" name="upChromeOSH149"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Upcoming change to ChromeOS release numbering&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>Starting with ChromeOS 154, ChromeOS will continue to be released every 4 weeks, but the release number will be incremented by 2 (instead of 1). This change is to align numbering with the new Chrome browser 2-week release cadence. You can find more details in the <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-two-week-release"><u>Chrome for Developers</u></a> blog post.</p>

    <p>For customers on the Long-term Support channel, the duration between LTS releases is not changing; LTS will continue to release every 6 months. With the transition to the new release numbering, LTS versioning will&nbsp; increment every 12 versions. For more information, see the <a href="https://chromiumdash.appspot.com/schedule"><u>Chromium release schedule</u></a> and <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/12239814"><u>Long-term Support (LTS) release notes</u></a> in the Chrome Enterprise and Education Help Center.</p>

    <p><img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/k8mx9CikAVGLAYHrS3DotQTdRGhK5T5k5-qXtv52-S-3n4nTRoxq6izsmJU_pfycS3A=w895" width="2048" height="854" alt="" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/k8mx9CikAVGLAYHrS3DotQTdRGhK5T5k5-qXtv52-S-3n4nTRoxq6izsmJU_pfycS3A"></p>
  </li>
</ul>
</div>

<h2>Chrome browser changes &nbsp;</h2>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Gemini in Chrome&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Gemini is now integrated into Chrome on macOS, Windows and selective ChromeOS devices, and can understand the content of your current page. Users can now seamlessly get key takeaways, clarify concepts, and find answers, all without leaving their Chrome tab. This integration includes both chat—where users can interact with Gemini via text, and <em>Gemini Live</em>, with which users can interact with Gemini via voice.</p>

    <p>In Chrome 143, <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16291696" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Gemini in Chrome</u></a> started to roll out to most Google Workspace users with access to the Gemini app in the US. Admins can turn off this feature (value 1) using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiSettings</u></a> policy or by using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> (value 2). For more details, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16291696" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Gemini in Chrome</u></a> in the Help Center or this <a href="https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/chrome-enterprise/supercharging-employee-productivity-with-ai-securely-with-gemini-in-chrome-enterprise" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>blog post</u></a>.</p>

    <p>Also in Chrome 143, we announced the multi-tab context feature. Gemini in Chrome can now see more of your opened tabs (10 max) so you can ask questions across multiple pages to help you compare, find information more efficiently. Gemini in Chrome also serves as a productivity agent. Gemini in Chrome automatically uses public information from these Google services: Google Search, Google Maps, YouTube. With your permission, Gemini in Chrome can help you connect your personal information and content in Google Workspace services (Gmail, Drive, Keep, Calendar, and Tasks).</p>

    <p>In Chrome 144, auto browse in Gemini in Chrome was made available to some users (non-enterprise). An enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiActOnWebSettings</u></a> will be available at launch.</p>
    <img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/tzECavmDds71fAkpXrShS2ODB9cLnbdgds98TZLfgZoN4K_lKBIuh6LW_vp-Bpe_K-s=w895" width="1004" height="567" alt="" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/tzECavmDds71fAkpXrShS2ODB9cLnbdgds98TZLfgZoN4K_lKBIuh6LW_vp-Bpe_K-s">

    <p>For more details, see the rollout steps below.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 144 on macOS, Windows: Auto browse in Gemini in Chrome available to some users (non-enterprise). Enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiActOnWebSettings</u></a> will be available at launch. Image upload context menu item available to enterprise users. Feature will respect rules set via the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DataControlsRules" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DataControlsRules</u></a> policy and the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnBulkDataEntryEnterpriseConnector" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>OnBulkDataEntryEnterpriseConnector</u></a> settings.</li>
      <li>Chrome 144 on macOS, Windows: Gemini in Chrome allows some 3P tools that are available as Gemini Extensions to be called.</li>
      <li>Chrome 145 on ChromeOS, macOS, Windows: Gemini in Chrome is now available to users in US, Canada, New Zealand and India in 50+ languages. More details in <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16291696" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>this</u></a> help center article.</li>
      <li>Chrome 147 on ChromeOS, macOS, Windows: As early as Chrome 147 on macOS, Windows, ChromeOS: auto browse in Gemini in Chrome available to enterprise users. Enterprise policies <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiActOnWebSettings</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebAllowedForURLs" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiActOnWebAllowedForURLs</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebBlockedForURLs" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiActOnWebBlockedForURLs</u></a> are available to control auto browse.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 148 on ChromeOS, macOS, Windows</strong>: Gemini in Chrome will be able to use Chrome Autofill to fill credit card and address forms (with user permission). This will respect the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AutofillAddressEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>AutofillAddressEnabled</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AutofillCreditCardEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>AutofillCreditCardEnabled</u></a> enterprise policies, as well as the general <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiActOnWebSettings</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebAllowedForURLs" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiActOnWebAllowedForURLs</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebBlockedForURLs" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiActOnWebBlockedForURLs</u></a> policies for agentic Gemini in Chrome.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome Autofill: Expanded support for Google Wallet pass types&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome Autofill currently populates web forms using data from select passes stored in Google Wallet. Beginning with Chrome 148, the range of supported pass types expands to include driver licenses, passports, national ID cards, Known Traveler Numbers, and redress numbers. Filling and saving of these new data types is governed by the existing <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AutofillAddressEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>AutofillAddressEnabled</u></a> policy.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 148 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Feature rolls out gradually</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Prompt API&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Prompt API gives web developers direct access to a browser-provided on-device AI language model. The API design offers fine-grained control, aligned with cloud API shapes, for progressively enhancing sites with model interactions tailored to individualized use cases. This complements task-based language model APIs, for example, Summarizer API, as well as a variety of APIs and frameworks for generalized on-device inference with developer-supplied ML models.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>The initial implementation supports text, image, and audio inputs. In addition, response constraints ensure that generated text conforms with predefined regex and JSON schema formats.</p>

    <p>This supports a variety of use cases, from generating image captions and performing visual searches to transcribing audio, classifying sound events, generating text following specific instructions, and extracting information or insights from multi-modal source material.</p>

    <p>This API has been shipped in <a href="https://chromewebstore.google.com/category/extensions" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Extensions</u></a>. An enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAILocalFoundationalModelSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAILocalFoundationalModelSettings</u></a> is available to disable the underlying model downloading, which would render this API unavailable. Enterprise admins can also set the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#BuiltInAIAPIsEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>BuiltInAIAPIsEnabled</u></a> policy to block Built-In AI API usage, while still permitting other on-device GenAI features.</p>

    <p>Language support log:</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 148 on Windows, macOS, Linux</strong>: No rollout step</li>
      <li>Chrome M139 and earlier only supported English ('en')</li>
      <li>Chrome M140 added support for Spanish and Japanese ('es' and 'ja')</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Extended lifetime shared workers&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This update adds a new option, extendedLifetime: true, to the SharedWorker constructor. This new option requests that the shared worker be kept alive even after all current clients have unloaded. This allows pages to perform asynchronous work that requires JavaScript after a page unloads, without needing to rely on a service worker.</p>

    <p><br>
      <strong>Chrome 148 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong>: No rollout step</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Increase HTTP/3 usage&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome introduces optimizations to increase the use of the HTTP/3 (<a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9000/"><u>QUIC</u></a>) protocol for communication. As a result, you might notice improved discovery of HTTP/3 (QUIC) support and an increase in the amount of HTTP/3 (QUIC) connections. These changes are designed to improve performance.</p>

    <p>No action is required from Admins as these optimizations are handled automatically by the browser. For organizations that prefer to disable or restrict the use of QUIC, the existing QuicAllowed enterprise policy remains sufficient to control this behavior.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 148 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Feature rolls out gradually</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

    <p>In Chrome 148, existing profile creation flows on Desktop (Windows, Mac, Linux) get a visual update to provide a contemporary and streamlined onboarding experience. During First Run and Secondary profile creation, we introduce a new design to the onboarding flow, which includes management screens, to harmonize with the current Chrome brand identity.</p>

    <p>From Chrome 137 onwards, some users can turn on <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/answer/142893"><u>Enhanced autofill</u></a>, a feature that helps users fill out online forms more easily. <h2>Chrome Enterprise Core changes</h2>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Block extensions based on third-party risk scores&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>As early as Chrome 147, admins can configure a risk threshold in the Google Admin Console's <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/6177447" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Apps and Extensions</u></a>&nbsp;settings to automatically block extensions using third-party risk assessments (<a href="https://spin.ai/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Spin.Ai</u></a> and <a href="https://layerxsecurity.com/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LayerX</u></a>). This feature simplifies extension management and reduces the manual work required to assess and block high-risk extensions. Extensions that exceed the configured risk score threshold will be automatically disabled on the client side, and new installations will be blocked.</p>

    <p>Chrome 148 allows a <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/engage/trusted-testers/sign-up/"><u>Trusted Tester</u></a> preview, with the feature gradually rolling out in Chrome 149.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 148 on Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Early preview available to Chrome Enterprise Trusted Tester</li>
      <li>Chrome 149 on Linux, macOS, Windows: Feature rolls out gradually</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Block extensions using Chrome Web Store categories&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>As early as Chrome 147, admins could enhance security by automatically blocking Chrome extensions based on their Chrome Web Store categories, for example, blocking all <em>Games</em> extensions. This feature prevents extensions from blocked categories being installed and disables them if already present. <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/6306504" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Force-installed</u></a> and allow-listed extensions remain unaffected.</p>

    <p>This setting is only available in the Google Admin console under <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/6177447" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Apps &amp; Extensions &gt; Settings</u></a>, within the new <strong>Advanced extension blocking</strong> section. The setting name is <strong>Block by category</strong>. It can also be configured using the <a href="https://developers.google.com/chrome/management" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Management APIs</u></a>. This setting is not available for locally-managed devices.</p>

    <p>Chrome 148 allows a <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/engage/trusted-testers/sign-up/"><u>Trusted Tester</u></a> preview, with the feature gradually rolling out in Chrome 149.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 148 on Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Early preview available to Chrome Enterprise Trusted Tester</li>
      <li>Chrome 149 on Linux, macOS, Windows: Feature rolls out gradually</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome client certificate support on iOS&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Built-in client certificate support in Chrome for iOS enables managed users to securely authenticate to corporate resources using mutual TLS (<a href="https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/mtls"><u>mTLS</u></a>). Historically, iOS isolated certificates within the system store accessible only to built-in Apple apps, but this launch allows Chrome to provision and manage its own hardware-backed certificates independently. By integrating with the iOS Secure Enclave for non-exportable private key storage, Chrome provides a high-assurance identity signal specifically for Zero Trust environments using Microsoft Entra ID and Conditional Access. These credentials are provisioned within the work-managed Chrome profile and are inaccessible to other applications or personal profiles on the device.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <p>To implement this feature, admins must enable the <strong>Apply supported user settings to Chrome on iOS toggle</strong> in the Google Admin console and configure the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ProvisionManagedClientCertificateForBrowser"><u>ProvisionManagedClientCertificateForBrowser</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ProvisionManagedClientCertificateForUser"><u>ProvisionManagedClientCertificateForUser</u></a> policies to initiate issuance and rotation. Finally, the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AutoSelectCertificateForUrls"><u>AutoSelectCertificateForUrls</u></a> policy should be used to automate certificate selection for designated corporate domains to ensure a seamless authentication flow.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 148 on iOS</strong>: Feature rolls out gradually</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Managed profile reporting support&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome Enterprise Core is launching cloud profile reporting support for the <strong>Apps &amp; extension usage</strong> report and the <strong>Versions</strong> report in the Google Admin console.</p>

    <p>On the <strong>Apps &amp; extension usage</strong> report, admins will be able to see a new total install count for managed profiles (work profiles). They will be able to see which extensions have the most installs across all managed profiles.</p>

    <p>On the <strong>Versions</strong> report, admins will be able to see the total number of managed profiles running each version of Chrome. For example, they will be able to see if managed profiles are using older versions of Chrome.</p>

    <p>To enable cloud profile reporting for both of these reports, admins have to enable the existing <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#CloudProfileReportingEnabled"><u>CloudProfileReportingEnabled</u></a> policy. If you have already turned on Managed profile reporting, the reports will automatically start reporting the data.</p>

    <p>How to find these reports? In the Admin console, navigate to <strong>Chrome browser &gt; Reports &gt; Apps &amp; extensions usage</strong> or <strong>Chrome browser &gt; Reports &gt; Versions</strong>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>
        <p><strong>Chrome 148 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Feature rolls out gradually</p>
      </li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<div class="no-margin"><h2>Chrome Enterprise Premium changes</h2>

<p>Read more about the differences between <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/products/chrome-enterprise-premium" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Enterprise Core and Chrome Enterprise Premium</u></a>.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome Enterprise Connectors API&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> &nbsp;

    <p>Chrome Enterprise expands programmatic management for <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/12166576"><u>Chrome Enterprise Connectors</u></a>. This update will introduce resources to define and assign connector configurations, complementing the existing connector policies to allow administrators to manage the full life-cycle of these integrations at scale.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <p>Previously, configuring Service Providers was a manual process in the Google Admin console. This update enables automation, which helps reduce manual errors and improve the efficiency of managing integrations with third-party security solutions.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <p>Administrators can now use the Chrome Management API to manage ConnectorConfiguration resources (defining the provider). Connector Selection is managed via the Chrome Policy API, enabling the assignment of these configurations to Organizational Units or Groups. This works in tandem with existing Policy API settings for event reporting and content analysis, including policies such as <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnSecurityEventEnterpriseConnector"><u>OnSecurityEventEnterpriseConnector</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnFileAttachedEnterpriseConnector"><u>OnFileAttachedEnterpriseConnector</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnFileDownloadedEnterpriseConnector"><u>OnFileDownloadedEnterpriseConnector</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnBulkDataEntryEnterpriseConnector"><u>OnBulkDataEntryEnterpriseConnector</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnPrintEnterpriseConnector"><u>OnPrintEnterpriseConnector</u></a>, and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#EnterpriseRealTimeUrlCheckMode"><u>EnterpriseRealTimeUrlCheckMode</u></a>. For technical details, developers should refer to the <a href="https://developers.google.com/chrome/management/reference/rest"><u>Chrome Management API</u></a> and <a href="https://developers.google.com/chrome/policy/reference/rest"><u>Chrome Policy API documentation</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>

<p><strong>Chrome Profile Bootstrapping via Custom URI</strong></p>

<p>This feature introduces a new custom URI scheme (google-chrome://) that allows external applications and web portals to launch Chrome directly into a specific managed profile. If the specified profile does not exist, the user will be guided through a streamlined profile creation flow pre-populated with their work email. This enables a seamless transition for users jumping from arbitrary browsers or built-in app catalogs into a secure, managed Chrome environment. Admins can control this behavior using the <strong>ChromeURILaunchEnabled</strong> policy. Chrome 149 will offer an early preview to <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/9036081"><u>Chrome Enterprise Trusted Testers</u></a>.</p>

</ul>

<p><strong>Chrome for ARM64 Linux devices</strong></p>

<p>We’re excited to announce that Google will launch Chrome for ARM64 Linux devices in Q2 2026, following the successful expansion of Chrome to Arm-powered macOS devices in 2020 and Arm-powered Windows devices in 2024.</p>

<p>Launching Chrome for ARM64 Linux devices allows more users to enjoy the seamless integration of Google’s most helpful services into their browser. This move addresses the growing demand for a browsing experience that combines the benefits of the open-source Chromium project with Google's ecosystem of apps and features.</p>

<p>To read more, see this <a href="https://blog.chromium.org/2026/03/bringing-chrome-to-arm64-linux-devices.html"><u>Chromium blog</u></a> post.</p>

<ul>

&nbsp;

<p><strong>PWA origin migration</strong></p>

<p>When a user installs a Progressive Web App (PWA), its identity and security context are tightly bound to its web origin, for example, app.example.com. This presents a significant challenge for developers who need to change their PWA's origin due to rebranding, domain restructuring, or technical re-architecture. Currently, such a change forces users to manually uninstall the old app and reinstall the new one, leading to a disruptive experience and potential user loss. Chrome 149 introduces a mechanism for developers to seamlessly migrate an installed PWA to a new, same-site origin, preserving user trust and permissions.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebAppInstallForceList"><u>WebAppInstallForceList</u></a> policy will block migration. Since enterprise policies around web applications are primarily based on URLs and origins, there is a risk that a migration would bypass certain policies an admin might have configured. No migration will be offered to the user when an app is force-installed by their enterprise administrator, and instead a banner will be shown explaining this to the user.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 149 on Windows, macOS, Linux</strong>: No rollout step</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Update to No HTTPS warning</strong></p>

<p>The warning displayed when a user opts in to the <strong>Always Use Secure Connections</strong> on chrome://settings/security is changing from an interstitial to a dialog. Full page load remains blocked, and the functionality remains the same. The URL content security indicator on the warning is changing from the *indicator to the broken lock. Some users may see this warning automatically when visiting HTTP sites. Users can opt in to the warning on chrome://settings/security.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 141 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: New warning design on desktop platforms.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 149 on Android</strong>: Similar updated warning design on Android, using a warning bubble instead of a full interstitial.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Always use secure connections by default</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 150 will enable the <strong>Always use secure connections</strong> setting in the <em>public sites only</em> mode by default. This means Chrome will ask for the user's permission before the first access to any public site without HTTPS. Public sites are defined as sites that have a globally unique name, and excludes direct navigation to <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1918"><u>RFC 1918</u></a> addresses (192.168.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8, and so on), as well as shortnames such as go/.</p>

<p>Prior to enabling it by default for all users, Chrome will enable <strong>Always use secure connections</strong> for the users who have opted-in to <a href="https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/11577602"><u>Enhanced Safe Browsing protections in Chrome</u></a>.</p>

<p>If you are a website developer or IT professional, and you have users who may be impacted by this feature, we very strongly recommend enabling the <strong>Always use secure connections</strong> setting today to help identify sites that you may need to work to migrate. Admins can use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HttpAllowlist"><u>HttpAllowlist</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HttpsOnlyMode"><u>HttpsOnlyMode</u></a> policies to override this behavior.</p>

<p>For more information, see our <a href="https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/docs/security/ask-before-http/ask-before-http-adoption-guide.md"><u>adoption guide</u></a> and <a href="https://security.googleblog.com/2025/10/https-by-default.html"><u>announcement blog post</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong>: Feature rolls out gradually. Enable "Always use secure connections" for users who have opted in to Enhanced Safe Browsing.</li>
  <li>Chrome 154 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: Feature rolls out gradually. Enable "Always use secure connections" by default for all users.</li>
</ul>

We have proactively reached out to users of the APIs with our deprecation plans. At the time of removal, Chrome 150, all the policies associated with these APIs will also be removed.</p>

<p><strong>Process isolation on Windows</strong></p>

<p>Chrome will apply Windows security ACLs to prevent other applications from reading or injecting into Chrome's memory space. This may cause interoperability issues with older antivirus, DLP, or accessibility software.</p>

<p>The admins will be able to control and disable this feature with the upcoming <strong>WindowsProcessIsolation</strong> policy.</p>

<p>Process isolation will eventually be enabled by default on all Windows installations.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Windows</strong>: Feature rolls out gradually</li>

<p><strong>SafeBrowsing API v4 to v5 migration</strong></p>

<p>Chrome calls into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/v4"><u>SafeBrowsing v4 API</u></a> will be migrated to call into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference"><u>v5 API</u></a> instead. The method names are also different between v4 and v5. If admins have any v4-specific URL allowlisting to allow network requests to https://safebrowsing.googleapis.com/v4*, these should be modified to allow network requests to the whole domain instead: safebrowsing.googleapis.com. Otherwise, rejected network requests to the v5 API will cause security regressions for users. For more details, see <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference/Migration.From.V4"><u>Migration From V4 - Safe Browsing</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Chrome will remove support for macOS 12</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 150 will be the last release to support macOS 12; Chrome 151+ will no longer support macOS 12, which is outside of its support window with Apple. Running on a supported operating system is essential to maintaining security.</p>

<p>On Macs running macOS 12, Chrome will continue to work, showing a warning infobar, but will not update any further. If a user wishes to have their Chrome updated, they need to update their computer to a supported version of macOS.</p>

<p>For new installations of Chrome 151+, macOS 13+ will be required.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 151 on Windows, macOS, Linux</strong>: No rollout step</li>
