<p><strong>Deprecate and remove XSLT</strong></p>

<p><a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/xslt-10/"><u>XSLT v1.0</u></a>, which all browsers adhere to, was standardized in 1999. In the meantime, XSLT has evolved to v2.0 and v3.0, adding features, and growing apart from the old version frozen into browsers. This lack of advancement, coupled with the rise of JavaScript libraries and frameworks that offer more flexible and powerful DOM manipulation, has led to a significant decline in the use of client-side XSLT. Its role within the web browser has been largely superseded by JavaScript-based technologies, such as JSON and React.</p>

<p>Chromium uses the libxslt library to process these transformations, and <a href="https://discourse.gnome.org/t/stepping-down-as-libxslt-maintainer/27615"><u>libxslt was unmaintained</u></a> for ~6 months of 2025. Libxslt is a complex, aging C codebase of the type notoriously susceptible to memory safety vulnerabilities like buffer overflows, which can lead to arbitrary code execution. Because client-side XSLT is now a niche, rarely-used feature, these libraries receive far less maintenance and security scrutiny than core JavaScript engines, yet they represent a direct, potent attack surface for processing untrusted web content. Indeed, XSLT is the source of several recent high-profile security exploits that continue to put browser users at risk.</p>

<p>For these reasons, Chromium (along with both other browser engines) plans to deprecate and remove XSLT from the web platform. For more details, <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/deprecating-xslt"><u>see this Chrome for Developers article</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 143 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Deprecation (but not removal) of the APIs.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Origin Trial (OT) and Enterprise Policy go live for testing. These allow sites and enterprises to continue using features past the removal date.</li>
  <li>Chrome 158 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: XSLT stops functioning on Stable releases, for all users other than Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy participants.</li>
  <li>Chrome 176 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy stop functioning. XSLT is disabled for all users.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Local network access restrictions</strong></p>

<p>Chrome 142 restricted the ability to make requests to the user's local network, gated behind a permission prompt. A local network request is any request from a public website to a local IP address or loopback, or from a local website (for example, intranet) to loopback.</p>

<p>Gating the ability for websites to perform these requests behind a permission mitigates the risk of cross-site request forgery attacks against local network devices such as routers, and reduces the ability of sites to use these requests to fingerprint the user's local network.</p>

<p>This permission is restricted to secure contexts. If granted, the permissions additionally relaxes mixed content blocking for local network requests (since many local devices are not able to obtain publicly trusted TLS certificates for various reasons).</p>

<p>This work supersedes a prior effort called <a href="https://chromestatus.com/feature/5737414355058688"><u>Private Network Access</u></a>, which used preflight requests to have local devices opt in. For more information on this feature, see <a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QQkqehw8umtAgz5z0um7THx-aoU251p705FbIQjDuGs/edit?usp=sharing"><u>Adapting your website for new Local Network Access restrictions in Chrome</u></a>.</p>

<p>Chrome 145 introduced more granular permissions for websites requesting access to a user's local network. The previous single local-network-access permission is being split into two distinct permissions:</p>

<ul>
  <li>local-network: Grants access to IP addresses in the local network space (for example, intranets, internal devices).</li>
  <li>loopback-network: Grants access to loopback IP addresses (for example, localhost, 127.0.0.1).</li>
</ul>

<p>The old local-network permission will remain as an alias, ensuring existing configurations and permissions policies continue to function as expected.</p>

<p>This change provides both users and Admins with more precise control over how websites interact with internal network resources. Current enterprise policies managing local network access will not be affected by this change.</p>

<p>Chrome 146 introduces two new enterprise policies for managing local network access restrictions: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides"><u>LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled"><u>LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled</u></a>. These policies can be set using <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/14749672"><u>custom configurations</u></a>.</p>

<p>Chrome 147 expands Local Network Access restrictions to include WebSocket and WebTransport connections.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 145 on Android, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: The permission split is rolled out.</li>
  <li>Chrome 146 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: Two new enterprise policies will be available for managing local network access restrictions: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides"><u>LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides</u></a> could be used to mark IPv4 and IPv6 address blocks as public or private. IP ranges that are treated as public will not cause permission prompts when accessed by other pages. For example, CGNAT 100.64.0.0/10 can be marked as public. This is useful for certain VPN and proxy setups. Marking 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 as public is equivalent to disabling the local network access restrictions. <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled"><u>LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled</u></a> can be used to cause the LNA permission to be automatically delegated to iframes by the parent frame, without requiring explicit annotation of the child iframes. This is useful in situations where local network access is performed by an embedded SaaS tool inside of a different SaaS tool. This includes certain locally hosted documentation and knowledgebase software.</li>
  <li>Chrome 147 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Local Network Access restrictions expanded to include WebSocket and WebTransport connections.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut"><u>LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut</u></a> policy will be removed.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>PostQuantum cryptography for DTLS in WebRTC</strong></p>

<p>This feature will enable the use of PostQuantum Cryptography (PQC) with WebRTC connections. The motivation for PQC is to get WebRTC media traffic up to date with the latest cryptography protocols and prevent <em>Harvest Now to Crack Later</em> scenarios.</p>

<p>Admins will be able to control this feature using an enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement"><u>WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement</u></a>, to allow enterprise users to opt out of PQC. The policy is temporary and is planned to be removed by Chrome 152.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 142 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: Feature rolls out gradually</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong>: Remove <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement"><u>WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement</u></a> enterprise policy</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Moving to a 2-week release cycle</strong></p>

<p>From September 2026 (Chrome 153), Chrome will move to a 2-week release cycle, from the current four-week cycle. The web platform is constantly advancing, and our goal at Chrome is to ensure developers and users have immediate access to the latest capabilities, fixes, and performance improvements. Building on our history of adapting our release process to match the demands of a modern web, we are announcing this significant step to further increase our development velocity and Chrome Stable is moving to a 2-week release cycle. You can find more details in the <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-two-week-release"><u>Chrome for Developers</u></a> blog post.&nbsp;</p>

<p>Extended Stable is available for customers who might have concerns about the maintenance costs. For more information about Extended Stable, see this <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16942104"><u>Help Center</u></a> article. The 2-week Stable option remains the most secure choice and should be utilized if security is a larger concern than maintenance costs.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 153 on Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Chrome moves to a 2-week release cycle</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Disallow spaces in non-file:// URL hosts</strong></p>

<p>According to the <a href="https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#forbidden-host-code-point"><u>URL Standard specification</u></a> URL hosts cannot contain the space character, but currently URL parsing in Chromium allows spaces in the host. This causes Chromium to fail several tests included in the <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/websockets?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2024-websockets"><u>Interop2024 HTTPS URLs for WebSocket</u></a> and <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/url?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2023-url"><u>URL focus</u></a> areas. To bring Chromium into spec compliance, we would like to remove spaces from URL hosts altogether, but a difficulty with this is that they are used in the host part in Windows file:// URLs. For more details, see this <a href="https://github.com/whatwg/url/issues/599"><u>Github discussion</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 157 on Android, ChromeOS, LaCrOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong></li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Isolated Web Apps</strong></p>

<p><a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/iwa/introduction"><u>Isolated Web Apps</u></a> (IWAs) are an extension of existing work on PWA installation and Web Packaging that provide stronger protections against server compromise and other tampering that is necessary for developers of security-sensitive applications. Rather than being hosted on live web servers and fetched over HTTPS, these applications are packaged into Web Bundles, signed by their developer, and distributed to end-users through one or more of the potential methods described in the <a href="https://github.com/WICG/isolated-web-apps/blob/main/README.md"><u>explainer</u></a>.</p>

<p>In Chrome 128, IWAs became installable through an admin policy only on enterprise-managed ChromeOS devices.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 161 on Windows</strong>: This rollout adds support for Isolated Web Apps in enterprise-managed browser configurations on Windows.</li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<h4><strong>Upcoming Chrome Enterprise Core updates</strong></h4>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><strong>Gen AI and SaaS app usage reporting</strong></p>

<p>As early as Chrome 147, admins will have access to a new <strong>Gen AI and SaaS app usage</strong> reporting feature in the Google Admin console. This report brings visibility into their organization's use of generative AI tools and SaaS sites, allowing admins to monitor usage of their enterprise IT resources.</p>

<p>This report is available for <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/products/chrome-enterprise-core/"><u>Chrome Enterprise Core (CEC)</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/products/chrome-enterprise-premium/"><u>Chrome Enterprise Premium (CEP)</u></a> customers only.</p>

<p>This new report tracks usage for 60 predefined sites (including <a href="https://www.xgen.ai/"><u>X Gen AI</u></a> sites), providing metrics on visits, unique managed profiles, unique managed browsers, and access to sensitive content transfer events. With these insights, admins can assess risk and restrict usage by making informed licensing decisions or creating usage restrictions, such as Data Loss Prevention (DLP) rules.</p>

<p>Chrome 147 allows a <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/engage/trusted-testers/sign-up/"><u>Trusted Tester</u></a> preview, with the feature gradually rolling out in Chrome 150.</p>
&nbsp;

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 147 on Linux, macOS, Windows: Early preview available to Chrome Enterprise Trusted Tester</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Feature rolls out gradually</li>
</ul>
</div>

<div class="no-margin"><p>&nbsp;</p>

<h4><strong>Upcoming Chrome Enterprise Premium updates</strong></h4>

<p><strong>&nbsp;</strong></p>

<p><strong>Hardening against local policy tampering</strong></p>

<p>Local settings on bring-your-own-device (BYOD) devices can sometimes conflict with corporate policy settings. To address this potential security gap, policy conflict signals in Chrome now detect and report whenever corporate policies are being overridden by local policy. Chrome 145 integrates these new policy conflict signals from the managed Chrome profile into existing security reports, controlled by the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UserSecuritySignalsReporting"><u>UserSecuritySignalsReporting</u></a> policy.</p>

<p>For more information on device reporting, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/1698333#zippy=%2Creporting-policies"><u>View ChromeOS device list and details - Chrome Enterprise and Education Help</u></a>.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 144 on Linux, macOS, Windows: Detection and reporting of policy conflict metadata begins.</li>
  <li>Chrome 145 on Linux, macOS, Windows: Visibility into Chrome policy hardening signals via the Devices API becomes available.</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Admin console UI is updated to display conflict signals and policy values begin reporting.</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Screenshot protections</strong></p>

<p>Admins can prevent users from taking screenshots or screen sharing specific web pages considered to contain sensitive data. Admins create a DLP URL filtering rule to block users taking screenshots or screen sharing specific URLs or categories of URLs.</p>

<p>This feature can be controlled via the same <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#EnterpriseRealTimeUrlCheckMode"><u>EnterpriseRealTimeUrlCheckMode</u></a> Chrome Enterprise policy that enables all real-time URL lookups.</p>

<ul>
  <li>Chrome 129 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Trusted Tester program</li>
  <li>Chrome 131 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Feature rolls out</li>
  <li><strong>Chrome 150 on iOS</strong>: Feature rolls out gradually. Feature becomes available on iOS and iPadOS</li>
</ul>
&nbsp;

<p><strong>Enterprise file download protection on iOS</strong></p>

<p>Admins can prevent users from downloading files considered to contain sensitive data by creating a DLP OnFileDownload rule to send a file for analysis when it is downloaded from a specific page. Based on the scanning result, it will warn or block the download if sensitive information is detected.</p>

<p>This feature can be controlled via the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnFileDownloadedEnterpriseConnector"><u>OnFileDownloadedEnterpriseConnector</u></a> Chrome Enterprise policy that enables the download connector.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome 151 on iOS</strong>: Feature rolls out gradually. Feature becomes available on iOS and iPadOS</li>
</ul>
</div>

<h2>Chrome browser changes &nbsp;</h2>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrA147" name="chromeBrsrA147">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>AI Mode enhancements</strong> <a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 143 integrates new AI Mode capabilities into Chrome on macOS and Windows. Users will be able to access AI Mode directly from the <strong>New tab</strong> page and the omnibox, allowing users to ask complex questions directly from where they start browsing. This will start rolling out in Chrome 143 on macOS and Windows. Admins can turn off these features (value 1) using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AIModeSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>AIModeSettings</u></a> policy or by using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> (value 2). For more details, see the relevant section in the <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/14443058#zippy=%2Cgemini-enterprise%2Cgoogle-lens%2Cai-mode"><u>Help Center</u></a>.</p>

    <p>Also coming in Chrome 144 is the multi-tab context feature. Users can choose to share the contents of one or more of their open tabs with AI Mode, helping them ask questions, compare, summarize, and find information more efficiently. Admins will be able to turn off these features (value 1) using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SearchContentSharingSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SearchContentSharingSettings</u></a> policy (available in Chrome 144) or by using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> (value 2).</p>

    <p>In Chrome 145, we rolled out the multi-tab context feature on AI Mode and Lens. Users can choose to share the contents of one or more of their open tabs, helping them ask questions, compare, summarize, and find information more efficiently. Admins can turn off these features (value 1) using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SearchContentSharingSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SearchContentSharingSettings</u></a> policy or by using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> (value 2). Also in Chrome 145 on Android and iOS, new AI Mode capabilities were integrated into Chrome browser.</p>

    <p>In Chrome 146, Google Drive files become available as context. Admins can turn off these features (value 1) using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SearchContentSharingSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SearchContentSharingSettings</u></a> policy.</p>

    <p>In Chrome 147, admins use <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SearchContentSharingSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SearchContentSharingSettings</u></a> to control these features. Google Lens policies are deprecated: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LensOverlaySettings"><u>LensOverlaySettings</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LensDesktopNTPSearchEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LensDesktopNTPSearchEnabled</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LensRegionSearchEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LensRegionSearchEnabled</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 143 on macOS, Windows: New AI Mode capabilities will be integrated into Chrome and can be controlled using <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AIModeSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>AIModeSettings</u></a> policy or the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> policy.</li>
      <li>Chrome 145 on macOS, Windows<strong>:</strong> The multi-tab context feature will be available and can be controlled using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SearchContentSharingSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SearchContentSharingSettings</u></a> policy or <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> policy.</li>
      <li>Chrome 145 on Android, iOS: New AI Mode capabilities will gradually become available on Android and iOS.</li>
      <li>Chrome 146 on macOS, Windows: Google Drive files become available as context. Admins can turn off these features (value 1) using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SearchContentSharingSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SearchContentSharingSettings</u></a> policy.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on macOS, Windows</strong>: The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LensOverlaySettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LensOverlaySettings</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LensDesktopNTPSearchEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LensDesktopNTPSearchEnabled</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LensRegionSearchEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LensRegionSearchEnabled</u></a> policies will be deprecated. Admins can use <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SearchContentSharingSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SearchContentSharingSettings</u></a> to control these features.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrB147" name="chromeBrsrB147">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Gemini in Chrome&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Gemini is now integrated into Chrome on macOS, Windows and selective ChromeOS devices, and can understand the content of your current page. Users can now seamlessly get key takeaways, clarify concepts, and find answers, all without leaving their Chrome tab. This integration includes both chat—where users can interact with Gemini via text, and <em>Gemini Live</em>, with which users can interact with Gemini via voice.</p>

    <p>In Chrome 143, <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16291696" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Gemini in Chrome</u></a> started to roll out to most Google Workspace users with access to the Gemini app in the US. Admins can turn off this feature (value 1) using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiSettings</u></a> policy or by using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> (value 2). For more details, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16291696" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Gemini in Chrome</u></a> in the Help Center or this <a href="https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/chrome-enterprise/supercharging-employee-productivity-with-ai-securely-with-gemini-in-chrome-enterprise" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>blog post</u></a>.</p>

    <p>Also in Chrome 143, we announced the multi-tab context feature. Gemini in Chrome can now see more of your opened tabs (10 max) so you can ask questions across multiple pages to help you compare, find information more efficiently. Gemini in Chrome also serves as a productivity agent. Gemini in Chrome automatically uses public information from these Google services: Google Search, Google Maps, YouTube. With your permission, Gemini in Chrome can help you connect your personal information and content in Google Workspace services (Gmail, Drive, Keep, Calendar, and Tasks).</p>

    <p>In Chrome 144, auto browse in Gemini in Chrome was made available to some users (non-enterprise). An enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiActOnWebSettings</u></a> will be available at launch.</p>
    <img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/tzECavmDds71fAkpXrShS2ODB9cLnbdgds98TZLfgZoN4K_lKBIuh6LW_vp-Bpe_K-s=w895" width="1004" height="567" alt="" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/tzECavmDds71fAkpXrShS2ODB9cLnbdgds98TZLfgZoN4K_lKBIuh6LW_vp-Bpe_K-s">

    <p>For more details, see the rollout steps below.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 144 on macOS, Windows: Auto browse in Gemini in Chrome available to some users (non-enterprise). Enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiActOnWebSettings</u></a> will be available at launch. Image upload context menu item available to enterprise users. Feature will respect rules set via the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DataControlsRules" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DataControlsRules</u></a> policy and the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnBulkDataEntryEnterpriseConnector" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>OnBulkDataEntryEnterpriseConnector</u></a> settings.</li>
      <li>Chrome 144 on macOS, Windows: Gemini in Chrome allows some 3P tools that are available as Gemini Extensions to be called.</li>
      <li>Chrome 145 on ChromeOS, macOS, Windows: Gemini in Chrome is now available to users in US, Canada, New Zealand and India in 50+ languages. More details in <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16291696" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>this</u></a> help center article.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on ChromeOS, macOS, Windows</strong>: As early as Chrome 147 on macOS, Windows, ChromeOS: auto browse in Gemini in Chrome available to enterprise users. Enterprise policies <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiActOnWebSettings</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebAllowedForURLs" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiActOnWebAllowedForURLs</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebBlockedForURLs" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiActOnWebBlockedForURLs</u></a> are available to control auto browse.</li>
      <li>Chrome 148 on ChromeOS, macOS, Windows: Gemini in Chrome will be able to use Chrome Autofill to fill credit card and address forms (with user permission). This will respect the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AutofillAddressEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>AutofillAddressEnabled</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AutofillCreditCardEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>AutofillCreditCardEnabled</u></a> enterprise policies, as well as the general <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiActOnWebSettings</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebAllowedForURLs" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiActOnWebAllowedForURLs</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GeminiActOnWebBlockedForURLs" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GeminiActOnWebBlockedForURLs</u></a> policies for agentic Gemini in Chrome.</li>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrC147" name="chromeBrsrC147">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>X25519Kyber768 key encapsulation for TLS&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 124 enabled by default on all desktop platforms a new post-quantum secure TLS key encapsulation mechanism <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-124-beta#x25519kyber768_key_encapsulation_for_tls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>X25519Kyber768</u></a>, based on a NIST standard (ML-KEM). This protects network traffic from Chrome with servers that also support ML-KEM from decryption by a future quantum computer. This change should be transparent to server operators. This cipher will be used for both <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8446" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>TLS 1.3</u></a> and <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9000/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>QUIC</u></a> connections.</p>

    <p>However, some TLS middleboxes might be unprepared for the size of a Kyber (ML-KEM) key encapsulation, or a new TLS ClientHello cipher code point, leading to dropped or hanging connections. This can be resolved by updating your middlebox, or disabling the key encapsulation mechanism via the temporary <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>PostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled</u></a> enterprise policy, which will be available through Chrome 145. However, long term, post-quantum secure ciphers will be required in TLS and the enterprise policy will be removed in Chrome 147. Post-quantum cryptography is required for CSNA 2.0. To learn more, see <a href="https://blog.chromium.org/2023/08/protecting-chrome-traffic-with-hybrid.html" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Protect Chrome Traffic with Hybrid Kyper KEM</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 131 on Linux, macOS, Windows: Chrome will switch the key encapsulation mechanism to the final standard version of ML-KEM.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled"><u>PostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled</u></a> enterprise policy will be removed.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrD147" name="chromeBrsrD147">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>CSS update: decoupling of Width and Style properties&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 147 aligns with updated <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/css-2025/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>CSS specifications</u></a> regarding the behavior of <code>border-width</code>, <code>outline-width</code>, and <code>column-rule-width </code>properties. Previously, if the corresponding <code>border-style</code>, <code>outline-style</code>, or <code>column-rule-style </code>was set to none or hidden, the computed width of these properties would be forced to 0px, regardless of the specified value.</p>

    <p>With this change, the computed values of <code>border-width</code>, <code>outline-width</code>, and <code>column-rule-width</code> will always reflect the author-specified values, independent of the <code>*-style</code> property. Additionally, the resolved values (as returned by <code>getComputedStyle()</code>) for <code>outline-width</code> and <code>column-rule-width</code> will also reflect the specified values.</p>

    <p>The change aligns Chrome with Firefox and WebKit, which have already implemented this behavior.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong>: No rollout step.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrE147" name="chromeBrsrE147">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome for iOS background customization for New tab page&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome for iOS will now allow users to customize their <strong>New tab</strong> page background. Admins can set <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#NTPCustomBackgroundEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>NTPCustomBackgroundEnabled</u></a> to True or False, which allows users to customize their <strong>New tab</strong> page background. The admin can set the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#BrowserThemeColor" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>BrowserThemeColor</u></a>, which supports a hex code for specifying a color. If a hex value is specified, the user will not be able to override it. Admins can also specify a recommended hex value, which the user can override. If fully enabled, users can also choose from the pre-selected gallery within Chrome, or from their phone's camera roll.</p>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrF147" name="chromeBrsrF147">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Device Bound Session Credentials&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>To enhance user security and combat session cookie theft, Chrome is introducing <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/device-bound-session-credentials" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC)</u></a>. This feature allows websites to bind a user's session to their specific device, which makes it significantly more difficult for stolen session cookies to be used on other machines.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 145 on Windows: Feature rolls out gradually.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on macOS</strong>: Feature rolls out gradually.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrG147" name="chromeBrsrG147">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Local network access restrictions&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 142 restricted the ability to make requests to the user's local network, gated behind a permission prompt. A local network request is any request from a public website to a local IP address or loopback, or from a local website (for example, intranet) to loopback.</p>

    <p>Gating the ability for websites to perform these requests behind a permission mitigates the risk of cross-site request forgery attacks against local network devices such as routers, and reduces the ability of sites to use these requests to fingerprint the user's local network.</p>

    <p>This permission is restricted to secure contexts. If granted, the permissions additionally relaxes mixed content blocking for local network requests (since many local devices are not able to obtain publicly trusted TLS certificates for various reasons).</p>

    <p>This work supersedes a prior effort called <a href="https://chromestatus.com/feature/5737414355058688" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Private Network Access</u></a>, which used preflight requests to have local devices opt in. For more information on this feature, see <a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QQkqehw8umtAgz5z0um7THx-aoU251p705FbIQjDuGs/edit?usp=sharing" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Adapting your website for new Local Network Access restrictions in Chrome</u></a>.</p>

    <p>Chrome 145 introduced more granular permissions for websites requesting access to a user's local network. The previous single local-network-access permission is being split into two distinct permissions:</p>

    <ul>
      <li>local-network: Grants access to IP addresses in the local network space (for example, intranets, internal devices).</li>
      <li>loopback-network: Grants access to loopback IP addresses (for example, localhost, 127.0.0.1).</li>
    </ul>

    <p>The old local-network permission will remain as an alias, ensuring existing configurations and permissions policies continue to function as expected. This change provided both users and Admins with more precise control over how websites interact with internal network resources. Current enterprise policies managing local network access will not be affected by this change.</p>

    <p>Chrome 146 introduces two new enterprise policies for managing local network access restrictions: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled</u></a>. These policies can be set using <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/14749672" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>custom configurations</u></a>.</p>

    <p>Chrome 147 expands Local Network Access restrictions to include WebSocket and WebTransport connections.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 145 on Android, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: The permission split is rolled out.</li>
      <li>Chrome 146 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: Two new enterprise policies will be available for managing local network access restrictions: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LocalNetworkAccessIpAddressSpaceOverrides</u></a> could be used to mark IPv4 and IPv6 address blocks as public or private. IP ranges that are treated as public will not cause permission prompts when accessed by other pages. For example, CGNAT 100.64.0.0/10 can be marked as public. This is useful for certain VPN and proxy setups. Marking 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 as public is equivalent to disabling the local network access restrictions. <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LocalNetworkAccessPermissionsPolicyDefaultEnabled</u></a> can be used to cause the LNA permission to be automatically delegated to iframes by the parent frame, without requiring explicit annotation of the child iframes. This is useful in situations where local network access is performed by an embedded SaaS tool inside of a different SaaS tool. This includes certain locally hosted documentation and knowledgebase softwares.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Local Network Access restrictions expanded to include WebSocket and WebTransport connections.</li>
      <li>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut</u></a> policy will be removed.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrJ147" name="chromeBrsrJ147">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>UI Automation accessibility framework provider on Windows&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 126 began to directly support accessibility client software that uses Microsoft Windows's UI Automation accessibility framework. Prior to this change, such software interoperated with Chrome by way of a compatibility shim in Microsoft Windows. This change is being made to improve the accessible user experience for many users. It provides complete support for Narrator, Magnifier, and Voice Access; and will improve third-party apps that use Windows's UI Automation accessibility framework. Users of Chrome will find reduced memory usage and processing overhead when used with accessibility tools. It will also ease development of software using assistive technologies.</p>

    <p>Administrators can use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> enterprise policy starting in Chrome 125 to either force-enable the new provider (so that all users receive the new functionality), or disable the new provider.</p>

    <p>This policy will be supported through Chrome 146 and will be removed in Chrome 147. This one-year period allowed enterprises sufficient time to work with third-party vendors so that they might fix any incompatibilities resulting from the switch from Microsoft's compatibility shim to Chrome's UI Automation provider.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 125 on Windows: The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> policy is introduced so that administrators can enable Chrome's UI Automation accessibility framework provider and validate that third-party accessibility tools continue to work.</li>
      <li>Chrome 126 on Windows: The Chrome variations framework will be used to begin enabling Chrome's UI Automation accessibility framework provider for users. It will be progressively enabled to the full stable population, with pauses as needed to address compatibility issues that can be resolved in Chrome. Enterprise administrators may continue to use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> policy to either opt-in early to the new behavior, or to temporarily opt-out through Chrome 146.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Windows</strong>: The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> policy will be removed from Chrome. All clients will use the browser's UI Automation accessibility framework provider.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<h2>Chrome Enterprise Core changes</h2>

<p><a id="chromeECA147" name="chromeECA147"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Block extensions based on third-party risk scores&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>As early as Chrome 147, admins can configure a risk threshold in the Google Admin Console's <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/6177447" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Apps and Extensions</u></a>&nbsp;settings to automatically block extensions using third-party risk assessments (<a href="https://spin.ai/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Spin.Ai</u></a> and <a href="https://layerxsecurity.com/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LayerX</u></a>). This feature simplifies extension management and reduces the manual work required to assess and block high-risk extensions. Extensions that exceed the configured risk score threshold will be automatically disabled on the client side, and new installations will be blocked. Chrome 147 allows a <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/engage/trusted-testers/sign-up/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Trusted Tester</u></a> preview, with the feature gradually rolling out in Chrome 148.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Linux, macOS, Windows -</strong> Early preview available to Chrome Enterprise Trusted Tester.</li>
      <li>Chrome 148 on Linux, macOS, Windows - Feature rolls out gradually.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeECB147" name="chromeECB147"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Block extensions using Chrome Web Store categories&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>As early as Chrome 147, admins could enhance security by automatically blocking Chrome extensions based on their Chrome Web Store categories, for example, blocking all <em>Games</em> extensions. This feature prevents extensions from blocked categories being installed and disables them if already present. <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/6306504" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Force-installed</u></a> and allow-listed extensions remain unaffected.</p>

    <p>This setting is only available in the Google Admin console under <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/6177447" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Apps &amp; Extensions &gt; Settings</u></a>, within the new <strong>Advanced extension blocking</strong> section. The setting name is <strong>Block by category</strong>. It can also be configured using the <a href="https://developers.google.com/chrome/management" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Management APIs</u></a>. This setting is not available for locally-managed devices.</p>

    <p>Chrome 147 allows a <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/engage/trusted-testers/sign-up/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Trusted Tester</u></a> preview, with the feature gradually rolling out in Chrome 148.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Linux, macOS, Windows - Early preview available to Chrome Enterprise Trusted Tester</strong>.</li>
      <li>Chrome 148 on Linux, macOS, Windows - Feature rolls out gradually.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeECC147" name="chromeECC147"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>New organization publishing option in the Chrome Web Store&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 147 introduces a new B2B domain publishing capability within the Chrome Web Store that enables developers to directly distribute extensions to specific enterprise domains. This unlocks secure, scalable deployment for custom-built enterprise solutions and improves the admin experience managing these deployments.</p>

    <p>Previously, enterprise developers could only publish extensions privately to their own enterprise. With the new option, developers will be able to deploy their extensions privately to external organizations that approve them, all from within the store.<br>
      For more information on how to get started, visit the <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/cws-new-enterprise-publishing-option#enable_the_new_option" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome for Developer Blog: New enterprise publishing option in the Chrome Web Store: Publish to external organizations</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>.</li>
    </ul>

The goal is to help Admins save time and more easily identify impactful changes and recommended actions.</p>

    <p>As early as Chrome 147, admins will have access to a new <strong>Gen AI and SaaS app usage</strong> reporting feature in the Google Admin console.     <p>This new report tracks usage for 60 predefined sites (including <a href="https://www.xgen.ai/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>X Gen AI</u></a> sites), providing metrics on visits, unique managed profiles, unique managed browsers, and access to sensitive content transfer events. <div class="no-margin"><h2>Chrome Enterprise Premium changes</h2>

<p>Read more about the differences between <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/products/chrome-enterprise-premium" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Enterprise Core and Chrome Enterprise Premium</u></a>.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Increased file size support for DLP scans&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> &nbsp;

    <p>Chrome Enterprise Premium will extend its Data Loss Prevention (DLP) and malware scanning capabilities to include large and encrypted files.</p>

    <p>Previously, files larger than 50 MB and all encrypted files were skipped during content scanning. This update closes that critical security gap.</p>

    <p>In Chrome 147, for policies configured to save evidence, files <strong>up to 2GB</strong> can now be sent to the <strong>Evidence Locker</strong>. This provides administrators with greater visibility and control, significantly reducing the risk of data exfiltration through large file transfers.</p>

    <p>Note: Because larger files are now being stored, customers may see an increase in Google Cloud Storage charges associated with their Evidence Locker bucket.</p>

    <p>No new policy is required to enable this feature. It is automatically controlled by your existing DLP rule configurations in the Google Admin console. If admins have rules that apply to file uploads, downloads, or printing, they will now also apply to large and encrypted files. For more information, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/11587610" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>What are ChromeOS data controls?</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>
        <p><strong>Chrome 147 on Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: This stage enables the collection of large (&gt;50 MB) and encrypted files for the Evidence Locker, closing a key Data Loss Prevention security gap.</p>
      </li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>New templates for Data Loss Prevention rules&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> &nbsp;

    <p>Deploying industry-leading data protection in Chrome is now faster and more intuitive. <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/products/chrome-enterprise-premium/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Enterprise Premium (CEP)</u></a> introduces ready-to-use Data Loss Prevention (DLP) rule templates to help customers implement robust data protection policies and realize the value of CEP’s security suite with minimal setup.</p>

    <p>With these templates, customers can quickly and easily implement essential DLP controls without starting from scratch. These templates provide a basis for common DLP use cases, such as:</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Protecting sensitive data like credit card numbers and social security numbers from being leaked accidentally or maliciously.</li>
      <li>Audit, block pasting or fully block categories of sites, such as Generative AI sites.</li>
      <li>Disable screen capture or watermark sites with sensitive information.</li>
    </ul>

    <p>The new data protection templates can be found in the Google Admin console using the <strong>Rules &gt; Templates</strong> option from the left navigation menu.</p>

    <p>Chrome 147 allows a <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/engage/trusted-testers/sign-up/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Trusted Tester</u></a> preview, with the feature gradually rolling out in Chrome 148.</p>
    <img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/O6Z7w67J2q0AYSEgNf0mZ6zPQ4dYu99_XYnsyQaXVPSOKjh7E3wUNNmHOHbfL3ZDNQ=w895" width="1600" height="1392" alt="" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/O6Z7w67J2q0AYSEgNf0mZ6zPQ4dYu99_XYnsyQaXVPSOKjh7E3wUNNmHOHbfL3ZDNQ">

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows - </strong>Early preview available to Chrome Enterprise Trusted Tester: Trusted tester access will begin as early as April 2026.</li>
      <li>Chrome 148 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows - Feature rolls out gradually.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Streamlined Chrome Enterprise to Google SecOps integration&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> &nbsp;

    <p>The new <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16731355" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Enterprise Connector</u></a> for Google Security Operations (Google SecOps) is now generally available.</p>

    <p>The connector provides a new integration experience that can optionally configure recommended Chrome Enterprise settings to forward Chrome data to Google SecOps. The connector now allows administrators to keep previously configured settings. Data from Chrome Enterprise Premium includes additional security context from <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/answer/13844634" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Safe Browsing</u></a>. Admins can choose to select an instance connected to their organization or use a one-time token (keyless) to send data to an external instance. This connector routes Chrome data to Google SecOps through Google Cloud.</p>

    <p>For additional details, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16731355" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Configure Chrome Enterprise Connectors for Google Security Operations</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 142 on iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows - Feature rolls out gradually</strong>: Chrome Enterprise Connector for Google Security Operations becomes generally available.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Support for allowlist and blocklist for Developer Tools&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> &nbsp;

    <p>Chrome will introduce two new policies, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DeveloperToolsAvailabilityAllowlist" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DeveloperToolsAvailabilityAllowlist</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DeveloperToolsAvailabilityBlocklist" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DeveloperToolsAvailabilityBlocklist</u></a>, which provide granular control over the availability of Developer Tools based on URL patterns.</p>

    <p>Previously, administrators could only allow or disallow Developer Tools globally. With these new policies, admins can now enforce a general block on Developer Tools to secure sensitive corporate data, while explicitly permitting access on specific internal URLs for development or troubleshooting purposes.</p>

    <p>These controls are available on Windows, Mac, Linux, and ChromeOS. If these new policies are not configured, the behavior of the existing <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DeveloperToolsAvailability" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DeveloperToolsAvailability</u></a> policy remains unchanged.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows - </strong>Feature rolls out gradually: Introduces the <strong>DeveloperToolsAvailabilityAllowlist</strong> and <strong>DeveloperToolsAvailabilityBlocklist</strong> policies on Desktop platforms.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Support for allowlist and blocklist for Incognito mode&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> &nbsp;

    <p>Chrome will introduce two new policies, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#IncognitoModeUrlBlocklist" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>IncognitoModeUrlBlocklist</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#IncognitoModeUrlAllowlist" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>IncognitoModeUrlAllowlist</u></a>, to provide administrators with more precise control over Incognito mode usage.</p>

    <p>As part of this change, Chrome is also updating the default behavior of wildcard patterns in the existing <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#URLBlocklist" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URLBlocklist</u></a> policy and in the new <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#IncognitoModeUrlAllowlist" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>IncognitoModeUrlAllowlist</u></a> to permit navigation to internal <code>chrome://</code> pages. If an administrator wants to block internal <code>chrome://</code> pages, they must explicitly block those and cannot depend on the wildcard. Note that access to internal <code>chrome:// </code>pages is necessary for the proper functioning of several Chrome features, like search, the new tab page and printing.</p>

    <p>These new policies function similarly to the existing <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#URLBlocklist" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URLBlocklist</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#URLAllowlist" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URLAllowlist</u></a> policies but are specifically designated for Incognito sessions. This allows organizations to restrict access to specific URLs in Incognito mode to protect sensitive information while permitting legitimate usage on other sites. Previously, administrators could only completely enable or disable Incognito mode via the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#IncognitoModeAvailability" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>IncognitoModeAvailability</u></a> policy.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows - </strong>Feature rolls out gradually: Introduces the <strong>IncognitoModeUrlBlocklist</strong> and <strong>IncognitoModeUrlAllowlist</strong> policies.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>
</div>

    <p>This update adds a new option, <code>extendedLifetime: true</code>, to the <code>SharedWorker</code> constructor. This requests that the shared worker be kept alive even after all current clients have unloaded. The primary use case is to allow pages to perform asynchronous work that requires JavaScript after a page unloads, without needing to rely on a service worker.</p>

  <li><strong>PWA origin migration&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>When a user installs a Progressive Web App (PWA), its identity and security context are tightly bound to its web origin, for example, app.example.com. This presents a significant challenge for developers who need to change their PWA's origin due to rebranding, domain restructuring, or technical re-architecture. Currently, such a change forces users to manually uninstall the old app and reinstall the new one, leading to a disruptive experience and potential user loss. Chrome 148 introduces a mechanism for developers to seamlessly migrate an installed PWA to a new, same-site origin, preserving user trust and permissions.</p>

    <p>The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebAppInstallForceList" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>WebAppInstallForceList</u></a> policy will block migration. Since enterprise policies around web applications are primarily based on URLs and origins, there is a risk that a migration would bypass certain policies an admin might have configured. No migration will be offered to the user when an app is force-installed by their enterprise administrator, and instead a banner will be shown explaining this to the user.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 148 on Windows, macOS, Linux</strong>: No rollout step.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>

    <p>The Prompt API is designed for interacting with an AI language model using text, image, and audio inputs. It supports various use cases, from generating image captions and performing visual searches to transcribing audio, classifying sound events, generating text following specific instructions, and extracting information or insights from text. It supports structured outputs which ensure that responses adhere to a predefined format, typically expressed as a JSON schema, to enhance response conformance and facilitate seamless integration with downstream applications that require standardized output formats.</p>

  <li><strong>Always Use Secure Connections&nbsp;by default&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 150 will enable the <strong>Always Use Secure Connections</strong> setting in the "public sites only" mode by default. This means Chrome will ask for the user's permission before the first access to any public site without HTTPS. Public sites are defined as sites that have a globally unique name, and excludes direct navigation to RFC 1918 addresses (192.168.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8, etc), as well as shortnames such as go/.</p>

    <p>If you are a website developer or IT professional, and you have users who may be impacted by this feature, we very strongly recommend enabling the "Always Use Secure Connections" setting today to help identify sites that you may need to work to migrate. Admins can use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HttpAllowlist" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>HttpAllowlist</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HttpsOnlyMode" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>HttpsOnlyMode</u></a> policies to override this behavior.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Isolated Web Apps&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p><a href="https://chromeos.dev/en/tutorials/getting-started-with-isolated-web-apps" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Isolated Web Apps</u></a> (IWAs) are an extension of existing work on PWA installation and Web Packaging that provide stronger protections against server compromise and other tampering that is necessary for developers of security-sensitive applications. Rather than being hosted on live web servers and fetched over HTTPS, these applications are packaged into Web Bundles, signed by their developer, and distributed to end-users through one or more of the potential methods described in the <a href="https://github.com/WICG/isolated-web-apps/blob/main/README.md" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>explainer</u></a>.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>As early as Chrome 150, IWAs will only be installable&nbsp;through an admin policy on enterprise-managed ChromeOS devices.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>SafeBrowsing API v4 to v5 migration&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome calls into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/v4" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SafeBrowsing v4 API</u></a> will be migrated to call into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>v5 API</u></a> instead. The method names are also different between v4 and v5. If admins have any v4-specific URL allowlisting to allow network requests to <code>https://safebrowsing.googleapis.com/v4*</code>, these should be modified to allow network requests to the whole domain instead: <code>safebrowsing.googleapis.com</code>. Otherwise, rejected network requests to the v5 API will cause security regressions for users. For more details, see <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference/Migration.From.V4" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Migration From V4 - Safe Browsing</u></a>.&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Deprecate and remove XSLT&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p><a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/xslt-10/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>XSLT v1.0</u></a>, which all browsers adhere to, was standardized in 1999. In the meantime, XSLT has evolved to v2.0 and v3.0, adding features, and growing apart from the old version frozen into browsers. This lack of advancement, coupled with the rise of JavaScript libraries and frameworks that offer more flexible and powerful DOM manipulation, has led to a significant decline in the use of client-side XSLT. Its role within the web browser has been largely superseded by JavaScript-based technologies, such as JSON+React.</p>

    <p>Chromium uses the libxslt library to process these transformations, and <a href="https://discourse.gnome.org/t/stepping-down-as-libxslt-maintainer/27615" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>libxslt was unmaintained</u></a> for ~6 months of 2025. Libxslt is a complex, aging C codebase of the type notoriously susceptible to memory safety vulnerabilities like buffer overflows, which can lead to arbitrary code execution. Because client-side XSLT is now a niche, rarely-used feature, these libraries receive far less maintenance and security scrutiny than core JavaScript engines, yet they represent a direct, potent attack surface for processing untrusted web content. Indeed, XSLT is the source of several recent high-profile security exploits that continue to put browser users at risk. For these reasons, Chromium (along with both other browser engines) plans to deprecate and remove XSLT from the web platform. For more details, see this article on&nbsp;<a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/deprecating-xslt" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Chrome for Developers</a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 143 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows: Deprecation (but not removal) of the APIs.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows:</strong> Origin Trial (OT) and Enterprise Policy go live for testing. These allow sites and enterprises to continue using features past the removal date.</li>
      <li>Chrome 160&nbsp;on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows: XSLT stops functioning on Stable releases, for all users other than Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy participants.</li>
      <li>Chrome 176&nbsp;on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows: Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy stop functioning. XSLT is disabled for all users.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>PostQuantum cryptography for DTLS in WebRTC&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature will enable the use of PostQuantum Cryptography (PQC) with WebRTC connections. The motivation for PQC is to get WebRTC media traffic up to date with the latest cryptography protocols and prevent <em>Harvest Now to Crack Later</em> scenarios.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>Admins will be able to control this feature using an enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement</u></a>, to allow enterprise users to opt out of PQC. The policy is temporary and is planned to be removed by Chrome 152.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 142 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: Feature rolls out</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong>: Remove enterprise policy</li>
    </ul>
  </li>

    <p>From September 2026 (Chrome 153) Chrome will move to a 2-week release cycle, from the current four-week cycle. The web platform is constantly advancing, and our goal at Chrome is to ensure developers and users have immediate access to the latest capabilities, fixes, and performance improvements. Building on our history of adapting our release process to match the demands of a modern web, we are announcing this significant step to further increase our development velocity and Chrome Stable is moving to a 2-week release cycle. You can find more details in the&nbsp;<a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-two-week-release" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Chrome for Developers</a>&nbsp;blog post.</p>

    <p>Extended Stable is available for customers who might have concerns about the maintenance costs. For more information about Extended Stable, see this&nbsp;<a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/16942104" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Help Center</a>&nbsp;article. The 2-week Stable option remains the most secure choice and should be used if security is a larger concern than maintenance costs.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Disallow spaces in non-file:// URL hosts&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>According to the <a href="https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#forbidden-host-code-point" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URL Standard specification</u></a> URL hosts cannot contain the space character, but currently URL parsing in Chromium allows spaces in the host. This causes Chromium to fail several tests included in the <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/websockets?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2024-websockets" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Interop2024 HTTPS URLs for WebSocket</u></a> and <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/url?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2023-url" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URL focus</u></a> areas. To bring Chromium into spec compliance, we would like to remove spaces from URL hosts altogether, but a difficulty with this is that they are used in the host part in Windows <code>file://</code> URLs. For more details, see this <a href="https://github.com/whatwg/url/issues/599" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Github discussion</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 157 on Android, ChromeOS, LaCrOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>
