  <li><strong>Device Bound Session Credentials&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrI145" name="chromeBrsrI145"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Introducing the Origin API&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>The <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc6454/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>origin</u></a> is a fundamental component of the web’s implementation, essential to both the security and privacy boundaries which user agents maintain. The concept is well-defined between HTML and URL, along with widely-used adjacent concepts like <em>site</em>.</p>

    <p>Origins, however, are not directly exposed to web developers. Though there are various origin getters on various objects, each of those returns the ASCII serialization of an origin, not the origin itself. This has a few negative implications. Practically, developers attempting to do same-origin or same-site comparisons when handling serialized origins often get things wrong in ways that lead to vulnerabilities. Philosophically, it seems like a missing security primitive that developers struggle to polyfill accurately.</p>

    <p>As early as Chrome 145, we plan to address this gap in the platform by introducing an Origin object that encapsulates the origin concept, and provides helpful methods for comparison, serialization, parsing, and so on.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 145 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrJ145" name="chromeBrsrJ145"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Local network access restrictions&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 142 restricted the ability to make requests to the user's local network, gated behind a permission prompt. A local network request is any request from a public website to a local IP address or loopback, or from a local website (for example, intranet) to loopback.</p>

    <p>Gating the ability for websites to perform these requests behind a permission mitigates the risk of cross-site request forgery attacks against local network devices such as routers, and reduces the ability of sites to use these requests to fingerprint the user's local network.</p>

    <p>This permission is restricted to secure contexts. If granted, the permissions additionally relaxes mixed content blocking for local network requests (since many local devices are not able to obtain publicly trusted TLS certificates for various reasons).</p>

    <p>This work supersedes a prior effort called <a href="https://chromestatus.com/feature/5737414355058688" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Private Network Access</u></a>, which used preflight requests to have local devices opt-in. For more information on this feature, see <a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QQkqehw8umtAgz5z0um7THx-aoU251p705FbIQjDuGs/edit?usp=sharing" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Adapting your website for new Local Network Access restrictions in Chrome</u></a>.</p>

    <p>Chrome 145 introduces more granular permissions for websites requesting access to a user's local network. The previous single local-network-access permission is being split into two distinct permissions:</p>

    <ul>
      <li>local-network: Grants access to IP addresses in the local network space (for example, intranets, internal devices).</li>
      <li>loopback-network: Grants access to loopback IP addresses (for example, localhost, 127.0.0.1).</li>
    </ul>

    <p>The old local-network permission will remain as an alias, ensuring existing configurations and Permissions Policies continue to function as expected. This change provides both users and Admins with more precise control over how websites interact with internal network resources. Current enterprise policies managing local network access will not be affected by this change.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 145 on Android, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong>: The permission split is rolled out.</li>
      <li>Chrome 147 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Local Network Access restrictions expanded to include WebSocket and WebTransport connections</li>
      <li>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut</u></a> policy will be removed.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrK145" name="chromeBrsrK145"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Reduced User-Agent strings by default&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Starting in Chrome 145, we will remove the <strong>UserAgentReduction</strong> policy. This policy was previously available to control whether Chrome sent a reduced or full User-Agent string.</p>

    <p>To enhance user privacy and reduce passive tracking capabilities, Chrome began reducing the information contained in the User-Agent header by default in Chrome version 110. The <strong>UserAgentReduction</strong> policy was provided as a temporary measure for enterprises to manage this transition.</p>

    <p>The recommended mechanism for websites to access browser and device information is now User-Agent Client Hints (UA-CH). UA-CH requires websites to actively request specific information, which is a more privacy-preserving approach than the legacy User-Agent string. For more details, see this article on web.dev, <a href="https://web.dev/articles/migrate-to-ua-ch" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Migrate to User-Agent Client Hints</u></a>.</p>

    <p>From Chrome 145 onwards, the <strong>UserAgentReduction</strong> policy will have no effect. Chrome will send a reduced User-Agent string by default. Systems or applications that relied on this policy to receive the full (legacy) User-Agent string may no longer receive the detailed information they expect.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 145 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Use of CssPixels in LayoutShift API&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature changes the attribution data (<code>prevRect</code> and <code>currentRect</code>) in the <a href="https://wicg.github.io/layout-instability/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LayoutShift API</u></a> to be reported in CSS pixels instead of physical pixels. The current behavior is inconsistent with other layout-related APIs, which all use CSS pixels. This change improves consistency, simplifies usage for developers, and aligns with expected units in debugging and tooling.</p>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrN145" name="chromeBrsrN145"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>WebRequest.SecurityInfo in Controlled Frame&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature introduces a WebRequest.SecurityInfo API for <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/iwa/controlled-frame" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ControlledFrame</u></a>. It allows a web app to intercept an HTTPS, WSS, or WebTransport request to a server, retrieve the server's certificate fingerprint (as verified by the browser), and then use that fingerprint to manually verify the certificate of a separate raw TCP/UDP connection to the same server. This provides a simple way for the app to confirm it's communicating with the correct server.</p>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrO145" name="chromeBrsrO145"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>2SV enforcement for Admin accounts&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>To better protect your organization’s information, Google now requires all accounts with access to <strong>admin.google.com</strong> to have 2-Step Verification (2SV) enabled. As a Google Workspace administrator, you need to confirm your identity with 2SV, which requires your password plus something additional, such as your phone or a security key. In Chrome 145, you should enable 2SV for the admin accounts in your organization before Google enforces it. For more information, see this <a href="https://support.google.com/a/answer/16271818" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>About 2SV enforcement for admins</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 137 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: 2SV enforcement starts</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 145 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: 2SV mandatory</li>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrP145" name="chromeBrsrP145"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Import data from Safari to Chrome for iOS made easier&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Users of Chrome for iOS can now import data (bookmarks, history, passwords, payment cards, and reading list entries) that they have previously exported from Safari. This helps users who are switching browsers to get set up faster and bring their existing data with them.</p>

    <p>Chrome cannot access this data directly; the user must provide a zip file containing their data, which can be exported through iOS settings. Chrome provides instructions on how to do so.</p>

    <p>When an on-device scam is detected using the visual features of the page, Chrome 145 now sends a request to <strong>Safe Browsing</strong> for a final verdict. Based on this verdict, Chrome decides whether to display a warning to the user.</p>

The feature is disabled for <strong>Standard Protection</strong> mode users or users with <strong>Safe Browsing</strong> disabled. Admins can control this <strong>Safe Browsing</strong> setting with the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SafeBrowsingProtectionLevel" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SafeBrowsingProtectionLevel</u></a> Chrome Enterprise policy.</p>

<div class="no-margin"><h2>Chrome Enterprise Premium changes</h2>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Hardening against local policy tampering&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> &nbsp;

    <p>Local settings on bring-your-own-device (BYOD) devices can sometimes conflict with corporate policy settings. To address this potential security gap, policy conflict signals in Chrome now detect and report whenever corporate policies are being overridden by local policy. Chrome 145 integrates these new policy conflict signals from the <strong>managed Chrome profile</strong> into existing security reports, controlled by the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UserSecuritySignalsReporting" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UserSecuritySignalsReporting</u></a> policy.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>For more information on device reporting, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/1698333#zippy=%2Creporting-policies" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>View ChromeOS device list and details - Chrome Enterprise and Education Help</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 144 on Linux, macOS, Windows: Detection and reporting of policy conflict metadata begins.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 145 on Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Visibility into Chrome policy hardening signals via the Devices API becomes available.</li>
      <li>Chrome 146 on Linux, macOS, Windows: Admin console UI is updated to display conflict signals and policy values begin reporting.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Upcoming Chrome browser changes</h4>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrA145" name="upChromeBrsrA145">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Bundled security settings&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature provides users with bundled security options to configure security settings based on their desired level of protection while using Chrome. Users can choose between <em>Enhanced</em> for the highest level of security and <em>Standard</em> for the default balanced protection. Users can still set custom values for the settings, as they can today. This simplifies the user experience and makes it easier for users to get the level of protection they want without needing to understand advanced configuration options. Existing enterprise policies take precedence over end-user bundle selections. If an existing policy is configured for security settings, the values will not be overridden by a user's choice of security bundle.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 146 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong></li>
    </ul>
    <img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/USADWrqac4uqKnJ0NpXfYHGqbfjM3m4cON5lq8SBBmfRAAd6pfsjmavSTG4z3d3si4M=w895" width="1080" height="563" alt="" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/USADWrqac4uqKnJ0NpXfYHGqbfjM3m4cON5lq8SBBmfRAAd6pfsjmavSTG4z3d3si4M"></li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrB145" name="upChromeBrsrB145">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>CSS update: decoupling of Width and Style properties&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome will soon align with updated <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/css-2025/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>CSS specifications</u></a> regarding the behavior of <code>border-width</code>, <code>outline-width</code>, and <code>column-rule-width</code> properties. Previously, if the corresponding <code>border-style</code>, <code>outline-style</code>, or <code>column-rule-style</code> was set to none or hidden, the computed width of these properties would be forced to 0px, regardless of the specified value.</p>

    <p>With this change, the computed values of <code>border-widt</code>h, <code>outline-width</code>, and <code>column-rule-width</code> will always reflect the author-specified values, independent of the *-style property. Additionally, the resolved values (as returned by <code>getComputedStyle()</code>) for <code>outline-width</code> and <code>column-rule-width</code> also will reflect the specified values.</p>

    <p>The change aligns Chrome with Firefox and WebKit, which have already implemented this behavior.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 146 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong>&nbsp;</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrC145" name="upChromeBrsrC145">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Remove third-party storage partitioning policies&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Third-party storage partitioning became the default in Chrome 115. The <code>chrome:// flag</code> that allowed users to disable this feature was removed in Chrome 128, and the deprecation trial ended with Chrome 139. In Chrome 146, the enterprise policies <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DefaultThirdPartyStoragePartitioningSetting" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DefaultThirdPartyStoragePartitioningSetting</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ThirdPartyStoragePartitioningBlockedForOrigins" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ThirdPartyStoragePartitioningBlockedForOrigins</u></a> will be removed. Users are advised to transition to alternative storage solutions, either by adapting to third-party storage partitioning or by using <code>document.requestStorageAccess({...})</code> where needed.</p>

    <p>If you have any feedback, you can add it <a href="https://g-issues.chromium.org/issues/425248669" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>here in the Chromium bug</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong><strong>Chrome 146 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong>: </strong>Removal of <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DefaultThirdPartyStoragePartitioningSetting" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DefaultThirdPartyStoragePartitioningSetting</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ThirdPartyStoragePartitioningBlockedForOrigins" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ThirdPartyStoragePartitioningBlockedForOrigins</u></a>&nbsp;policies&nbsp;</li>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrE145" name="upChromeBrsrE145">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>X25519Kyber768 key encapsulation for TLS&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 124 enabled by default on all desktop platforms a new post-quantum secure TLS key encapsulation mechanism <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-124-beta#x25519kyber768_key_encapsulation_for_tls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>X25519Kyber768</u></a>, based on a NIST standard (ML-KEM). This protects network traffic from Chrome with servers that also support ML-KEM from decryption by a future quantum computer. This change should be transparent to server operators. This cipher will be used for both <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8446" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>TLS 1.3</u></a> and <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9000/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>QUIC</u></a> connections.<br>
      However, some TLS middleboxes might be unprepared for the size of a Kyber (ML-KEM) key encapsulation, or a new TLS ClientHello cipher code point, leading to dropped or hanging connections. This can be resolved by updating your middlebox, or disabling the key encapsulation mechanism via the temporary <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>PostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled</u></a> enterprise policy, which will be available through Chrome 145. However, long term, post-quantum secure ciphers will be required in TLS and the enterprise policy will be removed as of Chrome 146. Post-quantum cryptography is required for CSNA 2.0. To learn more, see <a href="https://blog.chromium.org/2023/08/protecting-chrome-traffic-with-hybrid.html" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Protect Chrome Traffic with Hybrid Kyper KEM</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 131 on Linux, MacOS, Windows: Chrome will switch the key encapsulation mechanism to the final standard version of ML-KEM</li>
      <li><strong><strong>Chrome 146 on Linux, MacOS, Windows:</strong> </strong>Enterprise policy will be removed.&nbsp;</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrF145" name="upChromeBrsrF145">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Disallow spaces in non-file:// URL hosts&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>According to the <a href="https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#forbidden-host-code-point" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URL Standard specification</u></a> URL hosts cannot contain the space character, but currently URL parsing in Chromium allows spaces in the host. This causes Chromium to fail several tests included in the <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/websockets?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2024-websockets" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Interop2024 HTTPS URLs for WebSocket</u></a> and <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/url?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2023-url" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URL focus</u></a> areas. To bring Chromium into spec compliance, we would like to remove spaces from URL hosts altogether, but a difficulty with this is that they are used in the host part in Windows file:// URLs. For more details, see this <a href="https://github.com/whatwg/url/issues/599" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Github discussion</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Android, ChromeOS, LaCrOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrH145" name="upChromeBrsrH145">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Origin-Bound cookies (by default)&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>In Chrome 148, cookies are bound to their setting origin (by default) such that they're only accessible by that origin, that is, they are sent on a request or visible through document.cookie. Cookies might ease the host and port binding restrictions through use of the Domain attribute but all cookies will be bound to their setting scheme.</p>

    <p>Temporary enterprise policies <strong>LegacyCookieScopeEnabled</strong> and <strong>LegacyCookieScopeEnabledForDomainList</strong> will be made available to revert this change. These policies will stop working in Chrome 150.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 148 on Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Enterprise policies are available.</li>
      <li>Chrome 150 on Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Enterprise policies will be removed<span>&nbsp;</span></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrI145" name="upChromeBrsrI145">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>SafeBrowsing API v4 to v5 migration&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome calls into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/v4" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SafeBrowsing v4 API</u></a> will be migrated to call into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>v5 API</u></a> instead. The method names are also different between v4 and v5. If admins have any v4-specific URL allowlisting to allow network requests to <code>https://safebrowsing.googleapis.com/v4*</code>, these should be modified to allow network requests to the whole domain instead: <code>safebrowsing.googleapis.com</code>. Otherwise, rejected network requests to the v5 API will cause security regressions for users. For more details, see <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference/Migration.From.V4" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Migration From V4 - Safe Browsing</u></a>.&nbsp;</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 148 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: </strong>Feature would gradually roll out.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrJ145" name="upChromeBrsrJ145">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>UI Automation accessibility framework provider on Windows&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 126 began to directly support accessibility client software that uses Microsoft Windows's UI Automation accessibility framework. Prior to this change, such software interoperated with Chrome by way of a compatibility shim in Microsoft Windows. This change is being made to improve the accessible user experience for many users. It provides complete support for Narrator, Magnifier, and Voice Access; and will improve third-party apps that use Windows's UI Automation accessibility framework. Users of Chrome will find reduced memory usage and processing overhead when used with accessibility tools. It will also ease development of software using assistive technologies.</p>

    <p>Administrators can use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> enterprise policy starting in Chrome 125 to either force-enable the new provider (so that all users receive the new functionality), or disable the new provider.</p>

    <p>This policy will be supported through Chrome 147 and will be removed in Chrome 148. This one-year period is intended to give enterprises sufficient time to work with third-party vendors so that they may fix any incompatibilities resulting from the switch from Microsoft's compatibility shim to Chrome's UI Automation provider.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 125 on Windows:The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> policy is introduced so that administrators can enable Chrome's UI Automation accessibility framework provider and validate that third-party accessibility tools continue to work.</li>
      <li>Chrome 126 on Windows: The Chrome variations framework will be used to begin enabling Chrome's UI Automation accessibility framework provider for users. It will be progressively enabled to the full stable population, with pauses as needed to address compatibility issues that can be resolved in Chrome. Enterprise administrators may continue to use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> policy to either opt-in early to the new behavior, or to temporarily opt-out through Chrome 146.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 148 on Windows</strong>: The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> policy will be removed from Chrome. All clients will use the browser's UI Automation accessibility framework provider.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrK145" name="upChromeBrsrK145">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Deprecation and removal of Privacy Sandbox APIs&nbsp;&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome has <a href="https://privacysandbox.com/news/update-on-plans-for-privacy-sandbox-technologies/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>recently announced</u></a> that the current approach to third-party cookies is to be maintained, following which, we plan to deprecate and remove the following APIs.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Topics</li>
      <li>Protected Audience</li>
      <li>Shared Storage</li>
      <li>Attribution Reporting</li>
      <li>Private Aggregation</li>
      <li>Related Web Sites</li>
      <li>requestStorageAccessFor</li>
    </ul>

    <p>The following are the enterprise policies associated with the above APIs.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PrivacySandboxSiteEnabledAdsEnabled"><u>PrivacySandboxSiteEnabledAdsEnabled</u></a></li>
      <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PrivacySandboxAdTopicsEnabled"><u>PrivacySandboxAdTopicsEnabled</u></a></li>
      <li><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PrivacySandboxAdMeasurementEnabled"><u>PrivacySandboxAdMeasurementEnabled</u></a></li>
      <li>RelatedWebsiteSetsOverrides</li>
      <li>RelatedWebsiteSetsEnabled</li>
    </ul>

    <p>Deprecation began with Chrome 144, and removal is planned for Chrome 150. After deprecation, the APIs will continue to exist, and most users will see no disruptions. However, some users who rely on server-side integrations (such as k-anonymity server, or coordinators) will see a break in the services. We have proactively reached out to users of the APIs with our deprecation plans. At the time of removal, Chrome 150, all the policies associated with these APIs will also be removed.</p>

    <p>None of the APIs are enabled by default to enterprise users. Enterprise teams may want to review the status for any managed profile in their Admin console.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 144 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Deprecation launch.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: APIs and the associated Policies removal.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrL145" name="upChromeBrsrL145">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Enable "Always Use Secure Connections" by default&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 150 will enable the <strong>Always Use Secure Connections</strong> setting in the "public sites only" mode by default. This means Chrome will ask for the user's permission before the first access to any public site without HTTPS. Public sites are defined as sites that have a globally unique name, and excludes direct navigation to RFC 1918 addresses (192.168.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8, etc), as well as shortnames such as go/.</p>

    <p>Prior to enabling it by default for all users, Chrome will enable <strong>Always Use Secure Connections</strong> for the users who have opted in to <a href="https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/11577602" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Enhanced Safe Browsing protections in Chrome</u></a>.</p>

    <p>If you are a website developer or IT professional, and you have users who may be impacted by this feature, we very strongly recommend enabling the "Always Use Secure Connections" setting today to help identify sites that you may need to work to migrate. Admins can use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HttpAllowlist" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>HttpAllowlist</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HttpsOnlyMode" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>HttpsOnlyMode</u></a> policies to override this behavior.</p>

    <p>For more information, see our <a href="https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/docs/security/ask-before-http/ask-before-http-adoption-guide.md" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>adoption guide</u></a> and <a href="https://security.googleblog.com/2025/10/https-by-default.html" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>announcement blog post</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: </strong>Enable "Always Use Secure Connections" for users who have opted in to Enhanced Safe Browsing.</li>
      <li>Chrome 154 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: Enable "Always Use Secure Connections" by default for all users.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrM145" name="upChromeBrsrM145">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Isolated Web Apps&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p><a href="https://chromeos.dev/en/tutorials/getting-started-with-isolated-web-apps" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Isolated Web Apps</u></a> (IWAs) are an extension of existing work on PWA installation and Web Packaging that provide stronger protections against server compromise and other tampering that is necessary for developers of security-sensitive applications. Rather than being hosted on live web servers and fetched over HTTPS, these applications are packaged into Web Bundles, signed by their developer, and distributed to end-users through one or more of the potential methods described in the <a href="https://github.com/WICG/isolated-web-apps/blob/main/README.md" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>explainer</u></a>.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>As early as Chrome 150, IWAs will only be installable&nbsp;through an admin policy on enterprise-managed ChromeOS devices.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Windows </strong>This rollout adds support for Isolated Web Apps in enterprise-managed browser configurations on Windows.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrN145" name="upChromeBrsrN145">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome will remove support for macOS 12&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 150 will be the last release to support macOS 12; Chrome 151+ will no longer support macOS 12, which is outside of its support window with Apple. Running on a supported operating system is essential to maintaining security.</p>

    <p>On Macs running macOS 12, Chrome will continue to work, showing a warning infobar, but will not update any further. If a user wishes to have their Chrome&nbsp;updated, they need to update their computer to a support version of macOS.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>For new installations of Chrome 151+, macOS 13+ will be required.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 151 on Windows, MacOS, Linux</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrO145" name="upChromeBrsrO145">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Deprecate and remove XSLT&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p><a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/xslt-10/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>XSLT v1.0</u></a>, which all browsers adhere to, was standardized in 1999. In the meantime, XSLT has evolved to v2.0 and v3.0, adding features, and growing apart from the old version frozen into browsers. This lack of advancement, coupled with the rise of JavaScript libraries and frameworks that offer more flexible and powerful DOM manipulation, has led to a significant decline in the use of client-side XSLT. Its role within the web browser has been largely superseded by JavaScript-based technologies, such as JSON+React.</p>

    <p>Chromium uses the libxslt library to process these transformations, and <a href="https://discourse.gnome.org/t/stepping-down-as-libxslt-maintainer/27615" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>libxslt was unmaintained</u></a> for ~6 months of 2025. Libxslt is a complex, aging C codebase of the type notoriously susceptible to memory safety vulnerabilities like buffer overflows, which can lead to arbitrary code execution. Because client-side XSLT is now a niche, rarely-used feature, these libraries receive far less maintenance and security scrutiny than core JavaScript engines, yet they represent a direct, potent attack surface for processing untrusted web content. Indeed, XSLT is the source of several recent high-profile security exploits that continue to put browser users at risk. For these reasons, Chromium (along with both other browser engines) plans to deprecate and remove XSLT from the web platform. For more details, see this article on&nbsp;<a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/deprecating-xslt" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Chrome for Developers</a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 143 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows: Deprecation (but not removal) of the APIs.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows:</strong> Origin Trial (OT) and Enterprise Policy go live for testing. These allow sites and enterprises to continue using features past the removal date.</li>
      <li>Chrome 155 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows: XSLT stops functioning on Stable releases, for all users other than Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy participants.</li>
      <li>Chrome 164 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows: Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy stop functioning. XSLT is disabled for all users.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrP145" name="upChromeBrsrP145">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>PostQuantum cryptography for DTLS in WebRTC&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature will enable the use of PostQuantum Cryptography (PQC) with WebRTC connections. The motivation for PQC is to get WebRTC media traffic up to date with the latest cryptography protocols and prevent <em>Harvest Now to Crack Later</em> scenarios.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>Admins will be able to control this feature using an enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement</u></a>, to allow enterprise users to opt out of PQC. The policy will be temporary and is planned to be removed by Chrome 152.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 142 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: Feature rolls out</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong>: Remove enterprise policy</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<h4><strong>Upcoming Chrome Enterprise Core updates</strong></h4>

<p><a id="upChromeECA145" name="upChromeECA145">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Experimental cryptographic compliance policies&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p><strong>PreferSlowKEXAlgorithms</strong> and <strong>PreferSlowCiphers</strong> are two new, experimental enterprise policies that configure Chrome to order its preferred key agreement algorithms (supported groups) and encryption cipher algorithms, in <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8446" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>TLS 1.3</u></a>, to reflect a preference for algorithms that have been approved by a specific compliance regime. Currently, the only compliance regime is <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-becker-cnsa2-ssh-profile/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>CNSA2</u></a>. This does not guarantee that any specific algorithms will be negotiated. It allows server operators who want to support clients with and without compliance requirements to differentiate between clients, and only use certain non-default algorithms with increased cryptographic strength for those explicitly configured to prefer them. This policy is not required for security. The default cryptography used by Chrome is strong enough to withstand a brute force attack using the entire power of the sun. Setting this policy will cause Chrome to be slower when accessing websites. This policy only affects TLS 1.3 and <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9000/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>QUIC</u></a>, it does not affect earlier versions of TLS.</p>

    <p>These policies are temporarily available as a single combined flag, <code>chrome://#cryptography-compliance-cnsa</code>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 143 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: The policies are available but marked as <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/intl/en_ca/policies/#EnableExperimentalPolicies" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>experimental</u></a> for Chrome browser</li>
      <li>Chrome 144 on ChromeOS: The additional policies that apply to the ChromeOS device login screen are available but marked as experimental.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 146 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Around Chrome 146, the TLS servers for Google properties will be updated to negotiate ML-KEM-1024 when this flag is set. At that point, the policy will no longer be marked as experimental.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

<div class="no-margin"><h4><strong>Upcoming Chrome Enterprise Premium updates</strong></h4>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeEPA145" name="upChromeEPA145"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome Enterprise Connectors API&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome Enterprise will soon expand programmatic management for <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/12166576" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Enterprise Connectors</u></a>. This update will introduce resources to define and assign connector configurations, complementing the existing connector policies to allow administrators to manage the full life-cycle of these integrations at scale.</p>

    <p>Previously, configuring Service Providers was a manual process in the Google Admin console. This update enables automation, which helps reduce manual errors and improve the efficiency of managing integrations with third-party security solutions.</p>

    <p>Administrators can now use the Chrome Management API to manage ConnectorConfiguration resources (defining the provider). Connector Selection is managed via the Chrome Policy API, enabling the assignment of these configurations to Organizational Units or Groups. This works in tandem with existing Policy API settings for event reporting and content analysis, including policies such as <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnSecurityEventEnterpriseConnector" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>OnSecurityEventEnterpriseConnector</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnFileAttachedEnterpriseConnector" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>OnFileAttachedEnterpriseConnector</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnFileDownloadedEnterpriseConnector" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>OnFileDownloadedEnterpriseConnector</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnBulkDataEntryEnterpriseConnector" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>OnBulkDataEntryEnterpriseConnector</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnPrintEnterpriseConnector" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>OnPrintEnterpriseConnector</u></a>, and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#EnterpriseRealTimeUrlCheckMode" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>EnterpriseRealTimeUrlCheckMode</u></a>. For technical details, developers should refer to the <a href="https://developers.google.com/chrome/management/reference/rest" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Management API</u></a> and <a href="https://developers.google.com/chrome/policy/reference/rest" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Policy API documentation</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 143 on Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: This rollout adds support for programmatic management of Chrome Enterprise Connectors via a new API</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 146 on Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: This rollout introduces the ConnectorConfiguration and ConnectorSelection resources, enabling the creation of service provider instances and their assignment to organizational units.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeEPB145" name="upChromeEPB145"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Enterprise cache encryption&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome Enterprise Premium will offer Enterprise cache encryption, a feature designed to mitigate data exfiltration risks by encrypting browser data stored at rest, specifically the HTTP cache. Using OS-level APIs for key storage through App-Bound Encryption, this functionality renders locally stored data inaccessible to malware if a device is compromised.</p>

    <p>This feature operates transparently in the background, though it may impact performance due to real-time encryption. Administrators can manage this via the <strong>CacheEncryptionEnabled</strong> policy. Note that enabling or disabling this policy will automatically clear the existing cache to ensure data consistency.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 146 on Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Cache encryption becomes available on desktop platforms.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeEPC145" name="upChromeEPC145"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Support for AllowList and BlockList for DeveloperToolsAvailability policy&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome will introduce two new policies, <strong>DeveloperToolsAvailabilityAllowlist</strong> and <strong>DeveloperToolsAvailabilityBlocklist</strong>, which provide granular control over the availability of Developer Tools based on URL patterns.</p>

    <p>Previously, administrators could only allow or disallow Developer Tools globally. With these new policies, admins can now enforce a general block on Developer Tools to secure sensitive corporate data, while explicitly permitting access on specific internal URLs for development or troubleshooting purposes.</p>

    <p>These controls are available on Windows, Mac, Linux, and ChromeOS. If these new policies are not configured, the behavior of the existing <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DeveloperToolsAvailability" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DeveloperToolsAvailability</u></a> policy remains unchanged.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 146 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows -</strong> Feature rolls out gradually. Introduces the <strong>DeveloperToolsAvailabilityAllowlist</strong> and <strong>DeveloperToolsAvailabilityBlocklist</strong> policies on Desktop platforms.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeEPD145" name="upChromeEPD145"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Support for AllowList and BlockList for IncognitoModeAvailability policy&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome will introduce two new policies, <strong>IncognitoModeUrlBlocklist</strong> and <strong>IncognitoModeUrlAllowlist</strong>, to provide administrators with more precise control over Incognito mode usage. Previously, administrators could only completely enable or disable Incognito mode via the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#IncognitoModeAvailability" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>IncognitoModeAvailability</u></a> policy.</p>

    <p>These new policies function similarly to the existing <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#URLBlocklist" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URLBlocklist</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#URLAllowlist" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URLAllowlist</u></a> policies but are specifically designated for Incognito sessions. This allows organizations to restrict access to specific URLs in Incognito mode to protect sensitive information while permitting legitimate usage on other sites.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 146 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows - </strong>Feature rolls out gradually. Introduces the <strong>IncognitoModeUrlBlocklist</strong> and <strong>IncognitoModeUrlAllowlist</strong> policies.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeEPE145" name="upChromeEPE145"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Increased file size support for DLP scans&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome Enterprise Premium will extend its Data Loss Prevention (DLP) and malware scanning capabilities to include large and encrypted files. Previously, files larger than 50 MB and all encrypted files were skipped during content scanning. This update will close that critical security gap. For policies configured to save evidence, files <strong>up to 2GB</strong> can now be sent to the Evidence Locker. This provides administrators with greater visibility and control, significantly reducing the risk of data exfiltration through large file transfers.</p>

    <p>No new policy is required to enable this feature. It is automatically controlled by the existing DLP rule configurations in the Google Admin console. If admins have rules that apply to file uploads, downloads, or printing, they will now also apply to large and encrypted files. For more information, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/11587610" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>What are ChromeOS data controls?</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147&nbsp;on Linux, macOS, Windows: </strong>This stage enables the collection of large (&gt;50 MB) and encrypted files for the Evidence Locker, closing a key DLP security gap.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>
</div>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Upcoming ChromeOS changes</h4>

<p><a id="upChromeOSA145" name="upChromeOSA145"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>SkyVault Camera&nbsp;directory policy&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>Starting in ChromeOS 146, a new SkyVault policy will allow Admins specify a location for storing Camera files when local storage is deactivated on user devices.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p>

    <p>When&nbsp;<strong>Do not allow users to store and read local data</strong> (<a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalUserFilesAllowed" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LocalUserFilesAllowed</u></a>) is enabled, local storage is deactivated on user devices. This new SkyVault policy will allow Admins to extend&nbsp;that setting to apply for&nbsp;<strong>Camera files</strong>, using the <strong>Save to local Camera folder </strong>option.</p>
  </li>
</ul>
</div>

<p class="align-right"><a href="#top">↑ back to top</a> &nbsp;</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<div class="no-margin"><h2>Chrome browser changes &nbsp;</h2>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrA144" name="chromeBrsrA144"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>AI Mode and Lens enhancements&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Starting in Chrome 143 on macOS and Windows, new AI Mode capabilities are integrated into Chrome browser. Users can access AI Mode directly from the <strong>New tab</strong> page and the address bar, allowing users to ask complex questions directly from where they start browsing. Admins can turn off these features (value 1) using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AIModeSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>AIModeSettings</u></a> policy or by using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> (value 2). For more details, see this article in the <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/14443058#zippy=%2Cgemini-enterprise%2Cgoogle-lens%2Cai-mode:~:text=Google%20generative%20AI%20features%20available%20through%20Chrome" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Enterprise and Education Help Center</u></a>.</p>

    <p>In Chrome 144, we begin to roll out the multi-tab context feature on AI Mode and Lens. Users can choose to share the contents of one or more of their open tabs, helping them ask questions, compare, summarize, and find information more efficiently. Admins can turn off these features (value 1) using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SearchContentSharingSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SearchContentSharingSettings</u></a> policy or by using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> (value 2).</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 147 on MacOS, Windows: The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LensOverlaySettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LensOverlaySettings</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LensDesktopNTPSearchEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LensDesktopNTPSearchEnabled</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LensRegionSearchEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LensRegionSearchEnabled</u></a> policies will be deprecated. Admins can use <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SearchContentSharingSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SearchContentSharingSettings</u></a> to control these features.</li>
      <li>Chrome 143 on MacOS, Windows: New AI Model capabilities will be integrated into Chrome and can be controlled using <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AIModeSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>AIModeSettings</u></a> policy or the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> policy.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 144 on MacOS, Windows</strong>: The multi-tab context feature will be available and can be controlled using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SearchContentSharingSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SearchContentSharingSettings</u></a> policy or <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> policy.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrB144" name="chromeBrsrB144"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Preference tampering protection for enterprise users on Windows&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>To provide stronger, more consistent protection against malicious software, Chrome's encrypted preference tampering protection for enterprise-managed browsers is now available on Windows.</p>

    <p>Previously, this protection, which automatically resets tampered settings (like a hijacked search engine) to their default values, was not available for enterprise users on Windows. This exception was necessary because the legacy validation method was incompatible with roaming profiles, often causing incorrect resets.</p>

    <p>Chrome 144 implements a new, more secure system using an encryptor. This new encryption method is fully compatible with enterprise users. As this new system resolves the root cause of the original issue, we no longer need the legacy Windows enterprise exception.</p>

    <p>With this change, if Chrome detects that a sensitive preference has been modified by unauthorized software, it now automatically resets that preference to its default value. This behavior was previously disabled and is now being enabled. This change extends critical security protection to enterprise users, defending them against search hijacking and other malicious setting modifications.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 144 on Windows -</strong> Feature rolls out gradually</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrC144" name="chromeBrsrC144"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>CSS find-in-page highlight pseudos&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature exposes <strong>find-in-page</strong> search result styling to authors as a highlight pseudo-element, like selection and spelling errors. This allows authors to change the foreground and background colors or add text decorations, which can be especially useful if the browser defaults have insufficient contrast with the page colors or are otherwise unsuitable.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 144 on Windows, MacOS, Linux, Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrD144" name="chromeBrsrD144"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Deprecate savedTabGroups as individual value in SyncTypesListDisabled&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>To align desktop and ChromeOS behavior with mobile and to simplify sync management, the individual <code>savedTabGroups</code> datatype is now deprecated and is no longer an individually customizable value within the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SyncTypesListDisabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SyncTypesListDisabled</u></a> policy. Previously, the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SyncTypesListDisabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SyncTypesListDisabled</u></a> enterprise policy allowed administrators to disable the synchronization of <code>savedTabGroups</code> datatype on desktop and ChromeOS platforms. On mobile platforms, however, tab group synchronization is already managed by the tabs datatype.</p>

    <p>Starting with Chrome 144, if your <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SyncTypesListDisabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SyncTypesListDisabled</u></a> policy disables either tabs or <code>savedTabGroups</code>, both data types are now considered disabled. This means that disabling tabs also disables saved tab groups, and the other way around. The <code>savedTabGroups</code> value is entirely removed from the list of supported datatypes for this policy. For admins who have saved tab groups disabled, and intend to keep this behavior, make sure to explicitly disable the tabs datatype. This guarantees the desired behavior before the <code>savedTabGroups</code> value is fully removed.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 144 on ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrE144" name="chromeBrsrE144"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Happy Eyeballs V3&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p><a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-happy-happyeyeballs-v3/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Happy Eyeballs V3</u></a> is an algorithm used to reduce user-visible network connection delay. It performs DNS resolutions asynchronously and staggers connection attempts with preferable protocols (H3/H2/H1) and address families (IPv6/IPv4). Chrome 144 implements Happy Eyeballs V3 to achieve better network connection concurrency. You can control this feature using a temporary policy, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HappyEyeballsV3Enabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>HappyEyeballsV3Enabled</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 144 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrF144" name="chromeBrsrF144"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Multicast support for Direct Sockets API&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature allows <a href="https://chromeos.dev/en/web/isolated-web-apps" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Isolated Web Apps</u></a> (IWAs) to subscribe to multicast groups and receive User Datagram Protocol (UDP) packets from there. IWAs can now also specify additional parameters when sending UDP packets to multicast addresses.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 144 on Windows, MacOS, Linux</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrG144" name="chromeBrsrG144"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>ServiceWorkerAutoPreload browser mode&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p><code>ServiceWorkerAutoPreload</code> is a mode where the browser issues the network request in parallel with the service worker bootstrap. If the fetch handler returns the response with <code>respondWith()</code>, the browser consumes the network request result inside the fetch handler. If the fetch handler result is fallback, it passes the network response directly to the browser. <code>ServiceWorkerAutoPreload</code> is an optional browser optimization that changes the existing service worker behavior. Admins can control this feature using an enterprise policy called <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong><strong>Chrome 144 on Android, Windows:</strong> <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled</u></a> policy will be removed</strong></li>
      <li>Chrome 140 on Android, Windows: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled</u></a> policy will be available</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrH144" name="chromeBrsrH144"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Simplified New tab page&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature reduces visual clutter and enhances user control on the appearance of the <strong>New tab</strong> page (NTP). This simplification of the <strong>New tab</strong> page removes the <strong>Dismiss module</strong> button. Modules not managed by a policy can also be auto-removed after an extended period of inactivity.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong><strong>Chrome 144 on ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows</strong> - Feature rolls out gradually</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrI144" name="chromeBrsrI144"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Deprecation and removal of Privacy Sandbox APIs&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome has <a href="https://privacysandbox.com/news/update-on-plans-for-privacy-sandbox-technologies/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>recently announced</u></a> that the current approach to third-party cookies is to be maintained, following which, we plan to deprecate and remove the following APIs.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Topics</li>
      <li>Protected Audience</li>
      <li>Shared Storage</li>
      <li>Attribution Reporting</li>
      <li>Private Aggregation</li>
      <li>Related Web Sites</li>
      <li>requestStorageAccessFor</li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;

    <p>The following are the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/atomic-groups/#PrivacySandbox" rel="noopener" target="_blank">enterprise policies</a> associated with the above APIs.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>PrivacySandboxSiteEnabledAdsEnabled</li>
      <li>PrivacySandboxAdTopicsEnabled</li>
      <li>PrivacySandboxAdMeasurementEnabled</li>
      <li>RelatedWebsiteSetsOverrides</li>
      <li>RelatedWebsiteSetsEnabled</li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;

    <p>Deprecation will begin with Chrome 144, and removal is planned for Chrome 150. After deprecation, the APIs will continue to exist, and most users will see no disruptions. However, some users who rely on server-side integrations (such as k-anonymity server, or coordinators) will see a break in the services. We have proactively reached out to users of the APIs with our deprecation plans. At the time of removal, Chrome 150, all the policies associated with these APIs will also be removed.</p>

    <p>None of the APIs are enabled by default to enterprise users. Enterprise teams may want to review the status for any managed profile in their <strong>Admin console</strong>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 144 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows: </strong>Deprecation launch</li>
      <li>Chrome 150 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows: APIs and the associated Policies removal</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeECB144" name="chromeECB144"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Experimental cryptographic compliance policies&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p><strong>PreferSlowKEXAlgorithms</strong> and <strong>PreferSlowCiphers</strong> are two new, experimental enterprise policies that configure Chrome to order its preferred key agreement algorithms (supported groups) and encryption cipher algorithms, in <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8446" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>TLS 1.3</u></a>, to reflect a preference for algorithms that have been approved by a specific compliance regime. Currently, the only compliance regime is <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-becker-cnsa2-ssh-profile/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>CNSA2</u></a>. This does not guarantee that any specific algorithms will be negotiated. It allows server operators who want to support clients with and without compliance requirements to differentiate between clients, and only use certain non-default algorithms with increased cryptographic strength for those explicitly configured to prefer them. This policy is not required for security. The default cryptography used by Chrome is strong enough to withstand a brute force attack using the entire power of the sun. Setting this policy will cause Chrome to be slower when accessing websites. This policy only affects <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8446" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>TLS 1.3</u></a> and <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9000/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>QUIC</u></a>, it does not affect earlier versions of TLS.</p>

    <p>These policies are temporarily available as a single combined flag, <code>chrome://#cryptography-compliance-cnsa</code>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 143 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows, Fuchsia: The policies are available but marked as <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/intl/en_ca/policies/#EnableExperimentalPolicies" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>experimental</u></a> for Chrome browser</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 144 on ChromeOS:</strong> The additional policies that apply to the ChromeOS device login screen are available but marked as experimental.</li>
      <li>Chrome 146 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows: Around Chrome 146, the TLS servers for Google properties will be updated to negotiate ML-KEM-1024 when this flag is set. At that point, the policy will no longer be marked as experimental.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<div class="no-margin"><h2>Chrome Enterprise Premium changes</h2>

<p>Read more about the differences between <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/products/chrome-enterprise-premium" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Enterprise Core and Chrome Enterprise Premium</u></a>.</p>

<p><a id="chromeEPA144" name="chromeEPA144"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Copy and Paste rules protection&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> &nbsp;

    <p>To help organizations better prevent data exfiltration on mobile devices, Chrome is extending its existing desktop clipboard data controls. Administrators can now use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DataControlsRules" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DataControlsRules</u></a> policy to set rules that block or warn users when they attempt to copy or paste content that violates organizational policies.</p>

    <p>This feature allows admins to define data boundaries and prevent sensitive information from being pasted from a work context into personal apps or websites on their mobile fleet. This addresses a significant security gap and a frequently requested feature from enterprise customers who have cited the lack of mobile data controls as a concern.</p>

    <p>To use this feature, administrators can configure clipboard restrictions within the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DataControlsRules" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DataControlsRules</u></a> policy, providing a consistent management experience across desktop and mobile to strengthen their organization's overall security posture. For more details, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/11375053" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>this help center article</u></a>, which provides further context on how administrators can configure and manage Chrome Enterprise reporting connectors to forward browser security and data protection events to third-party services for analysis.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong><strong>Chrome 144 on iOS</strong>: Copy and Paste rules protection becomes available on iOS.</strong></li>
      <li>Chrome 140 on Android: Copy and Paste rules protection becomes available on Android.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeEPB144" name="chromeEPB144"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Hardening against local policy tampering&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> &nbsp;

    <p>Policy conflict detection signals for <a href="https://support.google.com/a/answer/9275380" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Context-Aware Access (CAA)</u></a>, closes a significant security gap by enabling the detection of corporate policies being overridden by conflicting local settings on BYOD devices.</p>

    <p>This is achieved by integrating new policy conflict signals from the managed Chrome profile into the existing security reporting pipeline, controlled by the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UserSecuritySignalsReporting" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UserSecuritySignalsReporting</u></a> policy.</p>

    <p>This visibility allows Admins to set CAA rules in Chrome Enterprise Premium's (CEP) Data and Threat Protection tools or Security Gateway to automatically block access to corporate applications if critical policies, such as DLP controls, Safe Browsing, or Extension blocklists, are found to be non-compliant.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 144 on Linux, MacOS, Windows:</strong> Detection and reporting of policy conflict metadata begins.</li>
      <li>Chrome 145 on Linux, MacOS, Windows: Enables the Context-Aware Access (CAA) evaluation flow to allow Admins to write enforcement rules based on the existence of a conflict.</li>
      <li>Chrome 146 on Linux, MacOS, Windows: Admin console UI is updated to display conflict signals and policy values begin reporting.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><span>&nbsp;</span><a id="chromeEPA143" name="chromeEPA143"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Enforced download to Cloud&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> &nbsp;

    <p>Admins can now configure a <a href="https://support.google.com/a/answer/10104358" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Data Loss Prevention (DLP) rule</u></a> that automatically redirects sensitive file downloads from a user's local device to their corporate Google Drive. This <strong>Force save to cloud storage</strong> action prevents sensitive data from resting on unmanaged local disks (for example, C:\Downloads), ensuring a secure chain of custody. When a user attempts to download a file flagged by DLP policies, the Secure Enterprise Browser extension intercepts the download and uploads it directly to the user's corporate drive.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><br>
        <strong>Chrome 144 on Linux, MacOS, Windows </strong>- Feature rolls out gradually: The <strong>Enforced download to Cloud</strong> remediation action becomes available in the Data Loss Prevention (DLP) rule builder.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeEPC144" name="chromeEPC144"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Proxy override rules&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> &nbsp;

    <p>To simplify proxy management in complex enterprise environments, Chrome 144 introduces two new policies: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ProxyOverrideRules" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ProxyOverrideRules</u></a> and <strong>EnableProxyOverrideRulesForAllUsers</strong>. Previously, organizations that used multiple proxy solutions (for example, a general proxy and a specific one for Google's Secure Gateway ) or have different admin teams (for example, for GPO and the Google Admin console) had to manually merge complex PAC files. This process is error-prone and creates significant administrative friction.</p>

    <p>The new <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ProxyOverrideRules" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ProxyOverrideRules</u></a> policy allows administrators to configure a list of routing rules that are evaluated before any existing proxy configuration, including PAC files set by the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ProxySettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ProxySettings</u></a> policy. This enables admins to easily <strong>prepend or override</strong> specific routes (for example, to send traffic for private web apps to a secure gateway ) without modifying the primary, company-wide PAC script.</p>

    <p>Users will see a notification in their chrome://settings page to inform them when these administrative proxy rules are active.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><br>
        <strong>Chrome 144 on ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows</strong>: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ProxyOverrideRules" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ProxyOverrideRules</u></a> becomes available.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>
</div>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Upcoming Chrome browser changes</h4>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrA144" name="upChromeBrsrA144">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>2SV enforcement for Admin accounts&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>To better protect your organization’s information, Google will soon require all accounts with access to <strong>admin.google.com</strong> to have 2-Step Verification (2SV) enabled. As a Google Workspace administrator, you need to confirm your identity with 2SV, which requires your password plus something additional, such as your phone or a security key. The enforcement will be rolled out gradually over the coming months. You should enable 2SV for the admin accounts in your organization before Google enforces it. For more information, see this <a href="https://support.google.com/a/answer/16271818" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>About 2SV enforcement for admins</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 145 on ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows:</strong> 2SV mandatory</li>
      <li>Chrome 137 on ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows: 2SV enforcement starts</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrC144" name="upChromeBrsrC144">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome removes support for obsolete virtual cameras on macOS&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>As early as Chrome 145, Chrome will remove support for obsolete virtual cameras for all macOS releases that it supports.</p>

    <p>On macOS, modern virtual cameras are built using the <a href="https://developer.apple.com/documentation/coremediaio" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Core Media IO</u></a> framework, which has been available since macOS 12.3. Apple has performed outreach, and all modern virtual camera software has been migrated to use this <a href="https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2022/10022/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Core Media IO framework</u></a>.</p>

    <p>Obsolete virtual cameras, built as DAL plugins, have been blocked by macOS itself starting with macOS 14.1 (2023), and have been unsupported in Safari since 2018, if not earlier.</p>

    <p>Chrome will remove support for obsolete virtual cameras for all macOS releases that it supports. This allows Chrome to improve security by fully disallowing loading of third-party libraries into Chrome processes.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 145 on Windows, MacOS, Linux</strong>&nbsp;</li>
