<p><a id="upChromeBrsrF144" name="upChromeBrsrF144">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Introducing the Origin API&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>The <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc6454/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>origin</u></a> is a fundamental component of the web’s implementation, essential to both the security and privacy boundaries which user agents maintain. The concept is well-defined between HTML and URL, along with widely-used adjacent concepts like <em>site</em>.</p>

    <p>Origins, however, are not directly exposed to web developers. Though there are various origin getters on various objects, each of those returns the ASCII serialization of an origin, not the origin itself. This has a few negative implications. Practically, developers attempting to do same-origin or same-site comparisons when handling serialized origins often get things wrong in ways that lead to vulnerabilities. Philosophically, it seems like a missing security primitive that developers struggle to polyfill accurately.</p>

    <p>As early as Chrome 145, we plan to address this gap in the platform by introducing an Origin object that encapsulates the origin concept, and provides helpful methods for comparison, serialization, parsing, and so on.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 145 on Windows, MacOS, Linux, Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

    <p>Chrome 145 will send a request to Safe Browsing for a final verdict when an on-device scam is detected using the visual features of the page. Based on this verdict, Chrome will decide whether to display a warning to the user.</p>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrH144" name="upChromeBrsrH144">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Reduced User-Agent strings by default &nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Starting in Chrome 145, the <strong>UserAgentReduction</strong> policy will be completely removed. This policy was previously available to control whether Chrome sent a reduced or full User-Agent string.</p>

    <p>To enhance user privacy and reduce passive tracking capabilities, Chrome began reducing the information contained in the User-Agent header by default in Chrome version 110. The <strong>UserAgentReduction</strong> policy was provided as a temporary measure for enterprises to manage this transition.</p>

    <p>The recommended mechanism for websites to access browser and device information is now User-Agent Client Hints (UA-CH). UA-CH requires websites to actively request specific information, which is a more privacy-preserving approach than the legacy User-Agent string. For more details, see this article on web.dev, <a href="https://web.dev/articles/migrate-to-ua-ch" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Migrate to User-Agent Client Hints</u></a>.</p>

    <p>From Chrome 145 onwards, the <strong>UserAgentReduction</strong> policy will have no effect. Chrome will send a reduced User-Agent string by default. Systems or applications that relied on this policy to receive the full (legacy) User-Agent string may no longer receive the detailed information they expect.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 145 on Windows, MacOS, Linux, Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Use of CssPixels in LayoutShift API&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature changes the attribution data (prevRect and currentRect) in the <a href="https://wicg.github.io/layout-instability/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LayoutShift API</u></a> to be reported in CSS pixels instead of physical pixels. The current behavior is inconsistent with other layout-related APIs, which all use CSS pixels. This change improves consistency, simplifies usage for developers, and aligns with expected units in debugging and tooling. The feature is gated behind a flag for experimentation and evaluation. <p><a id="upChromeBrsrL144" name="upChromeBrsrL144">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Local network access restrictions&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 142 restricts the ability to make requests to the user's local network, gated behind a permission prompt.</p>

    <p>A local network request is any request from a public website to a local IP address or loopback, or from a local website (for example, intranet) to loopback. Gating the ability for websites to perform these requests behind a permission mitigates the risk of cross-site request forgery attacks against local network devices such as routers, and reduces the ability of sites to use these requests to fingerprint the user's local network.</p>

    <p>This permission is restricted to secure contexts. If granted, the permissions additionally relaxes mixed content blocking for local network requests (since many local devices are not able to obtain publicly trusted TLS certificates for various reasons).</p>

    <p>This work supersedes a prior effort called <a href="https://chromestatus.com/feature/5737414355058688" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Private Network Access</u></a>, which used preflight requests to have local devices opt-in.</p>

    <p>For more information on this feature, see <a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QQkqehw8umtAgz5z0um7THx-aoU251p705FbIQjDuGs/edit?usp=sharing" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Adapting your website for new Local Network Access restrictions in Chrome</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut</u></a> will be removed.</strong></li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 146 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows</strong>: Local Network Access restrictions expanded to include WebSocket and WebTransport connections.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrO144" name="upChromeBrsrO144">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>X25519Kyber768 key encapsulation for TLS&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 124 enabled by default on all desktop platforms a new post-quantum secure TLS key encapsulation mechanism <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-124-beta#x25519kyber768_key_encapsulation_for_tls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>X25519Kyber768</u></a>, based on a NIST standard (ML-KEM). This protects network traffic from Chrome with servers that also support ML-KEM from decryption by a future quantum computer. This change should be transparent to server operators. This cipher will be used for both <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8446" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>TLS 1.3</u></a> and <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9000/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>QUIC</u></a> connections.</p>

    <p>However, some TLS middleboxes might be unprepared for the size of a Kyber (ML-KEM) key encapsulation, or a new TLS ClientHello cipher code point, leading to dropped or hanging connections. This can be resolved by updating your middlebox, or disabling the key encapsulation mechanism via the temporary <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>PostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled</u></a> enterprise policy, which will be available through the end of 2024. However, long term, post-quantum secure ciphers will be required in TLS and the enterprise policy will be removed. Post-quantum cryptography is required for CSNA 2.0. To learn more, see <a href="https://blog.chromium.org/2023/08/protecting-chrome-traffic-with-hybrid.html" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Protect Chrome Traffic with Hybrid Kyper KEM</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 131 on Linux, MacOS, Windows: Chrome will switch the key encapsulation mechanism to the final standard version of ML-KEM</li>
      <li><strong><strong>Chrome 146 on Linux, MacOS, Windows:</strong> Enterprise policy will be removed</strong></li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrP144" name="upChromeBrsrP144">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Disallow spaces in non-file:// URL hosts&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>According to the <a href="https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#forbidden-host-code-point" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URL Standard specification</u></a> URL hosts cannot contain the space character, but currently URL parsing in Chromium allows spaces in the host. This causes Chromium to fail several tests included in the <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/websockets?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2024-websockets" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Interop2024 HTTPS URLs for WebSocket</u></a> and <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/url?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2023-url" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URL focus</u></a> areas. To bring Chromium into spec compliance, we would like to remove spaces from URL hosts altogether, but a difficulty with this is that they are used in the host part in Windows file:// URLs. For more details, see this <a href="https://github.com/whatwg/url/issues/599" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Github discussion</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Android, ChromeOS, LaCrOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrQ144" name="upChromeBrsrQ144">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>UI Automation accessibility framework provider on Windows</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Starting in Chrome 126, Chrome will start directly supporting accessibility client software that uses Microsoft Windows's UI Automation accessibility framework. Prior to this change, such software interoperated with Chrome by way of a compatibility shim in Microsoft Windows. This change is being made to improve the accessible user experience for many users. It provides complete support for Narrator, Magnifier, and Voice Access; and will improve third-party apps that use Windows's UI Automation accessibility framework. Users of Chrome will find reduced memory usage and processing overhead when used with accessibility tools. It will also ease development of software using assistive technologies.</p>

    <p>Administrators may use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> enterprise policy starting in Chrome 125 to either force-enable the new provider (so that all users receive the new functionality), or disable the new provider. This policy will be supported through Chrome 147, and will be removed in Chrome 147. This one-year period is intended to give enterprises sufficient time to work with third-party vendors so that they may fix any incompatibilities resulting from the switch from Microsoft's compatibility shim to Chrome's UI Automation provider.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 125 on Windows: The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> policy is introduced so that administrators can enable Chrome's UI Automation accessibility framework provider and validate that third-party accessibility tools continue to work.</li>
      <li>Chrome 126 on Windows: The Chrome variations framework will be used to begin enabling Chrome's UI Automation accessibility framework provider for users. It will be progressively enabled to the full stable population, with pauses as needed to address compatibility issues that can be resolved in Chrome. Enterprise administrators may continue to use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> policy to either opt-in early to the new behavior, or to temporarily opt-out through Chrome 146.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Windows: </strong>The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> policy will be removed from Chrome. All clients will use the browser's UI Automation accessibility framework provider.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrR144" name="upChromeBrsrR144">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>WebRequest.SecurityInfo in Controlled Frame&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature introduces a WebRequest.SecurityInfo API for <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/iwa/controlled-frame" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ControlledFrame</u></a>. It allows a web app to intercept an HTTPS, WSS or WebTransport request to a server, retrieve the server's certificate fingerprint (as verified by the browser), and then use that fingerprint to manually verify the certificate of a separate raw TCP/UDP connection to the same server. This provides a simple way for the app to confirm it's talking to the correct server.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Windows, MacOS, Linux</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrS144" name="upChromeBrsrS144">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Origin-Bound cookies (by default)&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>In Chrome 148, cookies will be bound to their setting origin (by default) such that they're only accessible by that origin, that is, sent on a request or visible through <code>document.cookie</code>. Cookies might ease the host and port binding restrictions through use of the Domain attribute but all cookies will be bound to their setting scheme.</p>

    <p>Temporary enterprise policies <strong>LegacyCookieScopeEnabled</strong> and <strong>LegacyCookieScopeEnabledForDomainList</strong> will be available to revert this change. These policies will stop working in Chrome 150.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 148&nbsp;on Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Enterprise policies will be available</li>
      <li>Chrome 150 on Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Enterprise policies would be removed</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrT144" name="upChromeBrsrT144">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>SafeBrowsing API v4 to v5 migration&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome calls into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/v4" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SafeBrowsing v4 API</u></a> will be migrated to call into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>v5 API</u></a> instead. The method names are also different between v4 and v5. If admins have any v4-specific URL allowlisting to allow network requests to <code>https://safebrowsing.googleapis.com/v4*</code>, these should be modified to allow network requests to the whole domain instead: <code>safebrowsing.googleapis.com</code>. Otherwise, rejected network requests to the v5 API will cause security regressions for users. For more details, see <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference/Migration.From.V4" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Migration From V4 - Safe Browsing</u></a>.&nbsp;</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 148 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: </strong>Feature would gradually roll out.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrU143" name="upChromeBrsrU143">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Isolated Web Apps&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Isolated Web Apps (IWAs) are an extension of existing work on PWA installation and Web Packaging that provide stronger protections against server compromise and other tampering that is necessary for developers of security-sensitive applications. Rather than being hosted on live web servers and fetched over HTTPS, these applications are packaged into Web Bundles, signed by their developer, and distributed to end-users through one or more of the potential methods described in the <a href="https://github.com/WICG/isolated-web-apps/blob/main/README.md" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>explainer</u></a>.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>As early as Chrome 150, IWAs will only be installable through an admin policy on enterprise-managed ChromeOS devices.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Windows </strong>This rollout adds support for Isolated Web Apps in enterprise-managed browser configurations on Windows.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrV144" name="upChromeBrsrV144">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome will remove support for macOS 12&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 150 will be the last release to support macOS 12; Chrome 151+ will no longer support macOS 12, which is outside of its support window with Apple. Running on a supported operating system is essential to maintaining security.</p>

    <p>On Macs running macOS 12, Chrome will continue to work, showing a warning infobar, but will not update any further. If a user wishes to have their Chrome&nbsp;updated, they need to update their computer to a support version of macOS.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>For new installations of Chrome 151+, macOS 13+ will be required.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 151 on Windows, MacOS, Linux</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrW144" name="upChromeBrsrW144">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Deprecate and remove XSLT&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p><a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/xslt-10/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>XSLT v1.0</u></a>, which all browsers adhere to, was standardized in 1999. In the meantime, XSLT has evolved to v2.0 and v3.0, adding features, and growing apart from the old version frozen into browsers. This lack of advancement, coupled with the rise of JavaScript libraries and frameworks that offer more flexible and powerful DOM manipulation, has led to a significant decline in the use of client-side XSLT. Its role within the web browser has been largely superseded by JavaScript-based technologies, such as JSON+React.</p>

    <p>Chromium uses the libxslt library to process these transformations, and <a href="https://discourse.gnome.org/t/stepping-down-as-libxslt-maintainer/27615" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>libxslt was unmaintained</u></a> for ~6 months of 2025. Libxslt is a complex, aging C codebase of the type notoriously susceptible to memory safety vulnerabilities like buffer overflows, which can lead to arbitrary code execution. Because client-side XSLT is now a niche, rarely-used feature, these libraries receive far less maintenance and security scrutiny than core JavaScript engines, yet they represent a direct, potent attack surface for processing untrusted web content. Indeed, XSLT is the source of several recent high-profile security exploits that continue to put browser users at risk. For these reasons, Chromium (along with both other browser engines) plans to deprecate and remove XSLT from the web platform. For more details, see this article on&nbsp;<a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/deprecating-xslt" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Chrome for Developers</a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 143 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows: Deprecation (but not removal) of the APIs.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows:</strong> Origin Trial (OT) and Enterprise Policy go live for testing. These allow sites and enterprises to continue using features past the removal date.</li>
      <li>Chrome 155 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows: XSLT stops functioning on Stable releases, for all users other than Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy participants.</li>
      <li>Chrome 164 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows: Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy stop functioning. XSLT is disabled for all users.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrX144" name="upChromeBrsrX144">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>PostQuantum cryptography for DTLS in WebRTC&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature will enable the use of PostQuantum Cryptography (PQC) with WebRTC connections. The motivation for PQC is to get WebRTC media traffic up to date with the latest cryptography protocols and prevent <em>Harvest Now to Crack Later</em> scenarios.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>Admins will be able to control this feature using an enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement</u></a>, to allow enterprise users to opt out of PQC. The policy will be temporary and is planned to be removed by Chrome 152.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 142 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: Feature rolls out</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong>: Remove Enterprise Policy</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<div class="no-margin"><h4><strong>Upcoming Chrome Enterprise Premium updates</strong></h4>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeEPA144" name="upChromeEPA144"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Increased file size support for DLP scans&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome Enterprise Premium will extend its Data Loss Prevention (DLP) and malware scanning capabilities to include large and encrypted files. Previously, files larger than 50 MB and all encrypted files were skipped during content scanning. This update will close that critical security gap. For policies configured to save evidence, files <strong>up to 2GB</strong> can now be sent to the Evidence Locker. This provides administrators with greater visibility and control, significantly reducing the risk of data exfiltration through large file transfers.</p>

    <p>No new policy is required to enable this feature. It is automatically controlled by the existing DLP rule configurations in the Google Admin console. If admins have rules that apply to file uploads, downloads, or printing, they will now also apply to large and encrypted files. For more information, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/11587610" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>What are ChromeOS data controls?</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147&nbsp;on Linux, macOS, Windows: </strong>This stage enables the collection of large (&gt;50 MB) and encrypted files for the Evidence Locker, closing a key DLP security gap.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>
</div>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Current ChromeOS updates</h4>

<p><a id="chromeOSA144" name="chromeOSA144"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Class Tools wireless screen share and annotations for teachers&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>We're launching two powerful new features for teachers&nbsp; in Class Tools: Wireless Screen Share and Annotations.</p>

    <p>Teachers can now wirelessly project their screen, or a student's, to the classroom display. To connect, teachers enter a unique code into the Class Tools teacher app, which pairs with a dedicated ChromeOS receiver device (like a Chromebook, Chromebox, or ChromeOS Flex device) set up by your admin. This allows teachers to guide lessons and spotlight student work for the whole class to see.</p>

    <p>To make lessons more dynamic, the new Annotations feature allows teachers to draw or write on their device using a stylus, finger, trackpad, or mouse. Their notes and highlights appear in real-time on the mirrored display, perfect for emphasizing key points and engaging students directly with the material. We are increasing the maximum number of students in a Class Tools session to 100.</p>

    <p>For more information, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a?p=screenshare" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Use Class Tools</u></a> in the Help Center.</p>

    <p>This feature on ChromeOS 144 allows Progressive Web Apps (<a href="https://web.dev/articles/what-are-pwas" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>PWAs</u></a>) to declare handled protocols in the manifest and allows the user to select default handlers when multiple PWAs declare the same protocol. This change enables <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/best-practices/url-protocol-handler" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URL protocol handler registration for PWAs</u></a> as described on <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome for Developer docs for Web Platform</u></a>.</p>

    <p>In ChromeOS 144, Gemini will be integrated into Chrome on Chromebook Plus devices, and gradually rolls out as part of this release. <div class="no-margin"><h2>Chrome browser changes &nbsp;</h2>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrA143" name="chromeBrsrA143"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Deprecate and remove XSLT&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p><a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/xslt-10/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>XSLT v1.0</u></a>, which all browsers adhere to, was standardized in 1999. In the meantime, XSLT has evolved to v2.0 and v3.0, adding features, and growing apart from the old version frozen into browsers. This lack of advancement, coupled with the rise of JavaScript libraries and frameworks that offer more flexible and powerful DOM manipulation, has led to a significant decline in the use of client-side XSLT. Its role within the web browser has been largely superseded by JavaScript-based technologies, such as JSON+React.</p>

    <p>Chromium uses the libxslt library to process these transformations, but <a href="https://discourse.gnome.org/t/stepping-down-as-libxslt-maintainer/27615" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>libxslt has been unmaintained</u></a> for approximately 6 months of 2025. Libxslt is a complex, aging, C codebase that is susceptible to memory safety vulnerabilities like buffer overflows, which can lead to arbitrary code execution. Because client-side XSLT is now a niche, rarely-used feature, these libraries receive far less maintenance and security scrutiny than core JavaScript engines, yet they represent a direct, potent attack surface for processing untrusted web content. Indeed, XSLT is the source of several recent high-profile security exploits that continue to put browser users at risk.</p>

    <p>For these reasons, Chromium (along with both other browser engines) plans to deprecate and remove XSLT from the web platform. For more details, see this <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/deprecating-xslt" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome for Developers article</u></a>.&nbsp;</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 143 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Deprecation (but not removal) of the APIs&nbsp;</li>
      <li>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Origin Trial (OT) and Enterprise Policy go live for testing. These allow sites and enterprises to continue using features past the removal date.</li>
      <li>Chrome 155 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: XSLT stops functioning on Stable releases, for all users other than Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy participants.</li>
      <li>Chrome 164 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Origin Trial and Enterprise Policy stop functioning. XSLT is disabled for all users.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrB143" name="chromeBrsrB143"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>AI Mode enhancements&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 143 integrates new AI Mode capabilities into Chrome on macOS and Windows. Users will be able to access AI Mode directly from the <strong>New tab</strong> page and the omnibox, allowing users to ask complex questions directly from where they start browsing. This will start rolling out in Chrome 143 on macOS and Windows. Admins can turn off these features (value 1) using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AIModeSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>AIModeSettings</u></a> policy or by using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> (value 2). For more details, see the relevant section in the <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/14443058?hl=en&amp;ref_topic=14443801&amp;sjid=8990478865329402994-NA#zippy=%2Cgemini-enterprise%2Cgoogle-lens%2Cai-mode:~:text=Google%20generative%20AI%20features%20available%20through%20Chrome" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Help Center</u></a>.</p>

    <p>Also coming in Chrome 144 is the multi-tab context feature. Users can choose to share the contents of one or more of their open tabs with AI Mode, helping them ask questions, compare, summarize, and find information more efficiently. Admins will be able to turn off these features (value 1) using the <strong>SearchContentSharingSettings</strong> policy (available in Chrome 144) or by using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> (value 2).</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 143 on macOS, Windows</strong>: New AI Model capabilities integrated into Chrome and can be controlled using <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AIModeSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>AIModeSettings</u></a> policy or the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> policy</li>
      <li>Chrome 144&nbsp; on MacOS, Windows: The multi-tab context feature will be available and can be controlled using the SearchContentSharingSettings policy or <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> policy</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrC143" name="chromeBrsrC143"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>ICU version 77.1 (supporting Unicode 16)&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>The Unicode support library, International Components for Unicode (ICU), is upgraded from version 74.2 to version 77.1, adding support for Unicode 16 and updating locale data.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>Two changes could pose some risk for web applications that assume a specific format from the <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Internationalization" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Intl</u></a> JS APIs:</p>

    <ol>
      <li>The default Italian number formatting changed to omit the thousand separator for 4-digit numbers. For example new <code>Intl.NumberFormat("it").format(1234)</code> will return <em>1234</em> instead of <em>1.234</em>. The old behavior can be achieved with the <code>useGrouping</code> parameter for the <code>Intl.NumberFormat</code> constructor.&nbsp;</li>
      <li>In some English locales (en-AU, en-GB, and en-IN), a comma was added after full-length weekdays, for example, changing Saturday 30 April 2011 to Saturday, 30 April 2011. Web applications should avoid relying on the precise formatting of dates and they may change again in future.</li>
    </ol>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 143 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeECD143" name="chromeECD143"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Experimental cryptographic compliance policies&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>PreferSlowKEXAlgorithms and PreferSlowCiphers are two new, experimental enterprise policies that configure Chrome to order its preferred key agreement algorithms (supported groups) and encryption cipher algorithms, in TLS 1.3, to reflect a preference for algorithms that have been approved by a specific compliance regime. As of now, the only compliance regime is CNSA2. This does not guarantee that any specific algorithms will be negotiated. It allows server operators who want to support clients with and without compliance requirements to differentiate between clients, and only use certain non-default algorithms with increased cryptographic strength for those explicitly configured to prefer them. This policy is not required for security. The default cryptography used by Chrome is strong enough to withstand a brute force attack using the entire power of the sun. Setting this policy will cause Chrome to be slower when accessing websites. This policy only affects TLS 1.3 and QUIC, it does not affect earlier versions of TLS.</p>

    <p>These policies are temporarily available as a single combined flag, <code>chrome://#cryptography-compliance-cnsa</code>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 143 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: </strong>The policies are available but marked as <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/intl/en_ca/policies/#EnableExperimentalPolicies" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>experimental</u></a> for Chrome browser</li>
      <li>Chrome 144 on ChromeOS: The additional policies that apply to the ChromeOS device login screen are available but marked as experimental</li>
      <li>Chrome 146 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Around Chrome 146, the TLS servers for Google properties will be updated to negotiate ML-KEM-1024 when this flag is set. At that point, the policy will no longer be marked as experimental.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

Gemini in Chrome also serves as a productivity agent by enabling YouTube, Maps, Gmail, Drive, Keep, Calendar, and Tasks tools.</p>

    <p>This feature provides users with bundled security options to configure security settings based on their desired level of protection while using Chrome. Users can choose between Enhanced for the highest level of security and Standard for the default balanced protection. Users can still set custom values for the settings, as they can today. <p><a id="upChromeBrsrB143" name="upChromeBrsrB143">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Deprecating savedTabGroups as individual value in SyncTypesListDisabled&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Currently, the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SyncTypesListDisabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SyncTypesListDisabled</u></a> enterprise policy allows administrators to disable the synchronization of <code>savedTabGroups</code> datatype on desktop platforms. On mobile platforms, however, Tab Groups synchronization is already managed by the tabs datatype. To align desktop behavior with mobile and simplify sync management, the individual <code>savedTabGroups</code> datatype will be deprecated and will no longer be an individually customizable value within the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SyncTypesListDisabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SyncTypesListDisabled</u></a> policy.</p>

    <p>Action required by administrators:&nbsp;</p>

    <p>Starting with Chrome 144, if your <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SyncTypesListDisabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SyncTypesListDisabled</u></a> policy disables either tabs or <code>savedTabGroups</code>, both data types will now be considered disabled. This means that disabling tabs will also disable saved tab groups, and vice-versa. The <code>savedTabGroups</code> value will be entirely removed from the list of supported datatypes for this policy. Administrators who have saved tab groups disabled and intend to keep this behavior must explicitly disable the tabs datatype. This will ensure the desired behavior before the <code>savedTabGroups</code> value is fully removed.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 144 on Windows, macOS, Linux</strong></li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

    <p>This launch is an internal optimization in Chrome that implements <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-happy-happyeyeballs-v3/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Happy Eyeballs V3</u></a> to achieve better network connection concurrency. Happy Eyeballs V3 performs DNS resolutions asynchronously and staggers connection attempts with preferable protocols (H3/H2/H1) and address families (IPv6 or IPv4) to reduce user-visible network connection delay. This feature is gated by a temporary policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HappyEyeballsV3Enabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>HappyEyeballsV3Enabled</u></a>.</p>

    <p><em>ServiceWorkerAutoPreload</em> is a mode where the browser issues the network request in parallel with the service worker bootstrap, and consumes the network request result inside the fetch handler if the fetch handler returns the response with respondWith(). If the fetch handler result is fallback, it passes the network response directly to the browser. <em>ServiceWorkerAutoPreload</em> is defined as an optional browser optimization, which will change the existing service worker behavior. Admins can control this feature using an enterprise policy called <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled</u></a>.</p>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrN143" name="upChromeBrsrN143">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>X25519Kyber768 key encapsulation for TLS&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 124 enabled by default on all desktop platforms a new post-quantum secure TLS key encapsulation mechanism <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-124-beta#x25519kyber768_key_encapsulation_for_tls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>X25519Kyber768</u></a>, based on a NIST standard (ML-KEM). This protects network traffic from Chrome with servers that also support ML-KEM from decryption by a future quantum computer. This change should be transparent to server operators. This cipher will be used for both TLS 1.3 and QUIC connections.</p>

    <p>However, some TLS middleboxes might be unprepared for the size of a Kyber (ML-KEM) key encapsulation, or a new TLS ClientHello cipher code point, leading to dropped or hanging connections. This can be resolved by updating your middlebox, or disabling the key encapsulation mechanism via the temporary <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>PostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled</u></a> enterprise policy, which will be available through the end of 2024. However, long term, post-quantum secure ciphers will be required in TLS and the enterprise policy will be removed. Post-quantum cryptography is required for CSNA 2.0. To learn more, see <a href="https://blog.chromium.org/2023/08/protecting-chrome-traffic-with-hybrid.html" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Protect Chrome Traffic with Hybrid Kyber KEM</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 131 on Linux, macOS, Windows: Chrome will switch the key encapsulation mechanism to the final standard version of ML-KEM</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 146 on Linux, macOS, Windows:</strong> Enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>PostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled</u></a> will be removed</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrO143" name="upChromeBrsrO143">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Disallow spaces in non-file:// URL hosts&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>According to the <a href="https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#forbidden-host-code-point" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URL Standard specification</u></a>, URL hosts cannot contain the space character, but currently URL parsing in Chromium allows spaces in the host. This causes Chromium to fail several tests included in the <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/websockets?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2024-websockets" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Interop2024 HTTPS URLs for WebSocket</u></a> and <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/url?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2023-url" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URL focus</u></a> areas. To bring Chromium into spec compliance, we would like to remove spaces from URL hosts altogether, but a difficulty with this is that they are used in the host part in Windows <code>file://</code> URLs (<a href="https://github.com/whatwg/url/issues/599" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Github</u></a>).</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Android, ChromeOS, LaCrOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrP143" name="upChromeBrsrP143">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>UI Automation accessibility framework provider on Windows&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Starting in Chrome 126, Chrome will start directly supporting accessibility client software that uses Microsoft Windows's UI Automation accessibility framework. Prior to this change, such software interoperated with Chrome by way of a compatibility shim in Microsoft Windows. This change is being made to improve the accessible user experience for many users. It provides complete support for Narrator, Magnifier, and Voice Access; and will improve third-party apps that use Windows's UI Automation accessibility framework. Users of Chrome will find reduced memory usage and processing overhead when used with accessibility tools. It will also ease development of software using assistive technologies.</p>

    <p>Administrators can use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> enterprise policy starting in Chrome 125 to either force-enable the new provider (so that all users receive the new functionality), or disable the new provider. This policy will be supported through Chrome 146, and will be removed in Chrome 147. This one-year period is intended to give enterprises sufficient time to work with third-party vendors so that they may fix any incompatibilities resulting from the switch from Microsoft's compatibility shim to Chrome's UI Automation provider.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 125 on Windows: The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> policy is introduced so that administrators can enable Chrome's UI Automation accessibility framework provider and validate that third-party accessibility tools continue to work.</li>
      <li>Chrome 126 on Windows: The Chrome variations framework will be used to begin enabling Chrome's UI Automation accessibility framework provider for users. It will be progressively enabled to the full stable population, with pauses as needed to address compatibility issues that can be resolved in Chrome. Enterprise administrators may continue to use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> policy to either opt-in early to the new behavior, or to temporarily opt-out through Chrome 146.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Windows:</strong> The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> policy will be removed from Chrome. All clients will use the browser's UI Automation accessibility framework provider.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrQ143" name="upChromeBrsrQ143">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>SafeBrowsing API v4 to v5 migration&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome calls into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/v4" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SafeBrowsing v4 API</u></a> will be migrated to call into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>v5 API</u></a> instead. The method names are also different between v4 and v5. If admins have any v4-specific URL allowlisting to allow network requests to <code>https://safebrowsing.googleapis.com/v4*</code>, these should be modified to allow network requests to the whole domain instead: <code>safebrowsing.googleapis.com</code>. Otherwise, rejected network requests to the v5 API will cause security regressions for users. For more details, see <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference/Migration.From.V4" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Migration From V4 - Safe Browsing</u></a>.&nbsp;</p>

    <ul>

    </ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrR143" name="upChromeBrsrR143">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Isolated Web Apps&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Isolated Web Apps (IWAs) are an extension of existing work on PWA installation and Web Packaging that provide stronger protections against server compromise and other tampering that is necessary for developers of security-sensitive applications. Rather than being hosted on live web servers and fetched over HTTPS, these applications are packaged into Web Bundles, signed by their developer, and distributed to end-users through one or more of the potential methods described in the <a href="https://github.com/WICG/isolated-web-apps/blob/main/README.md" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>explainer</u></a>.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>In the initial release, IWAs will only be installable through an admin policy on enterprise-managed ChromeOS devices.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 150 on Windows </strong>This rollout adds support for Isolated Web Apps in enterprise-managed browser configurations on Windows.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrS143" name="upChromeBrsrS143">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>PostQuantum cryptography for DTLS in WebRTC&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature will enable the use of PostQuantum Cryptography (PQC) with WebRTC connections. The motivation for PQC is to get WebRTC media traffic up to date with the latest cryptography protocols and prevent <em>Harvest Now to Crack Later</em> scenarios.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>Admins will be able to control this feature using an enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement</u></a>, to allow enterprise users to opt out of PQC. The policy will be temporary and is planned to be removed by Chrome 152.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 142 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: Feature rolls out</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong>: Remove Enterprise Policy</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeBrsrT143" name="upChromeBrsrT143">&nbsp; &nbsp;</a></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Local network access restrictions&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 142 restricted&nbsp;the ability to make requests to the user's local network, gated behind a permission prompt.</p>

    <p>A local network request is any request from a public website to a local IP address or loopback address, or from a local website (for example, intranet) to loopback. Gating the ability for websites to perform these requests behind a permission mitigates the risk of cross-site request forgery attacks against local network devices such as routers, and reduces the ability of sites to use these requests to fingerprint the user's local network.</p>

    <p>This permission is restricted to secure contexts. If granted, the permission&nbsp;additionally relaxes mixed content blocking for local network requests (since many local devices are not able to obtain publicly trusted TLS certificates for various reasons).</p>

    <p>This work supersedes a prior effort called <a href="https://chromestatus.com/feature/5737414355058688" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Private Network Access</u></a>, which used preflight requests to have local devices opt in.</p>

    <p>For more information on&nbsp;this feature, see this guide to&nbsp;<a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QQkqehw8umtAgz5z0um7THx-aoU251p705FbIQjDuGs/edit?usp=sharing" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Adapting your website for new Local Network Access restrictions in Chrome</a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 152 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, MacOS, Windows: </strong><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut" rel="noopener" target="_blank">LocalNetworkAccessRestrictionsTemporaryOptOut</a> will be removed</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<h4><strong>Upcoming Chrome Enterprise Core updates</strong></h4>

<p>There are no Upcoming Chrome Enterprise Core updates.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<div class="no-margin"><h4><strong>Upcoming Chrome Enterprise Premium updates</strong></h4>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeEPA143" name="upChromeEPA143"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Copy and Paste rules protection&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>To help organizations better prevent data exfiltration on mobile devices, Chrome is extending its existing desktop clipboard data controls. Administrators can now use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DataControlsRules" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DataControlsRules</u></a> policy to set rules that block or warn users when they attempt to copy or paste content that violates organizational policies. This feature allows admins to define data boundaries and prevent sensitive information from being pasted from a work context into personal apps or websites on their mobile fleet. This addresses a significant security gap and a frequently requested feature from enterprise customers who have cited the lack of mobile data controls as a concern.</p>

    <p>To use this feature, administrators can configure clipboard restrictions within the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DataControlsRules" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DataControlsRules</u></a> policy, providing a consistent management experience across desktop and mobile to strengthen their organization's overall security posture. This <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/11375053" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Help Center article</u></a> provides further context on how administrators can configure and manage Chrome Enterprise reporting connectors to forward browser security and data protection events to third-party services for analysis.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 140 on Android:<strong> </strong>Copy/Paste Rules Protection becomes available on Android</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 144 on iOS: </strong>Copy/Paste Rules Protection becomes available on Android</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeEPB143" name="upChromeEPB143"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Proxy Override rules&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>To simplify proxy management in complex enterprise environments, Chrome 144 will introduce two new policies: <strong>ProxyOverrideRules</strong> and <strong>EnableProxyOverrideRulesForAllUsers</strong>. Currently, organizations that use multiple proxy solutions (for example, a general proxy and a specific one for Google's Secure Gateway ) or have different admin teams (for example, for GPO and the Google Admin console) must manually merge complex PAC files. This process is error-prone and creates significant administrative friction.</p>

    <p>The new <strong>ProxyOverrideRules</strong> policy allows administrators to configure a list of routing rules that are evaluated before any existing proxy configuration, including PAC files set by the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ProxySettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ProxySettings</u></a> policy. This enables admins to easily prepend specific routes (for example, to send traffic for private web apps to a secure gateway) without modifying the primary, company-wide PAC script. The <strong>EnableProxyOverrideRulesForAllUsers</strong> policy provides additional control over how these override rules apply to unaffiliated users on a device. End users will see a notification in their <code>chrome://</code>settings page to inform them when these administrative proxy rules are active.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 144 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong><br>
        Proxy Override Rules becomes available on Windows, macOS, ChromeOS and Linux</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeEPC143" name="upChromeEPC143"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Increased file size support for DLP scans&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome Enterprise Premium will extend its Data Loss Prevention (DLP) and malware scanning capabilities to include large and encrypted files. Previously, files larger than 50 MB and all encrypted files were skipped during content scanning. This update will close that critical security gap. For policies configured to save evidence, files <strong>up to 2GB</strong> can now be sent to the Evidence Locker. This provides administrators with greater visibility and control, significantly reducing the risk of data exfiltration through large file transfers.</p>

    <p>No new policy is required to enable this feature. It is automatically controlled by the existing DLP rule configurations in the Google Admin console. If admins have rules that apply to file uploads, downloads, or printing, they will now also apply to large and encrypted files. For more information, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/11587610" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>What are ChromeOS data controls?</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 145 on Linux, macOS, Windows: </strong>This stage enables the collection of large (&gt;50 MB) and encrypted files for the Evidence Locker, closing a key DLP security gap.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>
</div>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Current ChromeOS updates</h4>

<p><a id="chromeOSA143" name="chromeOSA143"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Manage&nbsp;USB printers in ChromeOS&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>Previously, admins could manage printers connected to ChromeOS over a network connection only. This new feature provides a way for managing printers connected to a ChromeOS device via the USB port. ChromeOS administrators can now specify the Vendor ID and Product ID of the USB printers to manage them for their organizations.</p>

    <p>For more information, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/7276100#zippy=%2Cmanage-who-can-use-printers%2Cadd-a-printer" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Manage local and network printers</u></a>.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeOSB143" name="chromeOSB143"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Pre-configured print settings&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Starting from ChromeOS 143, admins can pre-configure or limit print options per printer. The functionality applies to the paper size, paper type, duplex, color, DPI, print quality, and print as Image settings. Pre-configuring print settings helps to optimize workflows in domains like healthcare, retail, or logistics. A recurring example are label printers with a specific label size - by pre-setting the paper size, admins can save users the hassle of going through a manual configuration.</p>

    <p>For more information, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/7276100#zippy=%2Cmanage-who-can-use-printers%2Cadd-a-printer" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Manage local and network printers</u></a>.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<ul>

    <p><strong>Google Vids</strong>, an AI-powered video creation app for work, is now pre-installed for managed users. You can use Google Vids to create, write, produce, edit, collaborate, and share your videos.</p>

    <p>Managed users can find Google Vids in the ChromeOS Launcher. For more information, see <a href="https://workspace.google.com/products/vids/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Google Vids helps scale your message through video storytelling</u></a>.&nbsp;</p>
    <img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/YPyb88BtxJNfwRLEKmMWliDgALFngQ2QQ94mWolr54qThqPdfNs5XgZwxzhEZMIPMg=w172" width="172" height="36" alt="" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/YPyb88BtxJNfwRLEKmMWliDgALFngQ2QQ94mWolr54qThqPdfNs5XgZwxzhEZMIPMg"></li>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Upcoming ChromeOS changes</h4>

    <p><strong>Badge authentication enhancements&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

<div class="no-margin"><h2>Chrome browser changes &nbsp;</h2>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrA142" name="chromeBrsrA142"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Simplified sign-in and sync experience on Chrome Desktop&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome will launch a simplified and consolidated version of sign-in and sync in Chrome on Windows, Mac and Linux. Chrome sync will no longer be shown as a separate feature in settings or elsewhere. Instead, users can sign-in to Chrome to use and save data such as passwords, bookmarks and more in their Google Account, subject to the relevant enterprise policies. Additionally, users who are signed in to Chrome can also opt in to syncing their tabs and browsing history in their Google Account, here again subject to the relevant enterprise policies.</p>

    <p>As before, the functionality previously part of Chrome sync that saves and accesses Chrome data in the Google Account can be turned off via <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SyncDisabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SyncDisabled</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SyncTypesListDisabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SyncTypesListDisabled</u></a>. Sign-in to Chrome can be disabled via <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#BrowserSignin" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>BrowserSignin</u></a> as before.</p>

    <p>The changes do not affect users’ ability to sign in to Google properties on the web (for example, Gmail) without signing in to Chrome, their ability to remain signed out of Chrome, or their ability to control what information is synced with their Google Account.</p>

    <p>These changes are pretty similar to the simplified sign-in and sync experience that was launched on iOS in 117 and on Android in 127.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 142 on Linux, macOS, Windows:</strong> Gradual rollout</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrB142" name="chromeBrsrB142"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Disable force-installed extensions with non-malware violations&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature silently disables force-installed extensions exhibiting violations of Chrome Web Store policies (CWS) in unmanaged browser environments. Such violations include general program violations, unwanted software and potential security vulnerabilities not classified as malware. Users retain the ability to enable or disable these extensions, but will not be able to remove them.</p>

    <p>A new enterprise policy, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ExtensionForceInstallWithNonMalwareViolationsEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ExtensionForceInstallWithNonMalwareViolationEnabled</u></a>, will be added in 142 to preserve the existing behavior for unmanaged browser environments, but will be removed in 145.</p>

    <p>This change does not affect managed instances of Chrome that are joined to a Microsoft&nbsp;Active Directory&nbsp;domain, joined to Microsoft&nbsp;Azure&nbsp;Active Directory&nbsp;or enrolled in Chrome Enterprise Core. On macOS, this change does not affect instances of Chrome that are managed via MDM, joined to a domain or enrolled in Chrome Enterprise Core.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 142 on macOS, Windows:</strong> In Chrome 142 for Windows and macOS, force-installed extensions with minor policy violations will be silently disabled in low-trust environments.</li>
      <li>Chrome 145 on macOS, Windows: The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ExtensionForceInstallWithNonMalwareViolationsEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank">ExtensionForceInstallWithNonMalwareViolationsEnabled</a> policy will be removed.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrC142" name="chromeBrsrC142"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Multi-profile support in Share extension in Chrome on iOS&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>As early as Chrome 142 on iOS, Chrome Share extension allows users to see the currently-used profile and change it before opening a URL in Chrome or searching text or image. For users who have multiple profiles enabled, when they want to share a URL or select text or an image, then select Chrome they would be able to see Chrome Share extension with an account avatar. If users do nothing, it will open the share intent in the selected profile.</p>

    <p>To change the profile from the Chrome Share extension, users click on it and select the desired profile. Chrome then switches the profiles accordingly. If work profiles are allowed by enterprise policy, users can set the widgets profile. If only personal or if only corporate profiles are allowed, multi-profile support is not enabled, then widgets continue to function as before.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 142 on iOS</strong></li>
    </ul>
    <img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/lDBy00F9eLs_MaLJoAH_pmo4p6OJnEs12dNPJplAP9aC36uaDinty9FHcrNheH4rH6tS=w895" width="976" height="1012" alt="" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/lDBy00F9eLs_MaLJoAH_pmo4p6OJnEs12dNPJplAP9aC36uaDinty9FHcrNheH4rH6tS"></li>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrD142" name="chromeBrsrD142"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Client’s LLM assistance in mitigating scams&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Users on the webs are facing significant amounts of several kinds of scams&nbsp;on a daily basis. To combat these scams, Chrome leverages on-device Large Language Model (LLM) to identify scam websites for Enhanced Safe Browsing users. Chrome sends the page content to an on-device LLM to infer security-related signals of the page and send these signals to Safe Browsing server side for a final verdict. When enabled, Chrome may consume more bandwidth to download the LLM.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 134 on Linux, macOS, Windows: Gather the brand name and intent summary of the page that triggers keyboard lock to identify scam websites.</li>
      <li>Chrome 135 on Linux, macOS, Windows: Show the warnings to the user based on the server verdict which uses the brand and intent summary of the page that triggered keyboard lock.</li>
      <li>Chrome 137 on Linux, macOS, Windows: Gather brand and intent summary of the page based on server reputation scoring system.</li>
      <li>Chrome 138 on Linux, macOS, Windows: Show the warnings to the user based on the server verdict which uses the brand and intent of the pages that the server reputation system scored.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 142 on Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrE142" name="chromeBrsrE142"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Local network access restrictions&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 142 restricts the ability to make requests to the user's local network, gated behind a permission prompt.</p>

    <p>A local network request is any request from a public website to a local IP address or loopback, or from a local website (for example, Intranet) to loopback. Gating the ability for websites to perform these requests behind a permission mitigates the risk of cross-site request forgery attacks against local network devices such as routers, and reduces the ability of sites to use these requests to fingerprint the user's local network.</p>

    <p>This permission is restricted to secure contexts. If granted, the permission&nbsp;additionally relaxes mixed content blocking for local network requests (since many local devices are not able to obtain publicly trusted TLS certificates for various reasons).</p>

    <p>This work supersedes a prior effort called <a href="https://chromestatus.com/feature/5737414355058688,%20https://chromestatus.com/feature/5954091755241472" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Private Network Access</u></a>, which used preflight requests to have local devices opt-in.</p>

    <p>For more information on&nbsp;this feature, see this guide to&nbsp;<a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QQkqehw8umtAgz5z0um7THx-aoU251p705FbIQjDuGs/edit?usp=sharing" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Adapting your website for new Local Network Access restrictions in Chrome</a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 142 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrF142" name="chromeBrsrF142"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Origin-keyed process isolation&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 142 introduces a shift in the process isolation policy from locking processes to a site like <code>https://example.com</code> to locking them to a specific origin, such as, <code>https://foo.example.com</code>.</p>

    <p>To further enhance security, Chrome is moving to a more granular process isolation model called <strong>Origin Isolation</strong>. Previously, Chrome used <strong>Site Isolation</strong>, which grouped different origins from the same site (for example, <code>https://a.example.com</code> and <code>https://b.example.com</code>) into a single renderer process.</p>

    <p>With Origin Isolation, each individual origin (for example, <code>https://foo.example.com</code>) will be isolated in its own renderer process. This change strengthens Chrome's security architecture by better aligning process boundaries with the web's fundamental origin-based security model, offering greater protection against potential vulnerabilities within sites.</p>

    <p><strong>Potential performance considerations: </strong>While each individual process will be smaller, this increase in process granularity may lead to higher overall memory and CPU usage. To balance security and performance, Origin Isolation will be enabled by default only on devices with at least 4GB of RAM.</p>

    <p><strong>Enterprise Control: </strong>Admins can control this feature using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OriginKeyedProcessesEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>OriginKeyedProcessesEnabled</u></a> policy.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 142 on ChromeOS, Linux, Windows</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrG142" name="chromeBrsrG142"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>PostQuantum cryptography for DTLS in WebRTC&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature will enable the use of PostQuantum Cryptography (PQC) with WebRTC connections. The motivation for PQC is to get WebRTC media traffic up to date with the latest cryptography protocols and prevent <em>Harvest Now to Crack Later</em> scenarios.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>Admins will be able to control this feature using an enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreement</u></a>, to allow enterprise users to opt out of PQC. The policy will be temporary and is planned to be removed by Chrome 152.</p>

The lack of user activation in the post-navigation page prevents some use cases like showing virtual keyboards on auto-focus, and this has been a blocker for the developers who want to build Multi-page Applications (MPAs) over Single-page Applications (SPAs).</p>

<div class="no-margin"><h2>Chrome Enterprise Premium changes</h2>

<p>Read more about the differences between <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/products/chrome-enterprise-premium" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Enterprise Core and Chrome Enterprise Premium</u></a>.</p>

<p><a id="chromeEPA142" name="chromeEPA142"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome browser rule UX refactor&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> &nbsp;

    <p>To enhance the <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/13876556" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Data Loss Prevention (DLP)</u></a> rule creation experience, the Google Admin console is being updated to streamline how administrators define policies for different applications like Chrome and Workspace. This introduces mutually exclusive application groups, meaning that a single DLP rule can now only target one application group at a time—either Workspace apps (like Drive, Gmail), Chrome browser triggers (like file upload, URL visited), or ChromeOS triggers. This change simplifies rule configuration, eliminates potential conflicts from overlapping app selections, and lays the groundwork for more specialized and user-friendly workflows tailored to each platform's needs.</p>

    <p>Administrators will see an updated <strong>Apps</strong> selection interface using radio buttons to enforce this single-group selection for new rules. Existing rules that previously combined applications from multiple groups will be transparently migrated by the system into separate, compliant, single-platform rules to ensure continued protection and a seamless transition. Banners within the Admin console will provide information regarding these changes and the migration process. No new enterprise policies are introduced with this update; the changes are to the rule configuration interface. For more information, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/11587610" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>What are ChromeOS data controls? - Chrome Enterprise and Education Help</u></a>.&nbsp;</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 142 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: </strong>Enables mutually exclusive app selection for DLP rule configuration in Admin console</li>
    </ul>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Streamlined Chrome Enterprise to Google SecOps integration&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> &nbsp; &nbsp;

    <p>The new Chrome Enterprise Premium (CEP) and Google Security Operations (SecOps) integration provides a native, direct connection between the two systems. This feature transforms the browser into a primary security sensor, enabling organizations to prevent, detect, investigate, and respond to web-based threats (phishing, malware, and data exfiltration) by sending a richer set of security events and detailed browser telemetry from Chrome directly to SecOps.</p>

    <p>For administrators, the integration introduces enhanced security event types like URL navigation and suspicious URL visits, automatically enriched with Safe Browsing risk scores and threat intelligence. A new, streamlined <em>one-click</em> setup in the Admin Console replaces the previous manual workflow.&nbsp;</p>

    <p><strong>NOTE: </strong>The collection of high-volume events (for example, URL navigation) is opt-in. The feature requires no end-user-facing policy changes.</p>
    &nbsp;

      <li><strong>Chrome 142 on iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong></li>

<h2>Coming soon</h2>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Upcoming Chrome browser changes</h4>


<p><a id="upChromeBrsrB142" name="upChromeBrsrB142"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Deprecate and remove XSLT&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p><a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/xslt-10/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>XSLT v1.0</u></a>, which all browsers adhere to, was standardized in 1999. In the meantime, XSLT has evolved to v2.0 and v3.0, adding features, and growing apart from the old version frozen into browsers. This lack of advancement, coupled with the rise of JavaScript libraries and frameworks that offer more flexible and powerful DOM manipulation, has led to a significant decline in the use of client-side XSLT. Its role within the web browser has been largely superseded by JavaScript-based technologies, such as JSON+React.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <p>Chromium uses the libxslt library to process these transformations, and <a href="https://discourse.gnome.org/t/stepping-down-as-libxslt-maintainer/27615" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>libxslt was unmaintained</u></a> for ~6 months of 2025. Libxslt is a complex, aging C codebase of the type notoriously susceptible to memory safety vulnerabilities like buffer overflows, which can lead to arbitrary code execution. Because client-side XSLT is now a niche, rarely-used feature, these libraries receive far less maintenance and security scrutiny than core JavaScript engines, yet they represent a direct, potent attack surface for processing untrusted web content. Indeed, XSLT is the source of several recent high-profile security exploits that continue to put browser users at risk.</p>

    <p>For these reasons, Chromium (along with both other browser engines) plans to deprecate and remove XSLT from the web platform.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 143 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Deprecation (but not removal) of the APIs&nbsp;</li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>
