<div class="no-margin"><h4>Current ChromeOS updates</h4>

<p><a id="chromeOSA141" name="chromeOSA141"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Enhanced transparency for Data Recovery on ChromeOS&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Building on our commitment to security, ChromeOS now provides greater transparency into your device's data recovery history. Every recovery attempt is logged into a tamper-evident, privacy-preserving ledger, and we are now making it possible for that log to be reviewed.</p>

    <p>This allows you to verify that all attempts to recover local data on your device were made by you, ensuring unauthorized access attempts are easily detected and giving you complete peace of mind.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a name="chromeOSA141"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>New permissions policies for Device Attributes API&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Admins can now use&nbsp;two new permissions policies&nbsp; to restrict access to the Device Attributes API. The Device Attributes API is available for policy-installed kiosk web apps and policy-installed Isolated Web Apps (IWAs) only, on managed ChromeOS devices only. Additionally, the feature is controlled by content settings.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>Two new policies are introduced, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DeviceAttributesBlockedForOrigins" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DeviceAttributesBlockedForOrigins</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DefaultDeviceAttributesSetting" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DefaultDeviceAttributesSetting</u></a>, to complement the previously-introduced <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DeviceAttributesAllowedForOrigins" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DeviceAttributesAllowedForOrigins</u></a> policy. The feature is enabled by default for the supported scenarios described above.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a name="chromeOSA141"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Battery Charge Limit setting in UI&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>You can now take direct control of your Chromebook’s battery health to extend its lifespan with new charging optimization settings. These features help preserve your battery’s long-term health by adjusting how your device charges.</p>

    <p>To configure these user-accessible options, navigate to <strong>Settings &gt; Device &gt; Power</strong> and select <strong>Change</strong> next to Optimized Charging. You can choose between:</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Charge Limit:</strong> Maximizes your battery's lifespan by limiting the maximum charge to 80%.</li>
      <li><strong>Adaptive Charging:</strong> Intelligently delays charging to 100% until it's needed, based on your daily usage patterns.</li>
    </ul>

    <p>This update is the user-facing counterpart to the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DevicePowerBatteryChargingOptimization" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DevicePowerBatteryChargingOptimization</u></a> policy available in the Google <strong>Admin console</strong>. Administrators can set this policy to one of three options:</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Adaptive:</strong> The device delays charging to 100% until necessary.</li>
      <li><strong>Limited:</strong> The battery charges only to around 80%.</li>
      <li><strong>Standard:</strong> The battery charges normally to 100%, which disables all charging optimizations on the device.</li>
    </ul>

    <p>The policy set by an administrator overrides any setting selected by the user. A user can only benefit from adjusting the charge optimization options on their device if no overriding policy is enforced. By default, if no policy is enforced, <strong>Optimized Charging</strong> is enabled on the device with the <strong>Adaptive Charging</strong> option selected. For more information, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chromebook/answer/14236882" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>How to use Adaptive charging - Chromebook Help</u></a>.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a name="chromeOSA141"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Managed PPD files for printers&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Currently, there are 2 ways to set up a printer driverless configuration, or manufacturer and model.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>This new feature provides a third way to identify a printer, which is by using a custom PPD file.&nbsp; ChromeOS enterprise administrators can now specify custom PPD files when setting up managed printers for their organizations.</p>
    <img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/QIva5Vn4so_1vcdMvLecYMSmFygiSd5ri-Rm3mQS3IQ9pmC4b-dfNrlc3HgN6RVqDx3w=w895" width="1070" height="374" alt="" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/QIva5Vn4so_1vcdMvLecYMSmFygiSd5ri-Rm3mQS3IQ9pmC4b-dfNrlc3HgN6RVqDx3w"></li>
</ul>

<a class="zippy" name="140"><p>Chrome 140</p>
 </a>

<div>

<div class="no-margin"><h2>Chrome browser changes &nbsp;</h2>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrA140" name="chromeBrsrA140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Automated password change&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>When Chrome detects that a user has signed into a website with a known compromised password, it now offers to change it automatically. This feature is available on a set of eligible sites. The feature uses AI, and admins can control it using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AutomatedPasswordChangeSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>AutomatedPasswordChangeSettings</u></a> enterprise policy.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 140 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a href="https://screenshot.googleplex.com/3FX8Zc46htvBw3V.png"><strong><u><img height="317" src="//lh7-rt.googleusercontent.com/docsz/AD_4nXeWhTIWOEyarTmEqb6LOfTBTrr71e6G6O5vwJJukvGhMLFmXb1WOBAxuO_cEdI8zMzFgLL7vrLL04Wmiw_2m-oi-twT6Xghl_YzNH1ppH2Vm5I0IheEb_K7uMvhPVN4it_iFXD2SYxE9lv4KuGrwfPyN6dX5sdz?key=mteu4N1GlYLou4GHcpRftg" width="483"></u></strong></a></p>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrB140" name="chromeBrsrB140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Contextual search suggestions in Chrome address bar&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>With this feature, you can ask anything about the page you’re on, directly in context. Building on the existing Search habit of the address bar, users can ask a question with Google Lens by selecting anything on screen or asking with words. A Google Lens action in the address bar and contextual suggestions guide people to the feature when it’s most helpful. Admins can control this feature with the existing <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LensOverlaySettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LensOverlaySettings</u></a> policy.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 138 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Feature starts rollout</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 140 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows:</strong> If the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LensOverlaySettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LensOverlaySettings</u></a> policy is not set, this feature will respect the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> policy if present.</li>
    </ul>
    <img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/7z4RQSm0cLVlQXimjVYbrwok_ZRfZKDCMtAG21nIJYO9X2OC6pNapSU2fa3ynEhlRmU=w895" width="1600" height="647" alt="" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/7z4RQSm0cLVlQXimjVYbrwok_ZRfZKDCMtAG21nIJYO9X2OC6pNapSU2fa3ynEhlRmU"></li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrC140" name="chromeBrsrC140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>DSE Prewarming</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>DSE Prewarming optimizes the default search provider integration in the Omnibox. When the Omnibox gets a focus, Chrome starts prerendering the prewarm page that preload required resources for the search result page, and reuses the resources to accelerate navigating to the search result page in the next query. Admins can control this feature&nbsp; with the, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#NetworkPredictionOptions" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>NetworkPredictionOptions</u></a> enterprise policy.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 140 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows:</strong> Gradual roll-out</li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrD140" name="chromeBrsrD140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Enhanced autofill&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Starting in Chrome 137, some users can turn on <em>Autofill with AI</em>, a new feature that helps users fill out online forms more easily. On relevant forms, Chrome can use AI to better understand the form and offer users to automatically fill in previously-saved info. Admins can control the feature using the existing <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAiDefaultSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAiDefaultSettings</u></a> policy and a new <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AutofillPredictionSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>AutofillPredictionSettings</u></a> policy.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 137 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 140 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: </strong>The existing <em>Autofill with AI</em>&nbsp;feature will be renamed to <em>Enhanced autofill</em>, allow users to save and fill additional types of info, and become available in more countries and languages<span>&nbsp;</span></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrF140" name="chromeBrsrF140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Launch Chrome into new profile via command line&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature is designed for our enterprise partners and admins who need to launch web applications from their native app catalogs directly into a specific managed Chrome profile using Chrome-Cli. Currently, if the designated profile does not exist, Chrome defaults to the last-used profile, creating a disjointed user experience. With this new feature, when a specified profile is not found, Chrome initiates the existing profile creation flow, pre-populating the user's email address to streamline the setup process. This is a key technical enabler for admins aiming to onboard their enterprise users to Chrome Enterprise via managed profiles.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 140 on Linux, macOS, Windows</strong></li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrG140" name="chromeBrsrG140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Signed-in users: Autofill and&nbsp;settings from Google Account&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>As part of our effort to streamline Chrome’s identity model on Desktop, managed accounts that originally signed in to Chrome implicitly by signing in to a Google web property, and who are in a managed profile with user policies, can now save and use Autofill, settings and themes from their Google Account while signed in. Existing user policies continue to work as before, including <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SyncDisabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SyncDisabled</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SyncTypesListDisabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SyncTypesListDisabled</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#BrowserSignin" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>BrowserSignin</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AutofillAddressEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>AutofillAddressEnabled</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AutofillCreditCardEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>AutofillCreditCardEnabled</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PasswordManagerEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>PasswordManagerEnabled</u></a>.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 140 on Linux, macOS, Windows</strong></li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrH140" name="chromeBrsrH140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>ServiceWorkerAutoPreload mode&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>ServiceWorkerAutoPreload is a mode where the browser issues the network request in parallel with the service worker bootstrap, and consumes the network request result inside the fetch handler if the fetch handler returns the response with respondWith(). If the fetch handler result is fallback, it passes the network response directly to the browser. ServiceWorkerAutoPreload is defined as an optional browser optimization, which will change the existing service worker behavior. Admins can control this feature using an enterprise policy called <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled</u></a>.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 140 on Android, Windows: </strong><a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled</u></a> policy</li>
      <li>Chrome 144 on Android, Windows: <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ServiceWorkerAutoPreloadEnabled</u></a> policy will be removed</li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrI140" name="chromeBrsrI140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Shared tab groups&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Users can now collaborate on tabs using the shared tab groups feature. With this feature, users can create and use a set of tabs on their desktop or mobile device and their collaborative partners can browse the same tabs on their devices. When one person changes a tab in the group, the changes are reflected across all users’ browsers in the group. Admins can control this feature using an enterprise policy, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#TabGroupSharingSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>TabGroupSharingSettings</u></a>, in Chrome 140.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 138 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Rollout of the ability to join and use a shared tab group. Users on Stable Chrome will not be able to create a shared tab group (the entry point will not be available) - this part of the feature will only be available on Beta/Dev/Canary for this phase of rollout.&nbsp;</li>
      <li>Chrome 139 on iOS:<strong>&nbsp; </strong>As early as Chrome 139, support for iOS will rollout</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 140 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows:</strong> <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#TabGroupSharingSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>TabGroupSharingSettings</u></a><strong> </strong>enterprise policy will be available to the enterprise owner in the admin console. 100% of users on Stable will be able to join and use a shared tab group. However, the ability to create a shared tab group will remain exclusive to users on Beta/Dev/Canary, implying that only users on those channels could initiate a group (their friends and coworkers on Stable can then join).</li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrJ140" name="chromeBrsrJ140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Update to </strong><strong><em>No HTTPS</em></strong><strong> warning&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 140 updates the warning displayed when a user opts in to the <strong>Always use secure connections</strong> on <code>chrome://settings/security</code> from an interstitial to a dialog. The URL content security indicator on the warning changes from an asterisk to a broken lock, while the full page load remains blocked and the functionality remains unchanged. Some users might see this warning automatically when visiting HTTP sites. Users can opt in to the warning on <code>chrome://settings/security</code>.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 140 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows:</strong> New warning design on desktop platforms</li>
      <li>Chrome 141 on Android: New warning design on Android&nbsp;</li>
    </ul>

</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrK140" name="chromeBrsrK140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Stop sending </strong><strong><em>Purpose: prefetch</em></strong><strong> header from prefetches and prerenders&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Now that prefetches and prerenders are using the <code>Sec-Purpose</code> header for prefetches and prerenders, this change removes the legacy <code>Purpose: prefetch</code> header that is still currently passed. This update is behind a feature flag or kill switch to prevent compatibility issues.</p>

    <p>The scope includes speculation rules prefetch, speculation rules prerender, <code>&lt;link rel=prefetch&gt;</code>, and Chromium's non-standard <code>&lt;link rel=prerender&gt;</code>.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 140 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrL140" name="chromeBrsrL140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Deprecate special font size rules for H1 within some elements&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>The HTML spec contains a list of <a href="https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/rendering.html#sections-and-headings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>special rules for &lt;h1&gt; tags </u></a>nested within &lt;article&gt;, &lt;aside&gt;, &lt;nav&gt;, or &lt;section&gt; tags. Chrome 140 deprecates these special rules, because they can cause accessibility issues. For example, they can visually reduce the font size for nested &lt;h1&gt; tags so that they look like &lt;h2&gt; tags, but nothing in the accessibility tree reflects this demotion.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 140 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrP140" name="chromeBrsrP140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>SharedWorker inherits controller for blob URL&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>According to <a href="https://w3c.github.io/ServiceWorker/#control-and-use-worker-client" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Worker client case (github)</u></a>, workers should inherit controllers for the blob URL. However, existing code allows only dedicated workers to inherit the controller, and shared workers do not inherit the controller. This is the fix to make Chromium behavior adjust to the specification. An enterprise policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SharedWorkerBlobURLFixEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SharedWorkerBlobURLFixEnabled</u></a> is available to control this feature.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 140 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong><span>&nbsp;</span></li>
    </ul>
  </li>

<div class="no-margin"><h2>Chrome Enterprise Premium changes</h2>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Copy/Paste rules protection&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> &nbsp;

    <p>To help organizations better prevent data exfiltration on mobile devices, Chrome is extending its existing desktop clipboard data controls. Administrators can now use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DataControlsRules" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DataControlsRules</u></a> policy to set rules that block or warn users when they attempt to copy or paste content that violates organizational policies. This feature allows admins to define data boundaries and prevent sensitive information from being pasted from a work context into personal apps or websites on their mobile fleet. This addresses a significant security gap and a frequently requested feature from enterprise customers who have cited the lack of mobile data controls as a concern.</p>

    <p>To use this feature, administrators can configure clipboard restrictions within the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DataControlsRules" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DataControlsRules</u></a> policy, providing a consistent management experience across desktop and mobile to strengthen their organization's overall security posture. <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/11375053" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>This help center article</u></a> provides further context on how administrators can configure and manage Chrome Enterprise reporting connectors to forward browser security and data protection events to third-party services for analysis.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 140 on Android: </strong>Copy/Paste Rules Protection becomes available on Android<span>&nbsp;</span></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeEPB140" name="chromeEPB140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>DLP support for iFrames&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> &nbsp;

    <p>To enhance security and prevent data exfiltration, Chrome 140 extends Data Loss Prevention (DLP) capabilities to content within iFrames. With this change, when a user performs a DLP-triggering action (such as uploading a file) from a site loaded in an iFrame, Chrome now sends the entire URL hierarchy, from the source iFrame up to the top-level page, to be evaluated against all applicable DLP rules.</p>

    <p>No new enterprise policies are required to enable this functionality; it works with existing DLP rules configured via the <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/10106035?sjid=5991552215396607268-NA" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Connector policies</u></a>. Administrators should be aware that their existing rules now apply to iFrame contexts, which might block user actions that were previously permitted.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 139 on Linux, macOS, Windows:<strong> </strong>Initial launch of Data Loss Prevention support for iFrames. This phase adds enforcement for file upload events originating from within an iFrame context and it will work with existing DLP rules configured via the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#OnFileAttachedEnterpriseConnector" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>OnFileAttachedEnterpriseConnector</u></a> policy</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 140 on Linux, macOS, Windows:</strong> This expanded phase combines two feature rollouts, extending DLP iFrame support to include enforcement for both file download and printing actions.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Upcoming Chrome browser changes</h4>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrA140" name="upChromeBrsrA140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Add a search hijacking heuristic signal to extension telemetry</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Malicious Chrome extensions intercept and redirect Omnibox and Realbox (the search box in the <strong>New tab</strong> page) search queries from the Search Engine Results Page (SERP) to an attacker-controlled URL. This feature adds a client-side heuristic to detect such search hijacking. The core idea is to compare user-initiated searches with successful SERP landings; a significant discrepancy over time strongly indicates hijacking activity. This heuristic generates a new signal, uploaded to the Safe Browsing CRX telemetry server via the existing Extension Telemetry service in Chrome. Server-side analysis of signal data from multiple Chrome browsers can then identify potential search hijacking.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 141 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

This message often includes a link directly to the extension in the Chrome Web Store, making it easier to identify and manage unwanted extensions. If you're an administrator, you can disable this attribution using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#NTPFooterExtensionAttributionEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>NTPFooterExtensionAttributionEnabled</u></a> policy.</li>

This helps you understand how your browser is being managed. Administrators can disable this notice with the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#NTPFooterManagementNoticeEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>NTPFooterManagementNoticeEnabled</u></a> policy. Additionally, organizations can customize the footer's appearance using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#EnterpriseLogoUrlForBrowser" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>EnterpriseLogoUrlForBrowser</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#EnterpriseCustomLabelForBrowser" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>EnterpriseCustomLabelForBrowser</u></a> policies to display a custom logo and label.</li>

<ul>
  <li><strong>PostQuantum cryptography for DTLS in WebRTC</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature will enable the use of PostQuantum Cryptography (PQC) with WebRTC connections. The motivation for PQC is to get WebRTC media traffic up to date with the latest cryptography protocols and prevent <em>Harvest Now to Crack Later</em> scenarios.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>This feature will be controllable by an enterprise policy <strong>WebRtcPostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled</strong>,&nbsp; to allow enterprise users to opt out of PQC. The policy will be temporary and is planned to be removed by Chrome 151.</p>

    <ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrD140" name="upChromeBrsrD140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>CSS find-in-page highlight pseudos</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

This allows authors to change the foreground and background colors or add text decorations, which can be especially useful if the browser defaults have insufficient contrast with the page colors or are otherwise unsuitable.</p>

    <ul>

    </ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrE140" name="upChromeBrsrE140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Local network access restrictions</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 140 restricts the ability to make requests to the user's local network, gated behind a permission prompt. A local network request is any request from a public website to a local IP address or loopback, or from a local website (for example, Intranet) to loopback. Gating the ability for websites to perform these requests behind a permission mitigates the risk of cross-site request forgery attacks against local network devices such as routers, and reduces the ability of sites to use these requests to fingerprint the user's local network.</p>

    <p>This permission is restricted to secure contexts. If granted, the permissions additionally relaxes mixed content blocking for local network requests (since many local devices are not able to obtain publicly trusted TLS certificates for various reasons).</p>

    <p>This work supersedes a prior effort called <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/local-network-access?hl=en" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Private Network Access</u></a>, which used preflight requests to have local devices opt-in. Enterprises that need to disable or auto-grant the permission can do so using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessAllowedForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LocalNetworkAccessAllowedForUrls</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LocalNetworkAccessBlockedForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LocalNetworkAccessBlockedForUrls</u></a> policies. The value of '*' can be used to allow local network access on all URLs, matching the behavior prior to rolling out the restrictions.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 141 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrF140" name="upChromeBrsrF140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Origin-bound cookies (by default)&nbsp;</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>In Chrome 141, cookies are bound to their setting origin (by default) such that they're only accessible by that origin, that is, sent on a request or visible through document.cookie. Cookies might ease the host and port binding restrictions through use of the Domain attribute but all cookies will be bound to their setting scheme.</p>

    <p>Temporary enterprise policies <strong>LegacyCookieScopeEnabled</strong> and <strong>LegacyCookieScopeEnabledForDomainList</strong> are available to revert this change. These policies will stop working in Chrome 150.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Strict Same Origin policy for Storage Access API</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>We plan to adjust the <a href="https://privacysandbox.google.com/cookies/storage-access-api" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Storage Access API</u></a> semantics to strictly follow the Same Origin Policy, to enhance&nbsp; security. The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#CookiesAllowedForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>CookiesAllowedForUrls</u></a> policy or Storage Access Headers can still be used to unblock cross-site cookies.</p>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrI140" name="upChromeBrsrI140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>window.name property no longer preserved for cross-site navigations</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>The value of the window.name property is currently preserved throughout the lifetime of a tab, even with navigation that switches browsing context groups, which can leak information and potentially be used as a tracking vector. As early as Chrome 142,&nbsp; the window.name property will no longer be preserved in this case, which will mitigate this issue.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>This update will introduce a new temporary enterprise policy, <strong>ClearWindowNameCrossSiteBrowsing</strong>, which will stop working in Chrome 146.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 142 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS</strong></li>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrJ140" name="upChromeBrsrJ140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Deprecating savedTabGroups as individual value in SyncTypesListDisabled</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Currently, the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SyncTypesListDisabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SyncTypesListDisabled</u></a> enterprise policy allows administrators to disable the synchronization of savedTabGroups datatype on desktop platforms. On mobile platforms, however, Tab Groups synchronization is already managed by the tabs datatype. To align desktop behavior with mobile and simplify sync management, the individual savedTabGroups datatype will be deprecated and will no longer be an individually customizable value within the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SyncTypesListDisabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SyncTypesListDisabled</u></a> policy</p>
    &nbsp;

    <p>Action required by administrators:&nbsp;</p>

    <p>Starting with Chrome 142, if your <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SyncTypesListDisabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SyncTypesListDisabled</u></a> policy disables either tabs or savedTabGroups, both data types will now be considered disabled. This means that disabling tabs will also disable saved tab groups, and vice-versa. The <code>savedTabGroups</code> value will be entirely removed from the list of supported datatypes for this policy. Administrators who have saved tab groups disabled and intend to keep this behavior must explicitly disable the tabs datatype. This will ensure the desired behavior before the <code>savedTabGroups</code> value is fully removed.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 142 on Windows, macOS, Linux</strong>&nbsp;</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrL140" name="upChromeBrsrL140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>HSTS tracking prevention</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This update will mitigate user tracking by third-parties via the <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6797" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS)</u></a> cache. This feature only allows HSTS upgrades for top-level navigations and blocks HSTS upgrades for sub-resource requests. Doing so makes it infeasible for third-party sites to use the HSTS cache in order to track users across the web.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 142 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrM140" name="upChromeBrsrM140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Web App manifest: update eligibility algorithm</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>As early as Chrome 139, the Web App manifest will specify an update eligibility algorithm. This makes the update process more deterministic and predictable, giving the developer more control over whether (and when) updates should apply to existing installations, and allowing removal of the <em>update check throttle</em> that user agents currently need to implement to avoid wasting network resources.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Happy Eyeballs V3</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This launch is an internal optimization in Chrome that implements <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-happy-happyeyeballs-v3/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Happy Eyeballs V3</u></a> to achieve better network connection concurrency. Happy Eyeballs V3 performs DNS resolutions asynchronously and staggers connection attempts with preferable protocols (H3/H2/H1) and address families (IPv6 or IPv4) to reduce user-visible network connection delay. This feature is gated by a temporary policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HappyEyeballsV3Enabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>HappyEyeballsV3Enabled</u></a>.</p>

    <p>To better protect your organization’s information, Google will soon require all accounts with access to admin.google.com to have 2-Step Verification (2SV) enabled. As a Google Workspace administrator, you need to confirm your identity with 2SV, which requires your password plus something additional, such as your phone or a security key.</p>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrP140" name="upChromeBrsrP140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Disallow spaces in non-file:// URL hosts</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>According to the <a href="https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#forbidden-host-code-point" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URL Standard specification</u></a>, URL hosts cannot contain the space character, but currently URL parsing in Chromium allows spaces in the host. This causes Chromium to fail several tests included in the <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/websockets?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2024-websockets" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Interop2024 HTTPS URLs for WebSocket</u></a> and <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/url?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2023-url" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URL focus</u></a> areas. To bring Chromium into spec compliance, we would like to remove spaces from URL hosts altogether, but a difficulty with this is that they are used in the host part in Windows file:// URLs (<a href="https://github.com/whatwg/url/issues/599" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Github</u></a>).</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 145 on Android, ChromeOS, LaCrOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Remove Third-party storage partitioning policies</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Third-party storage partitioning became the default in Chrome 115. The <code>chrome:// flag</code> that allowed users to disable this feature was removed in Chrome 128, and the deprecation trial ended with Chrome 139. In Chrome 145, the enterprise policies <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DefaultThirdPartyStoragePartitioningSetting"><u>DefaultThirdPartyStoragePartitioningSetting</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ThirdPartyStoragePartitioningBlockedForOrigins"><u>ThirdPartyStoragePartitioningBlockedForOrigins</u></a> will be removed. Users are advised to transition to alternative storage solutions, either by adapting to third-party storage partitioning or by using&nbsp;<code>document.requestStorageAccess({...})</code> where needed.</p>

    <p>If you have any feedback, you can add it <a href="http://crbug.com/425248669" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>here in the Chromium bug</u></a>.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 145 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: </strong>Removal of <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DefaultThirdPartyStoragePartitioningSetting" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DefaultThirdPartyStoragePartitioningSetting</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ThirdPartyStoragePartitioningBlockedForOrigins" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ThirdPartyStoragePartitioningBlockedForOrigins</u></a></li>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrR140" name="upChromeBrsrR140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>SafeBrowsing API v4 → v5 migration</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome calls into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/v4" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SafeBrowsing v4 API</u></a> will be migrated to call into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>v5 API</u></a> instead. The method names are also different between v4 and v5. If admins have any v4-specific URL allowlisting to allow network requests to <code>https://safebrowsing.googleapis.com/v4*</code>, these should be modified to allow network requests to the whole domain instead: <code>safebrowsing.googleapis.com.</code> Otherwise, rejected network requests to the v5 API will cause security regressions for users. For more details, see <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference/Migration.From.V4" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Migration From V4 - Safe Browsing</u></a>.&nbsp;</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 145 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: </strong>Feature would gradually roll-out&nbsp;</li>
    </ul>
  </li>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrS140" name="upChromeBrsrS140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>X25519Kyber768 key encapsulation for TLS</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Starting in Chrome 124, Chrome enables by default on all desktop platforms a new post-quantum secure <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-124-beta#x25519kyber768_key_encapsulation_for_tls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>TLS key encapsulation mechanism X25519Kyber768</u></a>, based on a NIST standard (ML-KEM). This protects network traffic from Chrome with servers that also support ML-KEM from decryption by a future quantum computer. This change should be transparent to server operators. This cipher will be used for both TLS 1.3 and QUIC connections.</p>

    <p>However, some TLS middleboxes might be unprepared for the size of a Kyber (ML-KEM) key encapsulation, or a new TLS ClientHello cipher code point, leading to dropped or hanging connections. This can be resolved by updating your middlebox, or disabling the key encapsulation mechanism via the temporary <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>PostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled</u></a> enterprise policy, which will be available through the end of 2024. However, long term, post-quantum secure ciphers will be required in TLS and the enterprise policy will be removed. Post-quantum cryptography is required for CSNA 2.0. To learn more, see <a href="https://blog.chromium.org/2023/08/protecting-chrome-traffic-with-hybrid.html" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Protect Chrome Traffic with Hybrid Kyber KEM</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 131 on Linux, macOS, Windows: Chrome will switch the key encapsulation mechanism to the final standard version of ML-KEM</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 145 on Linux, macOS, Windows:</strong> Enterprise policy will be removed</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrT140" name="upChromeBrsrT140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Isolated Web Apps</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Isolated Web Apps (IWAs) are an extension of existing work on PWA installation and Web Packaging that provide stronger protections against server compromise and other tampering that is necessary for developers of security-sensitive applications. Rather than being hosted on live web servers and fetched over HTTPS, these applications are packaged into Web Bundles, signed by their developer, and distributed to end-users through one or more of the potential methods described in the <a href="https://github.com/WICG/isolated-web-apps/blob/main/README.md" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>explainer</u></a>.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>In this initial release, IWAs will only be installable through an admin policy on enterprise-managed ChromeOS devices.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 146 on Windows </strong>This rollout adds support for Isolated Web Apps in enterprise-managed browser configurations on Windows.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrU140" name="upChromeBrsrU140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>UI Automation accessibility framework provider on Windows</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Starting in Chrome 126, Chrome will start directly supporting accessibility client software that uses Microsoft Windows's UI Automation accessibility framework. Prior to this change, such software interoperated with Chrome by way of a compatibility shim in Microsoft Windows. This change is being made to improve the accessible user experience for many users. It provides complete support for Narrator, Magnifier, and Voice Access; and will improve third-party apps that use Windows's UI Automation accessibility framework. Users of Chrome will find reduced memory usage and processing overhead when used with accessibility tools. It will also ease development of software using assistive technologies.</p>

    <p>Administrators may use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> enterprise policy starting in Chrome 125 to either force-enable the new provider (so that all users receive the new functionality), or disable the new provider. This policy will be supported through Chrome 146, and will be removed in Chrome 147. This one-year period is intended to give enterprises sufficient time to work with third-party vendors so that they may fix any incompatibilities resulting from the switch from Microsoft's compatibility shim to Chrome's UI Automation provider.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 125 on Windows: The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> policy is introduced so that administrators can enable Chrome's UI Automation accessibility framework provider and validate that third-party accessibility tools continue to work.</li>
      <li>Chrome 126 on Windows: The Chrome variations framework will be used to begin enabling Chrome's UI Automation accessibility framework provider for users. It will be progressively enabled to the full stable population, with pauses as needed to address compatibility issues that can be resolved in Chrome. Enterprise administrators may continue to use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> policy to either opt-in early to the new behavior, or to temporarily opt-out through Chrome 146.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Windows:</strong> The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>UiAutomationProviderEnabled</u></a> policy will be removed from Chrome. All clients will use the browser's UI Automation accessibility framework provider. &nbsp;<br>
        &nbsp;</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeECB140" name="upChromeECB140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Chrome Enterprise Overview page</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>Chrome 137 introduced a new <strong>Overview</strong> page in the Chrome browser section of the Google Admin console. The Overview page allows IT administrators to quickly find key information about their deployment:</p>

    <p>- Active &amp; inactive profiles and enrolled browsers</p>

    <p>- Identify browsers out-of-date and with pending updates</p>

    <p>- Identify high-risk extensions (according to <a href="http://spin.ai" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Spin.AI</u></a>) and get a preview of most requested extensions</p>

    <p>- Security Insights (for example, sensitive file uploads or downloads)</p>
    &nbsp;

    <p>The Overview page also allows admins to quickly access key actions such as managing extensions, accessing the browser or profile list and setting update policies, to name a few.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 137 on Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Publicly Available to IT administrators</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 141 on Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: </strong>New filtering available on the Overview page for Organization Unit and Activity Dates</li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeECC140" name="upChromeECC140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Inactive profile deletion in Chrome Enterprise Core</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>In June 2025, the inactive period for profile deletion setting started to roll out. In September 2025, the setting will begin to automatically delete managed profiles in the Admin console that have been inactive for more than the defined inactivity period. When releasing the setting, the inactivity period of time has a default value of 90 days. Meaning that by default, all managed profiles that have been inactive for more than 90 days are deleted from your account. Administrators can change the inactive period value <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/2657289#inactive_period_for_profile_deletion&amp;zippy=%2Cinactive-period-for-profile-deletion" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>using this setting</u></a>. The maximum value to determine the profile inactivity period is 730 days and the minimum value is 28 days.</p>

    <p>If the set value is lowered, it might have a global impact on any currently managed profiles. All impacted profiles will be considered inactive and, therefore, be deleted. This does not delete the user account. If an inactive profile is reactivated on a device, that profile will reappear in the console.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 141 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: </strong>Policy was rolled out in June. Deletion will start in September and the initial wave of deletion will complete by the end of September. After the initial deletion rollout, inactive profiles will continue to be deleted once they have reached their inactivity period.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>
</div>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Upcoming Chrome Enterprise Premium changes</h4>

<p><a id="upChromeEPA140" name="upChromeEPA140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome browser rule UX refactor&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>To enhance the <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/13876556" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Data Loss Prevention (DLP)</u></a> rule creation experience, the Google Admin console is being updated to streamline how administrators define policies for different applications like Chrome and Workspace. This first introduces mutually exclusive application groups, meaning that a single DLP rule can now only target one application group at a time—either Workspace apps (like Drive, Gmail), Chrome browser triggers (like file upload, URL visited), or ChromeOS triggers. This change simplifies rule configuration, eliminates potential conflicts from overlapping app selections, and lays the groundwork for more specialized and user-friendly workflows tailored to each platform's needs.</p>

    <p>Administrators will see an updated <strong>Apps</strong> selection interface using radio buttons to enforce this single-group selection for new rules. Existing rules that previously combined applications from multiple groups will be transparently migrated by the system into separate, compliant, single-platform rules to ensure continued protection and a seamless transition. Banners within the Admin console will provide information regarding these changes and the migration process. No new enterprise policies are introduced with this update; the changes are to the rule configuration interface.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 141 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: </strong>Enables mutually exclusive app selection for DLP rule configuration in Admin Console</li>
    </ul>
    <br>
    <img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/hjsLukMkGqrhUhkFamzrynmoJEwqkbQ28d9p90KRRwInd7SWuBbWG5ab1U-j0CXbuwM=w895" width="1199" height="1205" alt="" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/hjsLukMkGqrhUhkFamzrynmoJEwqkbQ28d9p90KRRwInd7SWuBbWG5ab1U-j0CXbuwM"><br>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeEPB140" name="upChromeEPB140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Increased file size support for DLP scans&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome Enterprise Premium now extends its Data Loss Prevention (DLP) and malware scanning capabilities to include large and encrypted files. Previously, files larger than 50 MB and all encrypted files were skipped during content scanning. This update closes that critical security gap. For policies configured to save evidence, files <strong>up to 2GB</strong> can now be sent to the Evidence Locker. This provides administrators with greater visibility and control, significantly reducing the risk of data exfiltration through large file transfers.</p>

    <p>No new policy is required to enable this feature. It is automatically controlled by the existing DLP rule configurations in the Google Admin console. If admins have rules that apply to file uploads, downloads, or printing, they will now also apply to large and encrypted files.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 140 on Linux, macOS, Windows: </strong>Feature is rolled out</li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeEPC140" name="upChromeEPC140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Watermarking customization&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome Enterprise Premium now allows administrators to customize the appearance of watermarks. This enhancement is motivated by the need to improve user experience, addressing concerns such as eyestrain and readability on pages with existing watermarks.</p>

    <p>To control the watermark's appearance, administrators can use the new <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WatermarkStyle" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>WatermarkStyle</u></a> policy. Within this policy, admins can configure the following:</p>

    <ul>
      <li>'font_size': Sets the font size of the text in pixels.&nbsp;</li>
      <li>'fill_opacity': Sets the fill opacity of the text, from 0 (transparent) to 100 (opaque).&nbsp;</li>
      <li>'outline_opacity': Sets the outline opacity of the text, from 0 (transparent) to 100 (opaque).&nbsp;</li>
    </ul>

    <p>This provides administrators with greater flexibility to balance security requirements with user productivity.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 141 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: </strong>This launch enables administrators to customize watermark font size and opacity using the new <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WatermarkStyle" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>WatermarkStyle</u></a> policy in the Google Admin Console.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>
</div>

<ul>
  <li><strong>GoogleLocationServicesEnabled policy&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Early 2025, ChromeOS shipped a new system-wide geolocation control inside of Privacy and security settings that can be set to <strong>Allow</strong>, <strong>Only allowed for system services</strong> (for example, automatic time zone and local weather), or <strong>Off</strong>. Admins can choose to either set a default value that users can override, or enforce one of the settings. To change their device settings, users can select <strong>Settings &gt;&nbsp; Privacy and security &gt; Privacy control &gt; Location access &gt; Change access</strong>.</p>

    <p dir="ltr">If an extension or app relies on access to device location as part of your management strategy, you need to set the <strong>GoogleLocationServicesEnabled </strong>policy to enforce <strong>allow. </strong>Otherwise, devices might only be able to send location to these apps or extensions with precise IP address data.</p>
    <img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/3ApwiXoSR-hS1oCfiOHf8PZbpqxnge5K3aA5Qo-Y7BarY8RDJfOm7SgtgqaMZ-mdRWWO=w512" width="512" height="324" alt="" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/3ApwiXoSR-hS1oCfiOHf8PZbpqxnge5K3aA5Qo-Y7BarY8RDJfOm7SgtgqaMZ-mdRWWO"></li>
</ul>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Upcoming ChromeOS changes</h4>

<p><a id="upChromeOSA140" name="upChromeOSA140"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Battery Charge Limit setting in UI&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>As early as ChromeOS 143, users will be able to take direct control of their Chromebook’s battery health to extend its lifespan with new charging optimization settings. These features help preserve your battery’s long-term health by adjusting how your device charges.</p>

    <p>To configure these options, users can navigate to <strong>Settings &gt; System preferences &gt; Power</strong> and click <strong>Change</strong> next to <strong>Optimized charging</strong>. You can choose between:</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Adaptive charging</strong>: Intelligently delays charging to 100% until it's needed, based on your daily usage patterns.</li>
      <li><strong>Charge limit: </strong>Maximizes your battery's lifespan by limiting the maximum charge to 80%.</li>
    </ul>

    <p><img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/dI4AtREIG7N_c3Z_tT0xgl93EK5zIy1ta8QC870xpj7-2If3Zk6SxuHsd2ZGivDrDg4=w895" width="1600" height="976" alt="" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/dI4AtREIG7N_c3Z_tT0xgl93EK5zIy1ta8QC870xpj7-2If3Zk6SxuHsd2ZGivDrDg4"></p>

    <p>This feature is the user-facing counterpart to the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DevicePowerBatteryChargingOptimization" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DevicePowerBatteryChargingOptimization</u></a> policy available in the Google Admin console. Admins can set this policy to one of three options:</p>

    <ol>
      <li><strong>Adaptive:</strong> The device delays charging to 100% until necessary.</li>
      <li><strong>Limited:</strong> The battery charges only to around 80%.</li>
      <li><strong>Standard:</strong> If neither of the above optimized settings are selected, the battery charges normally to 100%<span>&nbsp;</span></li>
    </ol>

    <p>It is important to note that the policy set by an administrator overrides any setting selected by the user. A user can only benefit from adjusting the charge optimization options on their device if no overriding policy is enforced. By default, if no policy is enforced, Optimized Charging is enabled on the device with the Adaptive Charging option selected.</p>
  </li>
</ul>
</div>

<ul>
  <li><strong>AI Mode for search recommendations in Chrome&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>AI Mode is a feature that helps users dive deeper into topics they care about by showing AI Mode for search recommendations in Chrome. A new policy, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#AIModeSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>AIModeSettings</u></a>, is available to control search recommendations in the address bar and <strong>New tab</strong> page search box. This policy also controls AI Mode recommendations in the address bar and the new tab page omnibox.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 138 on ChromeOS, Linux,&nbsp; macOS, Windows: AI Mode recommendations starts rolling out in the address bar and the new tab page search box. The AI Mode entry point is also rolled out in the new tab page search box.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 139&nbsp;</strong>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>on Windows,&nbsp; macOS, Linux and ChromeOS: </strong>The AI Mode entrypoint button in the address bar begins rollout. AI Mode inline compose box in new tab page omnibox begins rollout.&nbsp;</li>
          <li><strong>on Android, iOS: </strong>The<strong> </strong>AI Mode entrypoint in the new tab page omnibox begins to roll out. And for iOS <strong>&nbsp;</strong>the AI Mode recommendations starts rollout in the address bar as well.&nbsp;</li>
        </ul>
      </li>
    </ul>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Admin-configurable site search&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Site search shortcuts are a way to use the address bar (omnibox) as a search box for a specific site without navigating directly to the site’s URL, similar to how you can use the omnibox to perform a broad Google search of the web. Administrators can now create site shortcuts for users to shortcut to the most critical enterprise sites. Users can initiate a search by typing the shortcut or @shortcut (for example, @work), followed by Space or Tab, in the address bar.</p>

    <p>Admins control these shortcut settings using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SiteSearchSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SiteSearchSettings</u></a> policy.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 128 on ChromeOS, Linux,&nbsp; macOS, Windows: Gradual rollout</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 139 on ChromeOS, Linux,&nbsp; macOS, Windows</strong>: Adding an additional policy parameter allowing admins to specify <strong>Allow user override</strong>, which allows users to edit, disable, or delete admin-set shortcuts</li>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrD139" name="chromeBrsrD139"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Malicious APK download checks&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome on Android now contacts Google servers about Android Package Kit (APK) files downloaded in Chrome, to get a verdict about their safety. If a downloaded APK file is determined to be dangerous, Chrome shows a warning and blocks the download, to protect users against mobile malware. Such download warnings are bypassable by the user through the Chrome UI. These malicious APK download checks are performed for users enrolled in Standard Protection or Enhanced Protection from Google Safe Browsing. This feature can be disabled by setting the Safe Browsing mode to <em>No Protection</em> using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SafeBrowsingProtectionLevel" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SafeBrowsingProtectionLevel</u></a> policy.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 139 on Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;

    <p><img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/PTguub5qft54jyYtwSfWABqWEm6hNOD3tC9wFP8vmRj-i2oarqPxdr_2cF42ptv9Hw=w316" width="316" height="530" alt="Chrome Web Store" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/PTguub5qft54jyYtwSfWABqWEm6hNOD3tC9wFP8vmRj-i2oarqPxdr_2cF42ptv9Hw"></p>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrE139" name="chromeBrsrE139"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Migrate extensions to Manifest V3 before June 2025&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Extensions must be updated to use Manifest V3. Chrome extensions are transitioning to a new manifest version, Manifest V3. This brings improved privacy for your users—for example, by moving to a model where extensions modify requests declaratively, without the ability to see individual requests. This also improves extension security, as remotely-hosted code is disallowed on Manifest V3.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>Beginning June 2024, Chrome gradually disables Manifest V2 extensions running in the browser. An enterprise policy - <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ExtensionManifestV2Availability" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ExtensionManifestV2Availability</u></a> - can be used to test Manifest V3 in your organization ahead of the migration. Additionally, machines on which the policy is enabled are not subject to the disabling of Manifest V2 extensions until June 2025 - at which point the policy is to be removed.</p>

    <p>You can see which Manifest version is being used by all Chrome extensions running on your fleet using the <strong>Apps &amp; extensions</strong> usage page in Chrome Enterprise Core.&nbsp;</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 127 on ChromeOS, LaCrOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Chrome will gradually disable Manifest V2 extensions on user devices. Only those with the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ExtensionManifestV2Availability" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ExtensionManifestV2Availability</u></a> enterprise policy enabled would be able to continue using Manifest V2 extensions in their organization.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 139 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: </strong>Remove <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ExtensionManifestV2Availability" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ExtensionManifestV2Availability</u></a> policy.</li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrF139" name="chromeBrsrF139"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>New tab page footer&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>An update to the <strong>New tab</strong> page includes a new footer designed to provide users with greater transparency and control over their Chrome experience.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 138 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows:<strong> </strong>Extension Attribution&nbsp; will begin to show on the NTP. If an extension has changed your default <strong>New tab</strong> page, you'll now see a message in the footer that attributes the change to that specific extension. This message often includes a link directly to the extension in the Chrome Web Store, making it easier to identify and manage unwanted extensions. If you're an administrator, you can disable this attribution using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#NTPFooterExtensionAttributionEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>NTPFooterExtensionAttributionEnabled</u></a> policy.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 139 on Linux, macOS, Windows</strong>: Browser management disclosure will be shown if one of the policies to customize the footer is set by an enterprise admin. For users whose Chrome browser is managed by a trusted source, the <strong>New tab</strong> page footer will now display a management disclosure notice. This helps you understand how your browser is being managed. Administrators can disable this notice with the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#NTPFooterManagementNoticeEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>NTPFooterManagementNoticeEnabled</u></a> policy. Additionally, organizations can customize the footer's appearance using the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#EnterpriseLogoUrlForBrowser" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>EnterpriseLogoUrlForBrowser</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#EnterpriseCustomLabelForBrowser" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>EnterpriseCustomLabelForBrowser</u></a> policies to display a custom logo and label.</li>
      <li>Chrome 140 on Linux, macOS, Windows: A default notice (<em>Managed by &lt;domain name&gt;</em>) will start to be shown in the <strong>New tab</strong> page footer for all managed browsers. Visibility can be changed with the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#NTPFooterManagementNoticeEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>NTPFooterManagementNoticeEnabled</u></a> policy.&nbsp;</li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;

    <p><img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/1t4shAyKRb8XlNZ76kd5s0jtkq2qEEzUwO6vfnQmt1oGl98z5JDiB3hoWU7IV_q8iao=w512" width="512" height="378" alt="Chrome Web Store" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/1t4shAyKRb8XlNZ76kd5s0jtkq2qEEzUwO6vfnQmt1oGl98z5JDiB3hoWU7IV_q8iao"></p>
    &nbsp;</li>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrG139" name="chromeBrsrG139"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Prevent accidental password deletions on Chrome&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>To reduce the risk of accidental deletion of passwords on <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/answer/2392709" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Delete browsing data</u></a>, Chrome 139 now points users to Google Password Manager settings, where they can better manage and delete passwords and passkeys. The feature removes the <strong>Passwords and other sign-in data</strong> selection in<img alt="More" height="19" src="//lh7-rt.googleusercontent.com/docsz/AD_4nXfDQ2hZnGpM7gu4FYsEIghflvjrep9ggi4185BQiFy0y0PY4uSncVBIH7YbXFXtYMxqJJNOfGj843_4vRiELYEcREcAb5-7qmhO_OzLO401kZ1B_UUYNzIOjdihRGuF4nhfNR_RgHfRa2xZkvUwbssL6mo76QU?key=mteu4N1GlYLou4GHcpRftg" width="19"> <img alt="and then" height="19" src="//lh7-rt.googleusercontent.com/docsz/AD_4nXfwsIIbiBAsd213q8-TFR4PktBPLntpiUwU6Z_mfUujpPAAaE8c-tcLrfM6je98xnxuzR9MWUndrlWaiCxGrNjOStklamzIo9iwLnrOjkIJKJhQQRhSm_IixzBE8qNQGonxnaKAzIdbegLFXiTBGbJ_Z8YRXb0P?key=mteu4N1GlYLou4GHcpRftg" width="19"> <strong>Delete browsing data</strong> and instead directs users to Google Password Manager where they can delete individually or in bulk.</p>

    <p>This feature does not impact the existing enterprise policies <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ClearBrowsingDataOnExitList" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ClearBrowsingDataOnExitList</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#BrowsingDataLifetime" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>BrowsingDataLifetime</u></a><strong>.&nbsp;</strong></p>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrH139" name="chromeBrsrH139"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Promotional notifications&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>In Chrome 128, new promotional OS-level notifications began to be shown to users. These notifications are governed by the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PromotionsEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>PromotionsEnabled</u></a> enterprise policy.</p>

Notifications will still be only shown to a subset of low-engaged users, and these can be disabled through the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PromotionsEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>PromotionsEnabled</u></a> enterprise policy.</li>
