<h2>Chrome Enterprise Core changes</h2>

<p><a id="chromeECA137" name="chromeECA137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>IP Address Logging &amp; Reporting&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome Enterprise will enhance security monitoring and incident response capabilities by collecting and reporting local and remote IP addresses and sending those IP addresses to the <a href="https://support.google.com/a/answer/7575955?sjid=9734593434977128193-NA" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Security Investigation Tool (SIT)</u></a> logs. In addition, Chrome Enterprise will allow admins to optionally send the IP addresses to first-party and third-party security information and event management (SIEM) providers via the Chrome Enterprise reporting connector. For more details, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/11375053?sjid=9734593434977128193-NA" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Manage Chrome Enterprise reporting connectors.</u></a> This will be available for Chrome Enterprise Core and Chrome Enterprise Premium customers.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 137 on Windows, macOS, Linux</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeECB137" name="chromeECB137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Chrome Enterprise Overview page&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome Browser Enterprise is introducing a new <strong>Overview</strong> page in the Chrome browser section of the Google Admin console. The Overview page allows IT administrators to quickly find key information about their deployment:</p>

    <p>- Active and inactive profiles and enrolled browsers</p>

    <p>- Identify browsers out-of-date and with pending updates</p>

    <p>- Identify high-risk extensions (according to Spin.AI) and get a preview of most requested extensions</p>

    <p>The Overview page also allows you to quickly access key actions, such as, managing extensions (block and allow) and accessing browser and profile lists.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 137 on Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong></li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;

    <p><img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/9jyVqKi3n6EARGNE91l4mRaNVfYlp3l511UCdJl9RqwkSyP6_Q744RcHgQjO-dqAVRI=w512" width="512" height="384" alt="&quot; &quot;" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/9jyVqKi3n6EARGNE91l4mRaNVfYlp3l511UCdJl9RqwkSyP6_Q744RcHgQjO-dqAVRI"></p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeECC137" name="chromeECC137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>New remote commands and CSV export for the Managed profiles list&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>The Admin console will support profile-level "Clear cache" and "Clear cookies" remote commands,&nbsp;and CSV export for the Managed Profiles list. You can select one or multiple profiles and perform a remote command.</p>

<div class="no-margin"><h2>Chrome Enterprise Premium changes</h2>

<p>Read more about the differences between <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/products/chrome-enterprise-premium" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Enterprise Core and Chrome Enterprise Premium</u></a>.</p>

<p><a id="chromeEPA137" name="chromeEPA137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>DLP download support for File System Access API (FSA)&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> &nbsp;

    <p>Chrome Enterprise Premium's Data Loss Prevention (DLP) content analysis and Safe Browse deep scans now extend to folder and directory downloads initiated via the <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/capabilities/web-apis/file-system-access" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>File System Access (FSA) API</u></a>, for example, in web-based IDEs. This addresses a gap, enhancing data security by applying existing DLP rules (configured via <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DataLeakPreventionRulesList" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DataLeakPreventionRulesList</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SafeBrowsingDeepScanningEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SafeBrowsingDeepScanningEnabled</u></a> policies) to these operations.</p>

    <p>If a download violates a DLP policy, it will be blocked, resulting in an empty file, and the website might indicate a <em>Blocked by Safe Browse</em> error. This change primarily benefits security by preventing data exfiltration through this vector. Administrators should test this with web applications using the FSA API to observe the behavior with their current DLP configurations.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 137 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows:</strong> Enables DLP content analysis for downloads initiated via File System Access API on selected platforms, governed by existing enterprise policies.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

    <p>The <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/11375053" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Enterprise Reporting Connector</u></a> is being updated to include security event reporting from Chrome on mobile devices (Android and iOS). This will provide IT admins with visibility into events such as unsafe site visits, sensitive data transfers (as per Data Protection rules), and URL Filtering matches occurring on mobile, achieving feature parity with existing desktop reporting. This enhancement aims to improve the organization's overall security posture by extending threat detection and data protection capabilities to mobile platforms.</p>

    <p>For customers utilizing the Security Investigation Tool (SIT), these new mobile browser events will be available for investigation; this SIT integration is a feature of Chrome Enterprise Premium. IT admins should be aware that these additional event types from mobile will begin to flow through their configured Reporting Connector.</p>

    <p>No new, specific enterprise policies are being introduced to control this mobile reporting extension itself; existing configurations for the Reporting Connector, Data Protection rules, and URL Filtering policies will determine the events generated and reported.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Per-extension user script toggle</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>In Chrome 138, the way that users and administrators control an extension’s ability to run user created scripts and use the <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/reference/api/userScripts" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>userScripts API</u></a> is changing. This change enhances security. End-users won’t unintentionally grant user script permissions to every extension when enabling <strong>Developer mode</strong> by explicitly deciding which extensions can run these potentially powerful scripts. For more detail on the motivation for the change, see this <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome for developers</u></a> blog.</p>

    <p>End users will now toggle this per extension on the <code>chrome://extensions</code> page via a <strong>Allow User Scripts</strong> toggle, replacing the global <strong>Developer mode</strong> toggle for more granular control. Existing extensions will have this toggle automatically enabled if <strong>Developer mode</strong> is on and the extension has been granted the User Scripts permission.</p>

    <p>Administrators who currently manage user scripts by disabling developer mode should now use the <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/9867568" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>`blocked_permissions` policy</u></a> or the <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/7515036" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Google Admin console</u></a> to independently control the User Scripts permission and extension <strong>Developer mode</strong>.</p>

    <p>Extension developers are advised to update their documentation to reflect the new toggle. See the <a href="https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/chromium-extensions" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chromium Extensions Google Groups</u></a> mailing list for more information and other changes to usage of the API.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 138 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: </strong>Feature rolls out</li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;

    <p><img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/wJH5g9SI6xVjjDfbR7hPwE4dv2CKVAyU_fhw49k4-LrLDm8SV13rd6YCtQD6gwB4HA=w512" width="512" height="70" alt="" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/png" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/wJH5g9SI6xVjjDfbR7hPwE4dv2CKVAyU_fhw49k4-LrLDm8SV13rd6YCtQD6gwB4HA"></p>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrC137" name="upChromeBrsrC137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Enhanced Safe Browsing as a synced setting</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome's Enhanced Safe Browsing is becoming a synced feature. This means that if a user opts into Enhanced Safe Browsing on one device, this protection level will automatically apply across all other devices where they are signed into Chrome with the same account. The goal is to provide stronger, more consistent security protection and a standardized user experience.</p>

    <p>Users who enable Enhanced Safe Browsing will benefit from its protections, for example, proactive phishing protection, improved detection of malware and malicious extensions) consistently across their synced Chrome instances on Desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS), Android, and iOS. Users will be notified of this change via UI elements when their Enhanced Safe Browsing setting is synced.</p>

    <p>The Safe Browsing protection level is an existing feature, controlled by the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SafeBrowsingProtectionLevel" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SafeBrowsingProtectionLevel</u></a> policy.</p>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrF137" name="upChromeBrsrF137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Removal of Private Network Access enterprise policies</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Private Network Access (PNA 1.0) is an unshipped security feature designed to limit website access to local networks. Due to deployability concerns, PNA 1.0 was never able to ship by default, as it was incompatible with too many existing devices.</p>

    <p>PNA 1.0 required changes to devices on local networks. Instead, Chrome is implementing an updated proposal, Private Network Access 2.0 (PNA 2.0) (<a href="https://github.com/explainers-by-googlers/local-network-access" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Github</u></a>). PNA 2.0 only requires changes to sites that need to access the local network, rather than requiring changes to devices on the local network. Sites are much easier to update than devices, and so this approach should be much more straightforward to roll out.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>The only way to enforce PNA 1.0 is via enterprise policy. To avoid regressing security for enterprise customers opting-in to PNA 1.0 prior to shipping PNA 2.0, we will maintain the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PrivateNetworkAccessRestrictionsEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>PrivateNetworkAccessRestrictionsEnabled</u></a> policy, which causes Chrome to send special preflight messages, until such time that it becomes incompatible with PNA 2.0.</p>

    <p>The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowedForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowedForUrls</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowed" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowed</u></a> policies, which loosen PNA 1.0 restrictions, will be removed immediately. These policies currently have no effect, since PNA 1.0 is not shipped, and they will have no meaning once PNA 1.0 is removed.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 135 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: Deprecate <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowedForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowedForUrls</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowed" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowed</u></a>, and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PrivateNetworkAccessRestrictionsEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>PrivateNetworkAccessRestrictionsEnabled</u></a> policies.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 138 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia:</strong> Removal of <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PrivateNetworkAccessRestrictionsEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>PrivateNetworkAccessRestrictionsEnabled</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowedForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowedForUrls</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowed" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowed</u></a>. There should be a PNA2 replacement policy available in Chrome 138.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrG137" name="upChromeBrsrG137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>TLS 1.3 Early Data</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>TLS 1.3 Early Data allows GET requests to be sent during the handshake when resuming a connection to a compatible TLS 1.3 server. The feature is expected to demonstrate performance improvements and will be available in Chrome 138 with a policy (<strong>TLS13EarlyDataEnabled</strong>) to control this change.</p>

    <p>TLS 1.3 Early Data is an established protocol. Existing TLS servers, middleboxes, and security software are expected to either handle or reject TLS 1.3 Early Data without dropping the connection. However, devices that do not correctly implement the TLS standard (RFC8446) may malfunction and disconnect when TLS 1.3 Early Data is in use. If this occurs, administrators should contact the vendor for a fix.</p>

    <p>This policy is a temporary measure to control the feature and will be removed in a future milestone. The policy may be enabled to allow you to test for issues and disabled while issues are being resolved.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 138 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrH137" name="upChromeBrsrH137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Predictable reported storage quota</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome 138 will introduce a predictable storage quota from StorageManager's estimate API for sites that do not have unlimited storage permissions.</p>

    <p>It is possible to detect a user's browsing mode via the reported storage quota because the storage space made available is significantly smaller in incognito mode than in regular mode. This is a mitigation that prevents detection of a user's browsing mode via the storage API by reporting an artificial quota, equal to usage + min(10 GiB, disk rounded up to the nearest 1 GiB), in all browsing modes for sites with limited storage permissions. Sites with unlimited storage permissions will be unaffected. Enforced quota will also be unaffected.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 138 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrI137" name="upChromeBrsrI137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Strict Same Origin Policy for Storage Access API</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>We plan to adjust the Storage Access API semantics to strictly follow the Same Origin Policy, to enhance&nbsp; security. Using <code>document.requestStorageAccess()</code> in a frame only attaches cookies to requests to the iframe's origin (not site) by default. The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#CookiesAllowedForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>CookiesAllowedForUrls</u></a> policy or Storage Access Headers can still be used to unblock cross-site cookies.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 138 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrJ137" name="upChromeBrsrJ137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Summarizer API</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Summarizer API is a JavaScript API for producing summaries of input text, backed by an AI language model. Browsers and operating systems are increasingly expected to gain access to a language model. By exposing this built-in model, we avoid every website needing to download their own multi-gigabyte language model, or send input text to third-party APIs. The summarizer API in particular exposes a high-level API for interfacing with a language model in order to summarize inputs for a variety of use cases (<a href="https://github.com/webmachinelearning/writing-assistance-apis/blob/main/README.md#summarizer-api" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Github</u></a>), in a way that does not depend on the specific language model in question.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>An enterprise policy,&nbsp;<a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAILocalFoundationalModelSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAILocalFoundationalModelSettings</u></a>,&nbsp;is available to disable the underlying model downloading which would render this API unavailable.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 138 on Windows, macOS, Linux</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrK137" name="upChromeBrsrK137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Language Detector API</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Language Detector API is a JavaScript API for detecting the language of text, with confidence levels. An important supplement to translation is language detection. This can be combined with translation, for example, taking user input in an unknown language and translating it to a specific target language. Browsers today often already have language detection capabilities, and we want to offer them to web developers through a JavaScript API, supplementing the translation API. An enterprise policy, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAILocalFoundationalModelSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAILocalFoundationalModelSettings</u></a>, is available to disable the underlying model downloading which would render this API unavailable.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 138 on Windows, macOS, Linux</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrL137" name="upChromeBrsrL137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Translator API</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>The Translator API is a JavaScript API to provide language translation capabilities to web pages. Browsers are increasingly offering language translation to their users. Such translation capabilities can also be useful to web developers. This is especially the case when the browser's built-in translation abilities cannot help. An enterprise policy, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#GenAILocalFoundationalModelSettings" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GenAILocalFoundationalModelSettings</u></a>, is available to disable the underlying model downloading which would render this API unavailable.</p>
    &nbsp;

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 138 on Windows, macOS, Linux</strong></li>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Web serial over Bluetooth on Android</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature allows web pages and web apps to connect to serial ports over Bluetooth on Android devices. Chrome on Android now supports Web Serial API over Bluetooth RFCOMM. Existing enterprise policies (<a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DefaultSerialGuardSetting" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DefaultSerialGuardSetting</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SerialAllowAllPortsForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SerialAllowAllPortsForUrls</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SerialAllowUsbDevicesForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SerialAllowUsbDevicesForUrls</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SerialAskForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SerialAskForUrls</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SerialBlockedForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SerialBlockedForUrls</u></a>) on other platforms are enabled in future_on states for Android. All policies except <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SerialAllowUsbDevicesForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SerialAllowUsbDevicesForUrls</u></a> will be enabled after the feature is enabled. <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SerialAllowUsbDevicesForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SerialAllowUsbDevicesForUrls</u></a> will be enabled in a future launch after Android provides system level support of wired serial ports.</p>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrMM137" name="upChromeBrsrMM137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Upcoming change for CA certificates included in the Chrome Root Store</strong><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml">

    <p>In response to sustained compliance failures, Chrome 139 changes how publicly-trusted TLS server authentication, that is, websites&nbsp;or certificates issued by Chunghwa Telecom and Netlock, are trusted by default. This applies to Chrome 139 and later on Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, Android, and Linux; iOS policies do not allow use of the Chrome Root Store in Chrome for iOS.</p>

    <p>Specifically, TLS certificates validating to the Chunghwa Telecom or Netlock root CA certificates included in the Chrome Root Store and issued:</p>

    <p>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;- after July 31, 2025, will no longer be trusted by default.</p>

    <p>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;- on or before July 31, 2025, will be unaffected by this change.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>If a Chrome user or an enterprise explicitly trusts any of the affected Chunghwa Telecom or Netlock certificates on a platform and version of Chrome relying on the Chrome Root Store, for example, when explicit trust is conveyed through a Windows Group Policy Object, the Signed Certificate Timestamp (SCT) constraints described above will be overridden and certificates will function as they do today.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p>

    <p>For additional information and testing resources, see <a href="https://security.googleblog.com/2025/05/sustaining-digital-certificate-security-chrome-root-store-changes.html" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Sustaining Digital Certificate Security - Upcoming Changes to the Chrome Root Store</u></a>.</p>

    <p>To learn more about the Chrome Root Store, see this <a href="https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/net/data/ssl/chrome_root_store/faq.md" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>FAQ</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 139 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows:</strong> All versions of Chrome 139 and higher that rely on the Chrome Root Store will honor the blocking action, but the blocking action will only begin for certificates issued after July 31, 2025.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

    <p>The last version of Chrome that supports Android Oreo or Android Pie is Chrome 138, and it includes a message to affected users informing them to upgrade their operating system. Chrome 139 and newer versions will not be supported on, nor shipped or available to, users running Android Oreo or Android Pie.<strong>&nbsp;</strong></p>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrO137" name="upChromeBrsrO137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Migrate extensions to Manifest V3 before June 2025</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Extensions must be updated to leverage Manifest V3. Chrome extensions are transitioning to a new manifest version, Manifest V3. This will bring improved privacy for your users—for example, by moving to a model where extensions modify requests declaratively, without the ability to see individual requests. This also improves extension security, as remotely hosted code will be disallowed on Manifest V3.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>Beginning June 2024, Chrome will gradually disable Manifest V2 extensions running in the browser. An Enterprise policy - <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ExtensionManifestV2Availability" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ExtensionManifestV2Availability</u></a> - can be used to test Manifest V3 in your organization ahead of the migration. Additionally, machines on which the policy is enabled will not be subject to the disabling of Manifest V2 extensions until the following year - June 2025 - at which point the policy will be removed.</p>

    <p>You can see which Manifest version is being used by all Chrome extensions running on your fleet using the Apps &amp; extensions usage page in Chrome Enterprise Core.&nbsp;</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 127 on ChromeOS, LaCrOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: Chrome will gradually disable Manifest V2 extensions on user devices. Only those with the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ExtensionManifestV2Availability" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ExtensionManifestV2Availability</u></a> enterprise policy enabled would be able to continue using Manifest V2 extensions in their organization.</li>
    </ul>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 139 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: </strong>Remove <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#ExtensionManifestV2Availability" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>ExtensionManifestV2Availability</u></a> policy.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

    <p>Chrome 138 will be the last release to support macOS 11; Chrome 139 and later&nbsp;will no longer support macOS 11, which is outside of its support window with Apple. Running on a supported operating system is essential to maintaining security.</p>

    <p>On Macs running macOS 11, Chrome will continue to work, showing a warning infobar, but will not update any further. If a user wishes to have their Chrome&nbsp;updated, they need to update their computer to a supported version of macOS. For new installations of Chrome 139 and later, macOS 12 or later&nbsp;will be required.</p>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrQ137" name="upChromeBrsrQ137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Happy Eyeballs V3</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This launch is an internal optimization in Chrome that implements Happy Eyeballs V3 to achieve better network connection concurrency. Happy Eyeballs V3 performs DNS resolutions asynchronously and staggers connection attempts with preferable protocols (H3/H2/H1) and address families (IPv6/IPv4) to reduce user-visible network connection delay. This feature is gated by a temporary policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#HappyEyeballsV3Enabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>HappyEyeballsV3Enabled</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrR137" name="upChromeBrsrR137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Isolated Web Apps</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Isolated Web Apps (IWAs) are an extension of existing work on PWA installation and Web Packaging that provide stronger protections against server compromise and other tampering that is necessary for developers of security-sensitive applications.</p>

    <p>Rather than being hosted on live web servers and fetched over HTTPS, these applications are packaged into Web Bundles, signed by their developer, and distributed to end-users through one or more of the potential methods described in the <a href="https://github.com/WICG/isolated-web-apps/blob/main/README.md" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>explainer</u></a>.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>In this initial release, IWAs will only be installable through an admin policy on enterprise-managed ChromeOS devices.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 140 on Windows:</strong> This rollout adds support for Isolated Web Apps in enterprise-managed browser configurations on Windows.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrS137" name="upChromeBrsrS137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Disallow spaces in non-file:// URL hosts</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>According to the <a href="https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#forbidden-host-code-point" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URL Standard specification</u></a>, URL hosts cannot contain the space character, but currently URL parsing in Chromium allows spaces in the host. This causes Chromium to fail several tests included in the <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/websockets?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2024-websockets" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Interop2024 HTTPS URLs for WebSocket</u></a> and <a href="https://wpt.fyi/results/url?label=master&amp;label=experimental&amp;aligned&amp;view=interop&amp;q=label%3Ainterop-2023-url" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>URL focus</u></a> areas. To bring Chromium into spec compliance, we would like to remove spaces from URL hosts altogether, but a difficulty with this is that they are used in the host part in Windows file:// URLs (<a href="https://github.com/whatwg/url/issues/599" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Github</u></a>).</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 141 on Android, ChromeOS, LaCrOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia</strong></li>
    </ul>
    <strong> </strong></li>
</ul>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrT137" name="upChromeBrsrT137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong><strong>Safe Browsing API v4 → v5 migration</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> </strong>

    <p>Chrome calls into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/v4" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Safe Browsing v4 API</u></a> will be migrated to call into the <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>v5 API</u></a> instead. The method names are also different between v4 and v5. If admins have any v4-specific URL allowlisting to allow network requests to <code>https://safebrowsing.googleapis.com/v4*</code>, these should be modified to allow network requests to the whole domain instead: <code>safebrowsing.googleapis.com</code>. Otherwise, rejected network requests to the v5 API will cause security regressions for users. For more details, see <a href="https://developers.google.com/safe-browsing/reference/Migration.From.V4" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Migration From V4 - Safe Browsing</u></a>.&nbsp;</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 145 on Android, iOS, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrU137" name="upChromeBrsrU137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li><strong><strong>UI Automation accessibility framework provider on Windows</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a> </strong>

    <p>Starting in Chrome 126, Chrome will start directly supporting accessibility client software that uses Microsoft Windows's UI Automation accessibility framework. Prior to this change, such software interoperated with Chrome by way of a compatibility shim in Microsoft Windows. This change is being made to improve the accessible user experience for many users. It provides complete support for Narrator, Magnifier, and Voice Access; and will improve third-party apps that use Windows's UI Automation accessibility framework. Users of Chrome will find reduced memory usage and processing overhead when used with accessibility tools. It will also ease development of software using assistive technologies.</p>

    <p>Administrators may use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank">UiAutomationProviderEnabled</a> enterprise policy starting in Chrome 125 to either force-enable the new provider (so that all users receive the new functionality), or disable the new provider. This policy will be supported through Chrome 146, and will be removed in Chrome 147. This one-year period is intended to give enterprises sufficient time to work with third-party vendors so that they may fix any incompatibilities resulting from the switch from Microsoft's compatibility shim to Chrome's UI Automation provider.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 125 on Windows: The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank">UiAutomationProviderEnabled</a> policy is introduced so that administrators can enable Chrome's UI Automation accessibility framework provider and validate that third-party accessibility tools continue to work.</li>
      <li>Chrome 126 on Windows: The Chrome variations framework will be used to begin enabling Chrome's UI Automation accessibility framework provider for users. It will be progressively enabled to the full stable population, with pauses as needed to address compatibility issues that can be resolved in Chrome. Enterprise administrators may continue to use the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank">UiAutomationProviderEnabled</a> policy to either opt-in early to the new behavior, or to temporarily opt-out through Chrome 146.</li>
    </ul>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 147 on Windows:</strong> The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#UiAutomationProviderEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank">UiAutomationProviderEnabled</a> policy will be removed from Chrome. All clients will use the browser's UI Automation accessibility framework provider</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><strong>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeECB137" name="upChromeECB137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong><strong>Inactive profile deletion in Chrome Enterprise Core</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></strong></p>

    <p>In June 2025, the inactive period for profile deletion setting started to roll out. In July 2025, the setting will begin to automatically delete managed profiles in the Admin console that have been inactive for more than the defined inactivity period. When releasing the setting, the inactivity period of time has a default value of 90 days. Meaning that by default, all managed profiles that have been inactive for more than 90 days are deleted from your account. Administrators can change the inactive period value using this setting. The maximum value to determine the profile inactivity period is 730 days and the minimum value is 28 days.</p>

    <p>If you lower the set value, it might have a global impact on any currently managed profiles. All impacted profiles will be considered inactive and, therefore, be deleted. This does not delete the user account. If an inactive profile is re-activated on a device, that profile will reappear in the console.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong><strong>Chrome 138 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows: </strong></strong>Policy will roll out in June. Deletion will start in July and the initial wave of deletion will complete by the end of August. After the initial deletion rollout, inactive profiles will continue to be deleted once they have reached their inactivity period.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

    <p>Chrome on iOS is introducing support for multiple accounts, particularly for managed (work or school) accounts. This update introduces separate browser profiles for each managed account, ensuring strict data separation between work and personal browsing. Regular accounts will continue to share a single profile.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>This change aims to improve Chrome's enterprise offering and provide a more secure and organized browsing experience, especially for end users with both personal and work accounts on their device. Users will experience a one-time onboarding flow when adding a managed account to the device. They will be able to switch between accounts by tapping on the account particle disk on the <strong>New tab</strong> page.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>Admins who enabled Chrome policies on iOS (instructions <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/6304822?hl=en" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>here</u></a>) can continue to leverage&nbsp;existing policies.&nbsp;&nbsp;</p>

<div class="no-margin"><h2>ChromeOS updates</h2>

<p><a id="chromeOSA137" name="chromeOSA137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Face Control policy on ChromeOS&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>With ChromeOS 137, we&nbsp;introduce a new policy, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#FaceGazeEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>FaceGazeEnabled</u></a>,&nbsp;to allow admins to have more control over access to Face Control on an organizational level.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>For more details, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chromebook/answer/15824371" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Use facial gestures &amp; head movements to control your Chromebook with Face control</u></a>.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeOSB137" name="chromeOSB137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Crosstalk cancellation&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>Crosstalk cancellation provides an immersive audio experience when using the internal speaker. Users can feel the audio surrounding their head instead of coming from the geometric position of the internal speaker. Any playable audio content benefits from this feature, especially when playing games or watching videos with spatialized audio. Users experience immersive, surround-sound audio, similar to wearing a headset.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeOSC137" name="chromeOSC137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>ChromeVox keyboard shortcut to caption audio with braille devices&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>ChromeVox now enables a command that displays spoken text as braille captions on connected (USB or Bluetooth) braille displays.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>The ChromeVox command is <strong>Search + O + C</strong> and stands for Search Open Captions.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>The braille command is space + dots 1-4-7. For more details, see <a href="https://support.google.com/accessibility/answer/7020014" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Use a braille device with your Chromebook - Google Accessibility Help</u></a>.&nbsp;</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="chromeOSD137" name="chromeOSD137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Event-based log collection&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>For event-based log collection, when an event occurs—for example, an OS crash or update failure—you'll see a notification on the device details page. You can also view device events in the device details page, to see when events occurred and to get detailed information. Google uploads any logs relevant to the specific event type, which makes troubleshooting more efficient.</p>

    <p>To enable this feature:</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Turn on the&nbsp;<a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/1375678#log_upload_enabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Device system log upload</a> setting.</li>
      <li>Turn on OS update status reporting—For the&nbsp;<a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/1375678?hl=en#zippy=%2Creport-device-os-information" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Report device OS information</a><strong> </strong>setting, select <strong>OS update status</strong>.</li>
      <li>Turn on device telemetry reporting on crash information—For the&nbsp;<a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/1375678?hl=en#zippy=%2Creport-device-telemetry" rel="noopener" target="_blank">Report device telemetry</a> setting, select <strong>Crash information</strong>.</li>
    </ul>

    <p>These uploads can happen at most two times per day on one device.</p>
    <img src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/vo83rE08SavN-7B-CQQLDh28B40pA0ZRuDgN_B780AsJIX4Jp8ei97l9sPF15hdcjDM=w512" width="512" height="235" alt="" class="screenshot" data-mime-type="image/gif" data-alt-src="//lh3.googleusercontent.com/vo83rE08SavN-7B-CQQLDh28B40pA0ZRuDgN_B780AsJIX4Jp8ei97l9sPF15hdcjDM"></li>
</ul>
</div>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Upcoming ChromeOS changes</h4>

<p><a id="upChromeOSA137" name="upChromeOSA137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Chrome apps changes&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>Starting with ChromeOS 138,&nbsp; planned for stable release on July 22nd, admin-installed Chrome apps in kiosk sessions will be disabled by default. A new policy, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#KioskChromeAppsForceAllowed" rel="noopener" target="_blank">KioskChromeAppsForceAllowed</a>,&nbsp;will be available prior to the release of ChromeOS 138 for administrators to re-enable Chrome apps in kiosk sessions. With this policy turned on, Chrome apps in kiosk sessions will be supported through ChromeOS 150.</p>

    <p>Additionally, as a reminder, as early as ChromeOS 139, planned for stable release on August 19th, user-installed Chrome apps will stop working.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>For more details, see <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/a/answer/15950395" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>End of support for Chrome apps</u></a>.</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p><a id="upChromeOSB137" name="upChromeOSB137"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Upcoming Native Client (NaCl) deprecation&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a></p>

    <p>ChromeOS 138 will be the final release to support <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/native-client" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Native Client (NaCl)</u></a> in managed environments with the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/?policy=NativeClientForceAllowed" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>NaCl allow policy</u></a> enabled. For devices on the Long-term Support (LTS) channel with this policy active, NaCl support will continue until the LTS Last Refresh in April 2026.</p>
  </li>
</ul>
</div>

<div class="no-margin"><h2>Chrome browser changes</h2>

<p><a id="chromeBrsrA136" name="chromeBrsrA136"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Google Lens result presentation updates&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Search results for Google Lens queries originating from the device camera and from searching images on web pages are presented on a native UI panel that slides from the bottom of the screen. Previously,&nbsp;these answers were presented on a separate web page on a new tab. Admins can control this feature with the existing policy <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#LensCameraAssistedSearchEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>LensCameraAssistedSearchEnabled</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 136 on iOS</strong></li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;

    <p><strong><img height="532" src="//lh7-rt.googleusercontent.com/docsz/AD_4nXeoYO9CynIctZ1M9xQ4A8XONIAn05CNQ1s1thZYj7QD5oDL7LMgqCZggJDUMtZPkFrVxWgYaFyJcNqwI5dHDS7xzn-u1uu6isDw6J3DKBJtkENGQ45i5Idi-gA2i_Zpjbpyb1WPmbI?key=K4zgJUdsr-h6SIfcdynrB6oK" width="247"></strong></p>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<p><a name="chromeBrsrB136"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Malicious APK download checks (telemetry-only)&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Chrome on Android now contacts Google about Android Package Kit (APK) files downloaded in Chrome, to verify their safety. This is a telemetry-only experimental state of a feature that will eventually show warnings and block downloads of malicious APK files, to protect users against mobile malware. At this time, the malicious APK download check is telemetry-only: no warnings will be shown and downloads will not be blocked. In telemetry-only mode, the malicious APK download check will only be performed for users enrolled in Enhanced Protection from Google Safe Browsing.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>This feature can be disabled by setting the Safe Browsing mode to <em>NoProtection </em><em>(value 0)</em> via the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SafeBrowsingProtectionLevel" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SafeBrowsingProtectionLevel</u></a> policy.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 136 on Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<p><a name="chromeBrsrC136"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Proactive notifications for Chrome Tips on iOS&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Users can now receive <a href="https://www.google.com/intl/en_ie/chrome/tips/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome Tips</u></a> as provisional notifications. Previously, only users who have explicitly opted into Chrome Tips notifications would receive these helpful notifications.</p>

    <p>In this release, Chrome sends these proactively as notifications to users who have installed Chrome on iOS, but have been inactive for several days. In this way, users won't even have to open the app to learn about useful features such as Google Lens&nbsp;or Enhanced Safe browsing. Admins can turn these off by using the policy <strong>ProvisionalNotificationsAllowed </strong>(policy will be available in Chrome 137).</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 136 on iOS</strong></li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<p><a name="chromeBrsrD136"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Custom data directory required for remote debugging&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Remote debugging via a TCP port or a pipe is no longer possible in Google Chrome with the default data directory on Windows, Linux, and macOS. A custom data directory must be specified to remotely debug Google Chrome using the <code>--user-data-dir</code> switch, when using the <code>--remote-debugging-pipe</code> or <code>--remote-debugging-port</code> switches.</p>

    <p>We’ve made this change because these remote debugging switches are being abused by infostealers and malware to extract data from Google Chrome. A custom user data directory uses a different encryption key and so it prevents malware stealing encrypted data such as cookies.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>This change does not affect Chrome for Testing and Chromium.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 136 on Linux, macOS, Windows</strong></li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<p><a name="chromeBrsrE136"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Partitioning </strong><strong><em>:visited</em></strong><strong> links history&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>To eliminate user browsing history leaks, anchor elements are styled as <code>:visited</code> only if they have been clicked from this top-level site and frame origin before. On the browser-side, this means that the VisitedLinks hashtable is now partitioned by triple-keying, that is, by storing the following for each visited link: &lt;link URL, top-level site, frame origin&gt;. By only styling links that have been clicked on this site and frame before, the many side-channel attacks that have been developed to obtain <code>:visited</code> links styling information are now obsolete, as they no longer provide sites with new information about users.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>There is an exception for <em>self-links</em>, where links to a site's own pages can be styled as <code>:visited </code>even if they have not been clicked on in this exact top-level site and frame origin before. This exemption is only enabled in top-level frames or subframes which are same-origin with the top-level frame. The privacy benefits above are still achieved because sites already know which of its subpages a user has visited, so no new information is exposed. This was a community-requested exception which improves user experience as well.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 136 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<p><a name="chromeBrsrF136"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Rename attr() type </strong><strong><em>string</em></strong><strong> keyword to </strong><strong><em>raw-string</em>&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>The <code>attr() </code>type argument specifies how the attribute value is parsed into a CSS value. In a recent decision by the <a href="https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/11645#issuecomment-2701601350" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>W3C CSS Working Group</u></a>,&nbsp;it was resolved to rename the <code>attr()</code> type <code>string</code> keyword to the more explicit <code>raw-string</code>. If the attribute value is given as the <code>raw-string</code> keyword, or omitted entirely, it causes the attribute’s literal value to be treated as the value of a CSS string, with no CSS parsing performed at all (including CSS escapes, whitespace removal, comments, etc). No value triggers fallback; only the lack of the attribute entirely does.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>For more details about <a href="https://drafts.csswg.org/css-values-5/#funcdef-attr" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>attr()</u></a> notation, see <a href="https://drafts.csswg.org/css-values-5/#attr-notation" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>CSS Values and Units Module Level 5</u></a>.&nbsp;</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 136 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<p><a name="chromeBrsrG136"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Update ProgressEvent to use double type for </strong><strong><em>loaded</em></strong><strong> and </strong><strong><em>total</em></strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>The <code>ProgressEvent</code> has attributes <code>loaded</code> and <code>total</code> indicating the progress, and their type is <code>unsigned long long</code> now.</p>

    <p>With this feature, the type for these two attributes is changed to double instead, which gives the developer more control over the value. For example, the developers can now create a <code>ProgressEvent</code> with the <code>total</code> of 1 and the <code>loaded</code> increasing from 0 to 1 gradually. This is aligned with the default behavior of the <code>&lt;progress&gt;</code> HTML element if the max attribute is omitted. For more details, see this <a href="https://whatwg.org/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Web Hypertext Application Technology working group (WHATWG)</u></a> discussion on <a href="https://github.com/whatwg/xhr/pull/394" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>GitHub</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 136 on Windows, macOS, Linux</strong></li>
    </ul>
    &nbsp;</li>
</ul>

<h2>Chrome Enterprise Core changes</h2>

<p><a id="chromeECA136" name="chromeECA136"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>WebAuthn support for Remote Desktop Clients on managed devices&nbsp;</strong><a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This change allows users on managed devices to securely access websites on remote hosts using their local security keys or passkeys. With the new <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#WebAuthenticationRemoteDesktopAllowedOrigins" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>WebAuthenticationRemoteDesktopAllowedOrigins</u></a> enterprise policy, administrators will be able to specify which remote desktop client applications can make WebAuthn requests on behalf of other origins.</p>

    <p>This addresses the challenge of using local authenticators with remote desktops, thereby enhancing both security and user experience. Administrators configure this policy by providing a comma-separated list of allowed remote desktop client app origins.</p>

<h2>Coming soon</h2>

<p><strong>Note:</strong> The items listed below are experimental or planned updates. They might change, be delayed, or canceled before launching to the Stable channel.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

<div class="no-margin"><h4>Upcoming Chrome browser changes</h4>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrA136" name="upChromeBrsrA136"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Removal of Private Network Access enterprise policies</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Private Network Access (PNA 1.0) is an unshipped security feature designed to limit website access to local networks. Due to deployability concerns, PNA 1.0 was never able to ship by default, as it was incompatible with too many existing devices.</p>

    <p>PNA 1.0 required changes to devices on local networks. Instead, Chrome is implementing an updated proposal, Private Network Access 2.0 (PNA 2.0). PNA 2.0 (<a href="https://github.com/explainers-by-googlers/local-network-access" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Github</u></a>) only requires changes to sites that need to access the local network, rather than requiring changes to devices on the local network. Sites are much easier to update than devices, and so this approach should be much more straightforward to roll out.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>The only way to enforce PNA 1.0 is via enterprise policy. To avoid regressing security for enterprise customers opting-in to PNA 1.0 prior to shipping PNA 2.0, we will maintain the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PrivateNetworkAccessRestrictionsEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>PrivateNetworkAccessRestrictionsEnabled</u></a> policy, which causes Chrome to send special preflight messages, until such time that it becomes incompatible with PNA 2.0.</p>

    <p>The <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowedForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowedForUrls</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowed" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowed</u></a> policies, which loosen PNA 1.0 restrictions, will be removed immediately. These policies currently have no effect, since PNA 1.0 is not shipped, and they will have no meaning once PNA 1.0 is removed.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>Chrome 135 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: Removal of <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowedForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowedForUrls</u></a> and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowed" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>InsecurePrivateNetworkRequestsAllowed</u></a> policies.</li>
    </ul>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 137 on Android, ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows, Fuchsia: </strong>Removal of <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PrivateNetworkAccessRestrictionsEnabled" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>PrivateNetworkAccessRestrictionsEnabled</u></a>. This is dependent on a not-yet-defined replacement policy to enable PNA 2.0 being available.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrB136" name="upChromeBrsrB136"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Remove --load-extension command line switch</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>To enhance the security and stability of the Chrome browser for our users, official Chrome branded builds will begin to deprecate the ability to load extensions using the <code>--load-extension</code> command-line flag, starting in Chrome 137. This change aims to mitigate the risks associated with harmful and unwanted extensions.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>Unpacked extensions can be loaded with the <strong>Load unpacked</strong> button on the <strong>Extensions</strong> management page (<code>chrome://extensions/</code>) with <strong>Developer mode</strong> enabled.</p>

    <p>Developers can still use the <code>--load-extension</code> switch in non-branded builds such as Chromium and <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-for-testing" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>Chrome For Testing</u></a>.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 137 on ChromeOS, Linux, macOS, Windows</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrC136" name="upChromeBrsrC136"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Remove SwiftShader fallback</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>Allowing automatic fallback to <a href="https://get.webgl.org/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>WebGL</u></a> backed by <a href="https://github.com/google/swiftshader" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SwiftShader</u></a> is deprecated and WebGL context creation will fail instead of falling back to SwiftShader. This was done for two primary reasons:</p>

    <ol>
      <li>SwiftShader is a high security risk due to JIT-ed code running in Chromium's GPU process.</li>
      <li>Users have a poor experience when falling back from a high-performance GPU-backed WebGL to a CPU-backed implementation. Users have no control over this behavior and it is difficult to describe in bug reports.</li>
    </ol>

    <p>SwiftShader is a useful tool for web developers to test their sites on systems that are headless or do not have a supported GPU. This use case will still be supported by opting in but is not intended for running untrusted content. To opt in to lower security guarantees and allow SwiftShader for WebGL, run the chrome executable with the <code>--enable-unsafe-swiftshader</code> command-line switch.</p>

    <p>During the deprecation period, a warning will appear in the javascript console when a WebGL context is created and backed with SwiftShader. Passing <code>--enable-unsafe-swiftshader</code> will remove this warning message.</p>

    <p>Chromium and other browsers do not guarantee WebGL availability. It is important to test and handle WebGL context creation failure and fall back to other web APIs such as Canvas2D or an appropriate message to the user. A temporary enterprise policy will be available to revert the change.&nbsp;</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 137 on Linux, macOS: </strong>Swiftshader will be disabled on macOS and Linux as early as Chrome 137. Users on machines without a GPU will not be able to use WebGL.</li>
      <li><strong>Chrome 137 on Windows: </strong>SwiftShader will be disabled and replaced with another software WebGL fallback, WARP. Tests depending on the exact pixel values generated by SwiftShader may start failing.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrD136" name="upChromeBrsrD136"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Align error type thrown for </strong><strong>payment</strong><strong> WebAuthn credential creation: SecurityError =&gt; NotAllowedError</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This change corrects the error type thrown during WebAuthn credential creation for payment credentials. Due to a historic specification mismatch, creating a payment credential in a cross-origin iframe without a user activation would throw a <code>SecurityError</code> instead of a <code>NotAllowedError</code>, which is what is thrown for non-payment credentials. Code that previously detected the type of error thrown, for example, <code>e instanceof SecurityError</code>, would be affected. Code that just generally handles errors during credential creation, for example, <code>catch (e)</code>, will continue to function correctly.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 137 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrE136" name="upChromeBrsrE136"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Blob URL Partitioning: Fetching/Navigation</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>As a continuation of Storage Partitioning, Chromium will implement partitioning of Blob URL access by Storage Key (top-level site, frame origin, and the <code>has-cross-site-ancestor</code> boolean), with the exception of top-level navigations which will remain partitioned only by frame origin. This behavior is similar to what’s currently implemented by both Firefox and Safari, and aligns Blob URL usage with the partitioning scheme used by other storage APIs as part of Storage Partitioning. In addition, Chromium will enforce noopener on renderer-initiated top-level navigations to Blob URLs where the corresponding site is cross-site to the top-level site performing the navigation. This aligns Chromium with similar behavior in Safari, and the relevant specs have been updated to reflect these changes.&nbsp;</p>

    <p>This change can be temporarily reverted by setting the <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#PartitionedBlobUrlUsage" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>PartitionedBlobURLUsage</u></a> policy. The policy will be deprecated when the other storage partitioning related enterprise policies are deprecated.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 137 on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>&nbsp;<a id="upChromeBrsrF136" name="upChromeBrsrF136"></a>&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Web serial over Bluetooth on Android</strong>&nbsp;<a href="#top"><img src="//storage.googleapis.com/support-kms-prod/875e9907-0d60-4f4e-a960-862bc24a29f4" height="18" alt="back to top" data-mime-type="image/svg+xml"></a>

    <p>This feature allows web pages and web apps to connect to serial ports over Bluetooth on Android devices. Chrome on Android now supports Web Serial API over Bluetooth RFCOMM. Existing enterprise policies (<a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#DefaultSerialGuardSetting" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>DefaultSerialGuardSetting</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SerialAllowAllPortsForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SerialAllowAllPortsForUrls</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SerialAllowUsbDevicesForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SerialAllowUsbDevicesForUrls</u></a>, <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SerialAskForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SerialAskForUrls</u></a>, and <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SerialBlockedForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SerialBlockedForUrls</u></a>) on other platforms are enabled in future_on states for Android. All policies except <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SerialAllowUsbDevicesForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SerialAllowUsbDevicesForUrls</u></a> will be enabled after the feature is enabled. <a href="https://chromeenterprise.google/policies/#SerialAllowUsbDevicesForUrls" rel="noopener" target="_blank"><u>SerialAllowUsbDevicesForUrls</u></a> will be enabled in a future launch after Android provides system level support of wired serial ports.</p>

    <ul>
      <li><strong>Chrome 137 on Android</strong></li>
    </ul>
